- [x] 🟡 M — **Contract-flow RPCs fan out multi-industry-tag recipients (duplicate/double-counted rows)** — The two contract-flow RPCs (chord_contract_flows_full and treemap_recipients_by_contracts_full) and the FIX-838 rollup rebuild that mirrors them LEFT JOIN entity_tags on the recipient WITHOUT a DISTINCT-ON. A financial_entity carrying more than one industry tag (1058 local / 1654 prod) fans out: in the treemap it becomes N duplicate entity_id rows, each with the entity FULL total (top-500 shows 7 dup entity_ids / 493 distinct in both envs); in the chord a single award is counted into EVERY one of the recipient sectors, inflating per-sector totals and the agency cross-sector sum. FIX-838 deliberately PRESERVED this fan-out (byte-exact materialization swap) and tracked the semantics fix here. Fix: pick ONE deterministic tag per recipient via a DISTINCT-ON CTE (mirror the FIX-836 ind CTE / fetchIndustryTagsByEntityId smallest-tag pick) in both _full bodies AND refresh_contract_flow_rollups(), so an entity appears once with a single industry and each award lands in exactly one sector. Re-run the FIX-838 equality proofs against the corrected _full afterward (they will legitimately change). The recipient rollup can then revert to a plain entity_id PRIMARY KEY. Verify total_cents conservation: SUM over sectors = SUM over agencies = raw contract SUM. See [[FIX-838]] [[FIX-836]]. <!--id:FIX-873-->
- [x] 🟠 L — **Audit the remaining unbounded .in() id-list reads (silent-empty-result class)** — **Bug hunt, unknown yield — needs a per-site investigation gate, NOT a blanket rewrite.** Filed by [[FIX-901]], which shipped the shared helper this audit remediates onto. **Mechanism (always the same, always silent):** supabase-js encodes an `.in()` filter into the request URL. Past roughly **200 uuids** the URL exceeds Kong's header limit and the gateway returns 414 `URI too long` **before PostgREST ever sees the query**. `withDbTimeout` converts that into `{data: null}`, and the near-universal `?? []` / `data?.x` fallback at the call site turns a hard failure into an empty result on an HTTP 200. Nothing logs, nothing 500s, the page renders — just missing. **The bound is URL LENGTH at ~200 ids. It is NOT the 1,000-row PostgREST `max_rows` cap** — do not reason about this class in terms of row counts, and do not assume a list under 1,000 is safe. **Four independent prior instances**, each found by accident rather than by monitoring: [[FIX-509]] (treemap, 414 verified at ~356 uuids / ~13 KB), [[FIX-514]], [[FIX-774]] (established the 200 bound), [[FIX-899]] (officials directory rendered ZERO tag pills for every official for months; ~1,000 ids / ~40 KB; surfaced only because [[FIX-897]] added pills to that surface and they did not appear). **Census at HEAD e5056d8b** — 248 total `.in(` call sites across `apps/` + `packages/` (excluding node_modules and tests); of those, on the order of **96–108 pass an id-list VARIABLE and are not obviously chunked** (96 under the strict single-line regex below; ~108 under a looser hand-classification that also catches multi-line and spread forms). Recipes: total = `grep -rn '.in(' --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx apps packages | grep -v node_modules | grep -v '.test.ts' | wc -l`; candidates = the same grep narrowed to `.in("col", identifier)` with chunk/batch/slice/page-named variables filtered out. **Most are probably bounded in practice — classifying them is the whole job.** Per site, the question is a BOUND ASSESSMENT: what feeds this id list, and can it exceed ~200? Note `.in("status", [...])` over a small literal enum list is fine and common — those are not in scope. Sites where the list is a fixed-arity literal, a `.slice(0, N<=200)`, or provably capped upstream should be marked bounded and left alone (ideally with a one-line note recording the bound, so the next auditor does not re-derive it). Sites where an unbounded or growth-prone collection feeds the filter are real latent bugs: migrate onto `fetchChunkedByIds` from `apps/civitics/src/lib/paginate.ts` ([[FIX-901]]), which chunks at 200 and **surfaces failed chunks in its result object instead of swallowing them**. Prioritise request-path renders and API routes that feed user-visible surfaces — those are where a silent empty result reads as 'this entity has no data' rather than as an error. **Deliberately NOT bundled into [[FIX-901]]:** that was a small mechanical PR migrating three sites whose correct behaviour was already verified; this is open-ended investigation over ~100 sites and would have swallowed it. **Explicitly out of scope here:** a lint rule or codemod banning raw `.in()`. Tempting, but it would have to distinguish id lists from small enum lists, and that discrimination is a design question of its own. <!--id:FIX-902-->
- [x] 🔴 S — **get_financial_entity_naics 504s over PostgREST — the nightly financial industry tagger cannot complete** — Surfaced while running the [[FIX-908]] run-twice verification. tagFinancialEntities() in packages/data/src/pipelines/tags/rules.ts fetches its NAICS rollup with db.rpc('get_financial_entity_naics') over PostgREST. That call **504s after exactly 60.0s** on local — reproduced with zero application code in the path (raw fetch to /rest/v1/rpc/get_financial_entity_naics with the secret key: status=504, 'The upstream server is timing out'). The SAME function over a direct psql connection returns in **537ms warm** (104s cold, 1 row). callWithRetry THROWS after 5 attempts, so the phase burns ~310s (5 x 60s) and then kills the whole function before it ever reaches clear_financial_entity_rule_tags + the upserts. Net effect: **the financial-entity industry tags are never rebuilt** — runRuleBasedTagger catches the throw and calls failSync, so the nightly reports a failure but the existing entity_tags rows are simply left frozen at whatever the last successful run wrote. Fails CLOSED (no data loss — the DELETE is downstream of the throw, which is the FIX-443 ordering working as designed), but the tagger is dead. **This is the FIX-443/444/651 class, and the fix is the one already applied to this function's two SIBLING reads:** the keyword fetch was migrated to selectDirect by FIX-444 for this exact reason ('the PostgREST path could never complete'), and both official rollups were migrated to rollupJsonbDirect by FIX-651. The NAICS rollup is the one read in tagFinancialEntities still going over the capped PostgREST path. Migrate it to selectDirect/rollupJsonbDirect (direct pg.Client, session statement_timeout raised) and the 60s gateway ceiling stops applying. **Deliberately NOT bundled into [[FIX-908]]/[[FIX-909]]** — those are a vocabulary change and this is a transport bug that predates them; bundling would have made a taxonomy PR responsible for a pipeline migration. **Verify on prod before assuming local-only**: prod's service_role carries an 8s statement_timeout (tighter than local's 60s gateway), so if the function is slow there too this has been failing on prod as well — check data_sync_log for tag_rules rows with a get_financial_entity_naics error. Cross-ref [[FIX-443]] [[FIX-444]] [[FIX-651]]. <!--id:FIX-910-->

- [x] 🟠 S — **upsertLegislatorsBatch clobbers officials.metadata wholesale — BOTH OpenStates pipelines destroy district_jurisdiction_id, and the API one never re-links** — Surfaced while implementing [[FIX-913]], and it means the RPC change alone provably cannot make SLD linkage durable. packages/data/src/pipelines/openstates/writer.ts buildOfficialInsert sets metadata: input.metadata and the update path is .upsert(records, { onConflict: 'id' }), so every legislator upsert REPLACES officials.metadata rather than merging it — district_jurisdiction_id is destroyed on contact. Both OpenStates pipelines share this one writer. runBulkPeoplePipeline (daily, openstates-bulk/people.ts) at least calls link_officials_to_districts() afterwards and repairs the numeric tier. runOpenStatesPipeline (weekly Sunday block, pipelines/index.ts line ~775, gated only on OPENSTATES_API_KEY) calls the SAME writer at openstates/index.ts line ~348 and NEVER calls the linker — verified, no reference to it exists anywhere in that file. So the weekly API run lands AFTER the daily repair and undoes it with no repair of its own; a perfect [[FIX-913]] RPC still ends Sunday night with links wiped. Fix is structural: extend the existing chunked external_source_refs lookup pass in upsertLegislatorsBatch to also select id, metadata from officials for the ids it finds, and merge {...existing, ...input.metadata} on the update path (PostgREST cannot express a server-side jsonb merge; insert path unchanged). Belt-and-braces, also call link_officials_to_districts() at the end of runOpenStatesPipeline mirroring openstates-bulk/people.ts lines ~264-274, so newly-seen legislators link in the same run. Blast radius verified small: state legislators carry exactly four metadata keys across the whole population — org_classification (7373), state (7373), district_jurisdiction_id (7313), state_abbr (1); only district_jurisdiction_id is being destroyed, the others are re-supplied by the upsert. With this landed [[FIX-913]] becomes the safety net for genuinely new or genuinely changed districts rather than a nightly repair job. Follow-up worth considering separately: district_jurisdiction_id belongs in a real column, not metadata. Cross-ref [[FIX-859]], [[FIX-217]]. <!--id:FIX-915-->
- [x] 🔴 S — **An out-of-vocabulary `other` tag reaching an official's top-3 kills the ENTIRE nightly rule tagger — live on local, latent on prod** — **Filed, not fixed** — found while running the [[FIX-916]] verification, and it is a strictly sharper consequence of [[FIX-911]] than that bullet's 'display wart' framing. `tagOfficials()` reads official_sector_affinity_rollup, excludes ONLY `'Untagged'`, and then calls `assertIndustryVocabulary()`, which THROWS on any value outside VALID_INDUSTRIES. `other` is written into entity_tags by ai-classifier.ts ([[FIX-911]]), flows into the rollup like any other tag, and is NOT in VALID_INDUSTRIES — so the moment an `other`-tagged donor lands in an ACTIVE official's top-3 by dollars, the assert fires and takes down the **entire nightly rule tagger**: proposals, officials AND financial entities, all three phases, because runRuleBasedTagger() catches the throw at the top level and calls failSync. **This is not hypothetical — it is LIVE on local today.** Measured 2026-07-28: 6 active officials carried `other` at rank<=3 on the local prod-clone before [[FIX-916]] and 7 after, so `pnpm data:tag-rules` cannot complete on local at all, and the [[FIX-916]] run-twice proof had to invoke tagFinancialEntities() in isolation to get around it. **Prod is currently safe but only by margin, not by design**: all 8 prod `other` rollup rows sit at rank 11-13 of 13 carrying $1,000-$5,500 against rank-3 values of $83k-$745k. A read-only simulation of the post-[[FIX-916]] state confirmed prod stays safe (rank 10-17, tightest margin Dave Min at $2,000 vs a rank-3 of $31,000, ~15x) — but the local 6->7 shift proves the promotion mechanism is real, and ANY change that reduces an official's classified mass (a de-tagging, a donor merge, a cycle rolling off) can push `other` up. **The asymmetry is the bug:** `'Untagged'` is excluded at the read as 'not an industry', and `other` is exactly the same kind of thing — an abstention — yet it is allowed through to an assert that kills the pipeline. Two candidate fixes, not exclusive: (1) stop writing `other` at all ([[FIX-911]]'s suggested shape) and delete the existing rows, which removes the input; (2) exclude non-vocabulary values at the rollup read the same way `'Untagged'` is excluded, so an out-of-vocabulary tag degrades to 'no pill' instead of 'no nightly'. (2) is the durable one — it makes the pipeline robust to the NEXT out-of-vocabulary writer rather than just this one — but it must not silently swallow real drift, so pair it with a logged count. Note the assert itself is correct and worth keeping; what is wrong is that a display-layer vocabulary violation is fatal to an unrelated data pipeline. Cross-ref [[FIX-911]] [[FIX-897]] [[FIX-916]] [[FIX-908]] [[FIX-890]]. <!--id:FIX-920-->

- [x] 🔴 S — **matchRow accepts a single-element name pool with no first-name check** — packages/data/src/pipelines/fec-bulk/index.ts matchRow() step 2 (weball name fallback) narrows the last-name pool by CAND_OFFICE_ST and then returns `pool[0]` outright when `pool.length === 1` — **the first names are never compared on that branch**. First-name narrowing only runs in the `pool.length > 1` arm below it, so the state narrowing makes the bug WORSE rather than safer: it collapses an ambiguous same-surname pool to one and thereby removes the very ambiguity guard that would otherwise have forced a skip. Consequence is a wrong binding between a FEC CAND_ID and a real named person on a public page, not a missing one. **Live case on the prod clone:** Ohio has three officials surnamed Brown. Before the `cn{yy}` candidate-tier row for S6OH00163 existed, the OH Brown pool was effectively just the sitting House member, so Sherrod Brown's SENATE CAND_ID bound to **Shontel M. Brown** (D-OH-11, source_ids congress_gov B001313). Her page carries 43,960 donation rows / 38,964 distinct donors / $50,998,289 spanning 2018-10-17..2026-03-31, against $2.26M on her own committee H2OH11169; her rendered top donors include NRSC ($52,800, cycle 2024) and OHIO SENATE VICTORY 2024 ($49,000). Because the writer upserts on financial_relationships_relcycle_unique (relationship_type, from_id, to_id, cycle_year), a later corrected binding writes a NEW row and never retires the old one — so every historical mis-binding is still resident. Fix is a first-name agreement gate on EVERY name-fallback match including single-element pools, mirroring the `normalizedLast|first3|state` key the sibling fallback loop at ~line 960 already uses correctly (do not modify that loop). A missed match is strictly better than a wrong match: an unbound official renders $0 plus a sync note; a mis-bound one renders another person's donors under their name. Enumeration of the residue is [[FIX-930]]; cleanup is a separate PR. <!--id:FIX-929-->

- [x] 🔴 M — **Merge SAME-PERSON duplicate officials — 47 pairs, $219.5M of double-counted FEC donations retired** — PR 2a of the [[FIX-930]] remediation. **LOCAL APPLIED 2026-07-30; PROD PENDING — leave open.** Implemented by `packages/data/src/scripts/merge-same-person-official-dupes.ts` (`pnpm --filter @civitics/data data:merge:official-dupes`, dry-run by default, `--apply` to commit, `--allow-prod` required for prod). Mechanism: `matchRow` binds a FEC CAND_ID to an official in memory and the writer upserts on `financial_relationships_relcycle_unique (relationship_type, from_id, to_id, cycle_year)`, so a CHANGED `to_id` writes a NEW row and never retires the old one — when the `cn{yy}` stage minted a candidate-tier row for a sitting member, that member's FEC money SPLIT across two officials rows and has been double-counted since. [[FIX-929]] stopped new bad bindings; this closes the residue for the one branch where remediation is mechanical (both rows hold the SAME human's money, and the survivor is decidable from role rather than from a name comparison). **The ELECTED row always survives** — votes, committee memberships, bioguide id, career history, promises, comments and every inbound user-facing link hang off it; the candidate row is the one the FEC pipeline minted. Note this is the OPPOSITE direction from `promote_candidate_to_elected()`, which rewrites elected→candidate because its job is a genuine promotion; reusing that RPC here would have moved a sitting Senator's whole record onto a stub literally named `T Ossoff`. Order is load-bearing: `fec_candidate_id` is merged onto the survivor FIRST (the `persistNewFecIds` server-side jsonb-merge shape, writer.ts:953), because moving the money while leaving the survivor unbound would let the next Sunday run re-mint the candidate row and re-split. Collisions resolve to the FRESHER row by `updated_at`, never summed — the two rows are the same FEC data under two bindings. **No officials row is deleted**: the duplicate ends up holding zero `financial_relationships` rows, which keeps the change reversible and every FK intact, and keeps this out of the officials-dedup design question. Manifest is RE-DERIVED live from the shared [[FIX-930]] classifier (extracted to `packages/data/src/scripts/fec-orphan-classify.ts` so the audit and the remediation can never diverge) and every pair is re-gated STRUCTURALLY server-side before any write; the 3 name-decided state-mismatch merge-blockers are excluded and go to [[FIX-934]]. Local measured: 47 pairs, 127,289 colliding losers deleted, 133,637 FR rows moved (donation + `ie_support` + `ie_oppose` — the IE money was split across these pairs too), platform donation dollars on officials $5,023,195,233 → $4,803,650,534, drop $219,544,699 = deleted-loser sum EXACTLY, zero `official_donor_totals` diffs outside the manifest. Reference case Jon Ossoff $14,585,287 + $14,627,225 → $15,633,810 (union taking the fresher side on each of 15,779 colliding pairs — a $29.2M result would have meant summing). Rebuilt in-transaction: `donor_rollup_rebuild_recipients` (official_donor_totals, official_donor_rollup_mv, official_small_dollar_rollup, official_sector_affinity_rollup, treemap_individuals_rollup, official_donor_bracket_totals), `rebuild_official_donation_totals`, `financial_entity_donation_totals_rebuild` + `donor_party_rollup_rebuild_donors` over the 105,732 affected donors (their incremental pg_cron paths key off `financial_relationships.updated_at` and a DELETE bumps nothing, so relying on them would silently skip any donor whose only change was a deletion), and 6 money-reading MVs; post-commit `rebuild_financial_entity_ie_totals`, `refresh_group_donor_rollup`, `rebuild_entity_search_index`, `refresh_treemap_individuals_global`. `entity_connections` money edges pointing at a duplicate are deleted (provably false once that row holds no money) and the twice-weekly rebuild repopulates the survivor; `entity_connection_stats(_mv)` and `browse_facet_counts` stay stale until their own pg_cron. Cross-ref [[FIX-930]], [[FIX-929]], [[FIX-934]], [[FIX-935]], [[FIX-936]], [[FIX-937]], [[FIX-938]], [[FIX-761]], [[FIX-544]]. <!--id:FIX-933-->
- [x] 🔴 M — **PR 2b — CROSS-PERSON MISATTRIBUTION branch: 60 officials render another person's donors ($113.2M)** — **File only — not implemented by [[FIX-933]].** The severe branch of the [[FIX-930]] audit: 60 officials holding **$113,233,132** of FEC donation money where BOTH same-person signals fail — the twin's first name disagrees AND the twin's CAND_ID does not describe the chamber+state this official actually holds. These are not double-counted copies of the official's own money; they are **someone else's donors rendered under this official's name**, so the remediation is the opposite of [[FIX-933]]'s: DELETE the mis-bound rows rather than merge them. Because deletion is destructive and name-only evidence is exactly what the [[FIX-930]] investigation proved unreliable (FEC files legal names — Ted/Rafael Cruz, Jack/John Reed — so a first-name disagreement is NOT proof of a different person), **this branch needs a reviewed, row-level manifest before anything is deleted**, not a heuristic sweep. Worst live cases from the clone: Shontel M. Prefer resolving Senators by bioguide (`source_ids->>'congress_gov'`) where the Senate XML permits it, so the name key is a fallback rather than the primary. **Do NOT simply move the existing 1,755 votes to the elected rows without fixing the map** — the next nightly would re-insert them onto the candidate row and re-split, since `votes` is unique on `(roll_call_id, official_id)`. [[FIX-933]] deliberately left these votes in place for exactly that reason. Same last-write-wins map-collision class as [[FIX-941]]. Note `official_vote_stats` is materialized off `votes`, so bipartisan/attendance figures for the affected Senators are understated too. Measured pre-[[FIX-933]] on the local prod-clone: Jon Ossoff's column read **$11,555,275** against a live rollup of **$14,585,287**, and his candidate row read **$0** against **$14,627,225** — i.e. the column was already ~21% low on a sitting Senator before any merge. **Read sites that render it directly:** `/api/graph/treemap` (route.ts ~400-513 — selects it per official and builds `totalByOfficial`, which sizes the treemap's cells) and `/api/graph/small-dollar` (route.ts ~87-120 — `totalReceivedCents` is the DENOMINATOR of the small-dollar share, so a low column inflates the reported small-dollar percentage). Durable fix: give the column a scheduled owner, shaped like the [[FIX-702]]/[[FIX-726]] incremental jobs rather than a full-table UPDATE — note `rebuild_official_donation_totals()` is a bare full-table `UPDATE … FROM (SELECT … GROUP BY to_id)`, so it is both expensive on Pro Small AND unable to zero an official whose last donation row was deleted (no aggregate row → no UPDATE → stale non-zero forever; [[FIX-933]] has to zero its duplicates explicitly for exactly this reason). Either fold it into the existing `donor-rollup-refresh` daily job (which already recomputes `official_donor_totals` per dirty recipient and is the natural place), or drop the column and read `official_donor_totals.total_cents` at the call sites — the rollup is already materialized, per-official, and correctly maintained. Prefer the latter: a denormalized copy of a materialized aggregate is a second source of truth with no benefit. - [x] 🟠 M — **Eight incremental rollups key their watermark off updated_at columns stamped by NOW() in a BEFORE trigger — rows written by a transaction that starts before and commits after a watermark read are excluded permanently** — **Found by the 2026-08-07 site-wide efficiency audit (`docs/audits/2026-08-07-efficiency-audit.md`), class 5 — lying timestamps (population 153 routines).** Unlike the rest of class 5 this is a **correctness** defect, not an observability one: it silently drops rows from incremental rollups. **The mechanism.** `financial_relationships.updated_at` and `votes.updated_at` are stamped by a `BEFORE` trigger (`financial_relationships_updated_at` → `public.set_updated_at()`) using `NOW()`, which is `transaction_timestamp()` — **the moment the writing transaction BEGAN**, not the moment it committed. An incremental rollup then reads `WHERE updated_at > last_watermark` and advances the watermark to the read time. Any transaction that **began before** the watermark read but **committed after** it stamps its rows with a timestamp *below* the new watermark while being invisible at read time — so those rows are never picked up by that run, and never by any later run either, because the watermark has already moved past them. **The loss is permanent and silent.** **Eight watermark read sites, enumerated from live bodies:** `donor_rollup_rebuild_bulk:101,127`; `rebuild_entity_connections_donations:26,28`; `rebuild_entity_connections_votes:23,27`; `refresh_donor_party_rollup_incremental:54,64`; `refresh_donor_party_rollup_mv:16,25`; plus `refresh_financial_entity_totals_incremental`. **Exposure window = the duration of the longest concurrent writing transaction on that table.** That is not small here: the FEC bulk pipeline's `INSERT INTO financial_relationships` measured `calls=1549, mean_exec_time=29,436 ms` on prod `pg_stat_statements` — a **~29-second mean per statement**, inside longer transactions — and the [[FIX-933]] money move ran ~12 minutes atomic. So a rollup firing during an FEC load can miss any row whose transaction spans the read. **Why it has not obviously bitten yet:** most of these rollups are also re-derived by periodic full passes, which paper over the gap — which is exactly the [[FIX-968]] shape where a frozen rollup makes deltas look clean while the absolute is wrong (playbook **E1**). **Fix shape:** the standard remedies, cheapest first — (a) subtract a safety lag from the watermark (`watermark - interval '1 hour'`), trading a little re-work for correctness, which is the smallest change and fits every one of the 8 sites; (b) stamp `updated_at` with `clock_timestamp()` so the value at least reflects statement time rather than transaction start — necessary but **not sufficient**, since the commit still lands later; (c) the rigorous fix is to advance the watermark to `min(backend_xmin)`-safe territory rather than to wall-clock, i.e. key the incremental read off a transaction-id horizon rather than a timestamp. **Verify before choosing:** confirm against a known-count run whether rows are actually being dropped today (playbook E2 — validate the sizing metric against a run whose true count is independently known), because the safety-lag fix costs re-work on every run and should be justified by a measurement rather than by the argument alone. Cross-ref [[FIX-972]], [[FIX-933]], [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-974]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-702]], [[FIX-726]]. <!--id:FIX-983-->

Real, permanent, silent, and small. (The 5 `super_pac` rows that do carry spend take the `ie>0` precedence branch and are unaffected.) **Fix shape:** (a) an arm must not DELETE what it cannot rebuild — either assert its source is non-empty before deleting, or scope the DELETE to the rows it actually owns (this is the [[FIX-808]]/[[FIX-692]] co-ownership rule applied to the EC arms); (b) fix the `'organization'` literal to `'other'`/`'nonprofit'` or drop the second arm, and add a **write-boundary vocab guard** the way [[FIX-889]]/[[FIX-891]] did for tag categories, so a predicate can never again name a value outside its own CHECK constraint — that guard is the mechanism-level fix and would have caught both this and FIX-073; (c) consider whether the six empty enum labels should be removed from the type or backfilled, since every predicate referencing them is dead code today. On the pg_cron path there is no such session setting, and per the FIX-1056 finding a SET statement_timeout inside a CALLed procedure is DECORATIVE — statement_timeout is armed at CALL start and a nested function cannot re-arm it. So the scheduled firing is effectively UNBOUNDED: instead of failing at 40 minutes it runs until something else breaks. FIX-965 has been reasoning about a budget the scheduled job does not have. RESOLUTION APPLIED: pg_cancel_backend on the treemap pid (ran 1h47m54s) restored the catalog query from a 60s timeout to 28ms immediately; refresh_financial_entity_totals_incremental was also cancelled at 1h31m58s; PostgREST did not self-recover so the project was restarted via the Management API and REST returned 200 in 0.12-0.25s. - [x] 🟡 M — **Prod statement_timeout audit + costed compute-tier upgrade memo** — Structural root of the whole timeout class. Audited prod 2026-06-14 (read-only psql, pg_roles.rolconfig): anon=3s, authenticated=8s, authenticator=8s(+lock 8s), service_role=none→inherits authenticator 8s, postgres-via-pooler=2min; shared_buffers=256MB, effective_cache_size=768MB, work_mem=3.4MB, max_connections=60. A role-level bump is UNSAFE (raising authenticator/service_role also raises request-path API routes using the admin client → slow queries hold buffers longer, worsening cache starvation — the [[FIX-505]] hazard) and wouldn't help the 100s-gateway class anyway. Direct-pg ([[FIX-586]]/[[FIX-587]]) is the durable per-pipeline fix. Remaining deliverable: a short costed memo — current Pro Small (256MB shared_buffers vs ~12.5GB top-3 working set, 2% buffer-hit on seq scans, see docs/audits/2026-05-24-iowait-diagnosis.md) → next compute tiers, shared_buffers/RAM each gives, expected effect on the timeout class, monthly $ delta. The only fix that addresses the cause vs routing around it. Cost decision is Craig's. <!--id:FIX-589-->

- [x] 🟠 S — **Hot-path tables accumulate dead tuples below their autovacuum trigger — six untuned tables at 42.7–85.4% all-visible** — **Found while preparing the [[FIX-933]] prod run.** **⚠️ CORRECTED 2026-08-01 — the original bullet's central number was wrong; see below.** Originally filed as "`financial_relationships` carries 411,555 dead tuples against a **1,663,805** threshold, so autovacuum mathematically never fires". **That arithmetic used the CLUSTER default scale factor (0.2), but `financial_relationships` already carries a per-table override of 0.05** (verified on prod AND local, 2026-08-01 — alongside `entity_connections`, `entity_tags`, `enrichment_queue`, presumably from the FIX-331/[[FIX-884]] work). Its real trigger is `50 + 0.05 × 8,208,155` = **410,458**, so the 411,555 dead tuples measured on 07-30 were ~1,100 PAST the line, not 1.25M short of it — and prod confirms autovacuum did fire (`last_autovacuum` 2026-07-30 05:28, `autovacuum_count` 7). The table was never in a "never fires" state. **The real defect is the one the wrong number pointed at anyway, and it is a CLASS, not this table:** the trigger is a *floor of tolerated bloat*, and a heap page loses its all-visible mark if ANY tuple on it is dead — these tables carry 4.6–60 tuples per page, so a few-percent dead ratio un-marks most of the heap and every index-only scan degrades to a per-row heap fetch. Sorting every large prod table by visibility map settles it: **`donor_party_rollup_mv` 42.7%, `votes` 61.1%, `external_source_refs` 63.8%, `external_relationships_review_queue` 65.0%, `financial_entities` 77.3%, `proposals` 85.4%, `external_relationships` 97.3% — every one untuned — against `financial_relationships`, `entity_connections`, `entity_tags` and `enrichment_queue` all at 100.0%, every one tuned.** The correlation is total: the tuning works and was simply never extended past the tables [[FIX-884]] happened to touch. Two tables are textbook near-misses sitting *just* under their line (`donor_party_rollup_mv` 261,534 dead vs 262,622; `proposals` 16,145 vs 17,323) and two have **never been autovacuumed in their lives** (`votes` and `external_source_refs`, `autovacuum_count` = 0 — autoANALYZE runs because its trigger is 0.1, half the vacuum trigger, so they cross the analyze line forever and the vacuum line never). The one that matters most is **`financial_entities`**: 13.12% dead, 77.3% all-visible, no custom setting at all, 2.9M rows across 19 indexes — and it is the large table in the donor-rollup join path that dominates that job's runtime today (`financial_entities_pkey`, 11,780 ms of arm 1b). **This is NOT [[FIX-884]]**, which was `entity_connections` stranded at `autovacuum_enabled=false` by the rebuild (an explicitly-disabled flag, since fixed); here autovacuum is enabled and simply never fires. Same *consequence* as FIX-884 though — a stale visibility map kills index-only scans, which is how FIX-884's 0.9% all-visible turned a clean plan into 34,534 heap fetches. Measured impact on the local prod-clone: the [[FIX-930]] audit's suspect query went from completing in ~8 min to **blowing its 600s `statement_timeout`** purely from ~260k additional dead tuples left by the [[FIX-933]] merge, and completed again after a VACUUM. So this already degrades a read path today at 411k, before any migration adds to it. Fix (shipped, `20260801000000_fix943_autovacuum_hot_path_tables.sql`): extend the per-table scale factors to the hot-path class, **sized per table from its measured write pattern and index footprint rather than a blanket value** — `financial_relationships` 0.05→0.02 (410,458→**164,213**), `financial_entities` →0.05 (582,987→**145,784**), `votes` →0.05 (193,681→**48,458**), `donor_party_rollup_mv` →0.02 (262,622→**26,307**), `external_source_refs` →0.05 (114,191→**28,585**), `proposals` →0.05 (17,323→**4,368**). Note the original bullet's `autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 50000` suggestion is a **no-op for this purpose** — the formula is `threshold + scale_factor × reltuples`, i.e. additive, so the threshold only raises the trigger and only matters on small tables; lowering the *scale factor* is the only lever on a large one. `entity_connections` is deliberately **left at 0.05** (not 1.07M — it too is already tuned, real trigger 259,648): 2,919 MB heap / 3,544 MB across 10 indexes means every extra pass is real standing I/O on an already-I/O-bound Small instance, and it has both the monthly `ec-vacuum-analyze` backstop and the [[FIX-885]] startup reconcile. Five self-maintaining rollups (`entity_connection_stats_mv`, `entity_search_index`, `group_donor_rollup`, `official_donor_rollup_mv`, `treemap_individuals_rollup`) are untuned yet all at 100.0% all-visible — their rebuilds delete millions of rows and clear even the 0.2 trigger every run — so they are left alone, as is pipeline-only `external_relationships_review_queue`. Note Pro Small has limited I/O and a VACUUM on this table took **>17 min on local Docker**, so tune the thresholds rather than scheduling blanket full-table VACUUMs, and prefer off-peak (cf. the no-heavy-prod-ops-during-active-hours rule). [[FIX-933]]'s script ends with an explicit `VACUUM (ANALYZE)` on `financial_relationships`/`entity_connections`/`officials` — filed here as "a workaround local to one script, not the fix", and that framing was **too modest**: autovacuum tuning narrows the window but cannot close it (a bulk rewrite lands its whole dead-tuple load inside the remaining floor at once), and that vacuum running on 07-31 02:35 is the *only* reason [[FIX-944]]'s four-day backlog cleared. So it is now a **standing convention, not a workaround** — "any script that bulk-rewrites a table ends by vacuuming what it rewrote", landed in root `CLAUDE.md` (Data-state changes) with the reference table and sizing rules in `packages/db/CLAUDE.md`. **[[FIX-934]] is the next bulk `financial_relationships` rewrite and must carry a vacuum tail regardless of these settings.** Also shipped: `check_rebuild_autovacuum_status()` ([[FIX-650]]/[[FIX-885]]) now watches the whole tuned class instead of only `entity_connections` — which is how `donor_party_rollup_mv` sat at 42.7%, *below the canary's own 50% escalation floor*, completely unseen — and gains `bloat`/`bloat_degraded` keys reporting dead tuples against each table's computed trigger. `bloat_degraded` is **report-only by design**: a table can sit under its trigger harmlessly, so `vm_degraded` remains the escalating signal and this exists to make the cause greppable before the consequence arrives. Cross-ref [[FIX-884]], [[FIX-650]], [[FIX-885]], [[FIX-590]], [[FIX-933]], [[FIX-934]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-702]], [[FIX-726]]. <!--id:FIX-943-->

So any drift renders as wrong money on two graph surfaces and as a wrong percentage on the third. **The structural hazard is in the refresh function, not the value:** `rebuild_official_donation_totals()` — the variant the FEC pipeline calls after each wave — is `UPDATE officials … FROM (SELECT … GROUP BY to_id) agg WHERE o.id = agg.official_id`, i.e. it only touches officials that still HAVE donation rows. An official whose `financial_relationships` rows were all deleted (exactly what [[FIX-933]]'s merge does to the neutralised duplicate) keeps its last non-zero value forever; only `rebuild_official_donation_totals_full()`, which zeroes first, can clear it, and nothing on the schedule calls `_full()`. **Measured on the local prod-clone 2026-07-31 (post-FIX-933): ZERO drift** — all 4,321 officials in `official_donor_totals` match the column exactly (Ossoff $15,633,810 both sides), and ZERO officials carry a non-zero column value with no surviving donation rows. The prompt that surfaced this reported Ossoff at $11,555,275 in the column against $15,633,810 in the rollup; that gap is not present locally, so **re-derive on prod first** — if prod also measures clean, the bullet collapses to the design question alone. That design question is the durable part and is worth answering either way: now that `official_donor_totals` exists, is refreshed daily and is authoritative, the column is a second source of truth for the same quantity with a refresh function that structurally cannot converge. Options: (a) point the two graph routes at `official_donor_totals` and leave the column as a legacy no-read; (b) swap the pipeline's post-wave call from the incremental to `_full()` so it can converge; (c) drop the column and its `officials_total_received_cents` index. Note (c) also touches `20260715000000_fix776_materialize_official_small_dollar_rollup.sql`, which references it. Cross-ref [[FIX-933]], [[FIX-836]], [[FIX-702]], [[FIX-776]], [[FIX-940]]. <!--id:FIX-947-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **Donor-rollup throughput numbers in FIX-944's migration comment and the sweep script are a measurement artifact (2.5x undercount)** — **Found while running the [[FIX-944]] per-arm regression diagnosis (2026-08-01).** The "~1,000 recipients per 6h window" figure that FIX-944's migration comment and `packages/data/src/scripts/donor-rollup-sweep.ts` both state as measured fact is a **measurement artifact**, and it is the number a future session would use to justify a 50-hour break-glass sweep that is not needed. The proxy was "count DISTINCT official_id in `official_small_dollar_rollup` / `official_donor_totals` with `updated_at` inside the run window". Both tables hold **4,336 rows total**, because only recipients that actually have donation rows get one — so the proxy can never report more than 4,336 no matter how many recipients a run processes, and it undercounts every partial run by the same unknown factor. Falsified against a run whose true count is known: the 2026-07-31 09:00 run (`cron.job_run_details` runid 135) processed **8,381 recipients in 42 chunks, status `complete`** — and the same proxy reports **3,339**, a 2.5x undercount on a fully successful run. The downstream claims are therefore all wrong: "a 6h window completes ~1,000", "8,382 needs ~50h of compute", "about 9 nightly runs". Corrected numbers, measured: 07-22 = 1,992 recipients / 10 chunks / 1h54m = **685 s/chunk**; 07-31 = 8,381 recipients / 42 chunks / 3h08m = **269 s/chunk**, i.e. the job is now **2.5x faster per chunk than the 07-22 baseline**, not 6-8x slower, and it clears the whole dirty set in **one 6h window with 2h52m to spare**. Two artifacts carry the bad numbers: `supabase/migrations/20260731000000_fix944_resumable_donor_rollup.sql` (the "Why it can never converge" and "Convergence" comment blocks) — **frozen, it is an applied migration and must not be edited** — and the sweep script's header comment, which is editable and should be corrected. Also worth correcting the procedure's `COMMENT ON` text in a future migration if one touches it anyway. **Lesson worth keeping**: when a proxy metric is used to size a multi-hour remediation, validate it against a run whose true count is independently known before quoting it as measured — a rollup table's row count is a ceiling on any "rows touched" proxy built from it. Consequence worth stating plainly: **a split schedule provides NO isolation once a run overruns** — 09:00 and 12:00 chain into one continuous block rather than acting as two bounded windows — so **a per-run budget must sit BELOW the gap between firings**, or the second firing simply inherits the first's overrun. Full write-up: docs/audits/2026-08-07-fix974-bulk-regime.md. **The per-recipient regime is the wrong shape for a backlog, and this is the measurement that proves it.** [[FIX-973]] measured refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental() at 19.0 s/recipient on 08-06 (~33 ms per FR row, about one random page per row); the 9,086 recipients then outstanding needed ~48 h of pure compute, naive ETA ~Aug 12, with Sunday fec_bulk due to refill the dirty set first. **New procedure donor_rollup_rebuild_bulk()** (migration 20260807000000) generalises the [[FIX-965]] resumable-global-rebuild pattern to the whole six-arm family: to_id RANGE chunks (default 32, GUC civitics.donor_rollup_bulk_chunks) instead of scattered to_id = ANY(uuid[]) probes, and ONE scan per chunk landing in UNLOGGED staging from which ALL SIX arms are derived, instead of six arms each re-scanning FR for the same recipients through a 256 MB shared_buffers. Mode via civitics.donor_rollup_bulk_mode (dirty default, full), budget via civitics.donor_rollup_bulk_budget_seconds; cursor advances inside each chunk transaction, predictive between-chunk budget is the only clean stop (status=partial, resumable), a chunk failure ABORTS rather than skipping, and it takes the SAME advisory lock as the incremental. **⚠ CLARIFIED 2026-08-09 — the original wording said a 09:00/12:00 firing "defers behind it", which names the wrong outcome.** Both procedures acquire the lock with `pg_try_advisory_lock` (NON-blocking), so a scheduled firing that finds the lock held by a bulk run does NOT wait: it INSERTs a `data_sync_log` row with `status='skipped'` and `skip_reason='advisory lock held by a concurrent donor-rollup refresh'`, then RETURNs. **That firing's work is LOST until the NEXT scheduled firing — it is not delayed into this one.** Three distinct behaviours are being described with one word across this family, and that conflation has now produced two falsified bullets ([[FIX-968]], and this one), so name the one you mean: **(a) QUEUED** — same jobid, a firing due while the previous one still runs: pg_cron keeps ONE task per jobid and runs them back-to-back, `cron.job_run_details.start_time` landing ~1.0s after the prior `end_time`, NO `skipped` row written and nothing at all visible in `data_sync_log` ([[FIX-968]], [[FIX-1002]]); **(b) SKIPPED** — a DIFFERENT session holds the advisory lock (the `data:donor-rollup:bulk` driver, or any manual sweep): `pg_try_advisory_lock` returns false, a `status='skipped'` row IS written, and that firing is forfeited; **(c) "defers"** — used in this repo for both (a) and (b), and precise about neither. Do not use it. **This bullet's case is (b), not (a).** The same conflation is frozen into the header comment of migration `20260807000000_fix974_donor_rollup_bulk_regime.sql` (~line 88: "defers behind it exactly as the two firings already chain behind each other"), which states the equivalence between (a) and (b) outright and cites the [[FIX-972]] chaining premise that [[FIX-1002]] later falsified; the live `COMMENT ON PROCEDURE` text is clean (it claims only that the lock is shared). Migrations are applied and therefore frozen, so this bullet is the correction of record. Driver packages/data/src/scripts/donor-rollup-bulk.ts (data:donor-rollup:bulk / :prod) lifts statement_timeout, re-CALLs while partial, and VACUUM (ANALYZE)s all six rewritten arms ([[FIX-943]] rule; VACUUM cannot run inside a procedure). **The unlock is an equivalence, measured not assumed:** arms 2-6 filter fr.to_type = official, and to_type is NOT in financial_relationships_donor_rollup_idx, so every such row would need a heap visit — but across all 6,457,535 rows in that index scope there are ZERO rows with to_type=official lacking an officials row and ZERO rows with another to_type whose to_id IS an official. Resolving official-ness through the target table instead of the heap column keeps the whole scan INDEX-ONLY (FR was 94.1% all-visible). Prod EXPLAIN of chunk 0: Index Only Scan, 184,067 rows to 150,437 groups in 21.8 s = **0.118 ms/FR row vs FIX-973 33.0 ms/row**. **Result: all 15,316 recipients (6,947 officials) in 926 s, one CALL, 32/32 chunks, slowest chunk 59 s, 1,006,285 arm-1 rows, 13 s vacuum tail — 0.060 s/recipient vs 19.0, about 314x.** The backlog was cleared as a superset (a full pass, not just the 9,086 owed) and the dirty set the next firing will build is 0. **Correctness is equality, not deltas:** locally the bulk output is BYTE-IDENTICAL to the live per-recipient path over the same 827 recipients — row-wise set difference both directions, 0/0 on every arm including the 50,733-row arm 1 — and identical again after a forced-budget park at chunk 0 plus resume. On prod: named-three published==live to the cent (Mike Johnson had been understating by $524,106, Emmer by $1,349,979), a 60-official sample from the reconstructed pre-run backlog with 0 mismatches on all six arms (arm 5 row-identical over 10,216 rows), all five platform-level sums exactly equal to a live FR aggregation, and financial_relationships itself byte-identical before/after (10,280,280 rows / 377,497,303,748,122 cents / same max updated_at) so nothing here touched attribution. GLOBAL treemap scope preserved at 3,034 rows. **Deliberate deviation from FIX-965: no whole-table publish swap.** FIX-965 needs one because its chunks are keyed by donor while its output is partitioned by state; here the chunk key IS the output partition key (every arm is keyed by official_id/scope_id = to_id), so a chunk output is final and there is no cross-chunk merge to protect. Writing straight into the live arms per chunk halves the write volume and the dead-tuple load on a box whose measured problem is I/O, and one chunk is one transaction so an official is either wholly old or wholly new consistently ACROSS all six arms. **dirty vs full was measured, not assumed:** locally full 13,139 targets 86 s vs dirty 4,885 targets 88 s — dirty is marginally SLOWER because the range walk dominates and the semi-join removes none of it. Chose full. **One latent divergence found and guarded** (migration 20260807010000): arm 2 official_donor_totals is the only arm whose live body has NO from_type predicate, so it is defined more broadly than the rollup index can see. Measured empty on prod (all 4,098,213 donation-to-official rows are from_type=financial_entity, single group), which is why byte-identity passed — but donor_rollup_bulk_assert_invariants() now asserts it BEFORE any arm is written, so a future violation fails loud instead of silently understating that official. **This is the bulk half of [[FIX-969]] regime split**; auto-selecting bulk vs trickle by dirty-set size is still 969 PR. Does NOT close [[FIX-973]] — it routes around the regression rather than explaining it, and the per-recipient path is still what the daily trickle uses; see the dated measurement line added to that bullet. [[FIX-970]] untouched (arm 1 deliberately still not scoped to officials, matching the live body). - [x] 🔴 M — **financial_entities has no VACUUM owner anywhere on the schedule — 53.7% all-visible and falling ~2,800 pages/min, 3.7 points from the canary's escalation floor** — **Found by the 2026-08-07 site-wide efficiency audit (`docs/audits/2026-08-07-efficiency-audit.md`), class 2 — heap-forced read shapes.** [[FIX-943]] landed the standing convention *"any script that bulk-rewrites a table ends by vacuuming what it rewrote"* and named `financial_entities` as **"the one that matters most"**. Nobody was ever assigned to it, and the table has degraded ever since. **Enumerated by mechanism, not by site:** every `public` table over 200 MB (18 tables) joined against `pg_class.relallvisible/relpages`, `pg_stat_user_tables.vacuum_count` and `pg_stat_user_indexes`. Sorting by *whether any script, cron job or procedure ever issues a manual `VACUUM`* separates them completely — `entity_connections` (vacuum_count 6) **98.4%** all-visible, `financial_relationships` (5) **96.8%**, `official_donor_rollup_mv` (1) 100%, `treemap_individuals_rollup` (1) 100%; and with **vacuum_count = 0**: `financial_entities` **53.7%**, `donor_party_rollup_mv` **74.9%**, `external_relationships_review_queue` **65.0%**. `entity_tags` is the one clean exception (97.1% at vacuum_count 0) because it is DELETE-dominated — 14,785,744 deletes clear its trigger constantly (61 autovacuums) — and that exception is what makes the rest a mechanism rather than a coincidence. **The degradation is live and fast.** Two readings the same session, `relpages` **unchanged** at 208,903: relallvisible **145,898 → 112,162** (69.8% → 53.7%) in ~13 minutes, i.e. **33,736 heap pages lost their all-visible mark**, ~2,800 pages/min, while `n_dead_tup` went 140,224 → 164,110. FIX-943 measured this table at **77.3% on 2026-08-01**; it is 53.7% six days later, *after* being tuned. **Why the FIX-943 tuning cannot hold it:** FE is UPDATE-dominated — `n_tup_upd` **3,410,204** vs `n_tup_ins` 739,201 — and its trigger is `50 + 0.05 × 3,630,602` = **181,580** against 164,110 dead, i.e. *under* the line, so autovacuum will not fire. The trigger also **grew 25% as the table grew** (FIX-943 computed 145,784 against 2.9M rows): a table that steps raises its own tolerance for bloat, which is [[FIX-972]]'s stale-quantum defect (playbook D5) applied to autovacuum itself. **Writers with no tail, enumerated from prod `pg_proc`:** 13 live functions mass-UPDATE `financial_entities` (`rebuild_financial_entity_donation_totals`, `rebuild_financial_entity_ie_totals`, `refresh_spending_totals`, `financial_entity_recipient_count_rebuild`, `reconcile_financial_entity_totals`, `rebuild_all_primary_sources`, …) and **none contains `VACUUM`**; `grep -rn "VACUUM" packages/data/src/pipelines/` returns **zero matches**, so no ingest pipeline vacuums anything; the only pg_cron vacuum job, `ec-vacuum-analyze`, covers `entity_connections` alone. **Measured consequence** — the covering index that exists *specifically* to enable index-only scans, `financial_entities_nonindividual_id` = `btree(id) INCLUDE (display_name, entity_type) WHERE entity_type <> 'individual'` (33 MB, ~4,224 pages): `Index Only Scan … actual rows=226640, **Heap Fetches: 108419** (47.8% of rows), Buffers: shared hit=205784 read=50837, Execution Time: **47,042.959 ms**` — **256,621 buffers to return 226,640 rows, 61× the index's own size**, all of the excess heap. Against the tables that DO have vacuum owners, same box same night: EC's `entity_connections_donation_to_official_idx` 26.5% heap fetches, FR's `financial_relationships_donor_rollup_idx` (the [[FIX-974]] path) **4.8%** — a **10× spread tracking vacuum ownership exactly**. **Blast radius:** `financial_entities_pkey` is the **most-scanned index on the instance**, 84,990,056 scans at 80.6% heap-fetched; every donor rollup, graph query, tagger pass and treemap build joins through it. **It is 3.7 points from paging someone** — `check_rebuild_autovacuum_status()` escalates `vm_degraded` at `relpages > 1000 AND pct_all_visible < 50.0`, and FIX-943 called `donor_party_rollup_mv` at 42.7% "the worst table on the instance". **Fix shape:** give the three ownerless tables a vacuum owner the way [[FIX-974]]'s `donor-rollup-bulk.ts` owns its six arms — cheapest first: (a) add `financial_entities` to the FEC/USASpending/LittleSis/IRS990/EDGAR pipeline tails and to `merge-cross-source-fe-collisions.ts`; (b) add a `financial_entities` arm to the monthly `ec-vacuum-analyze` cron (rename it — the job name already lies about its scope); (c) `donor_party_rollup_mv` should be vacuumed by `refresh_donor_party_rollup_incremental`'s driver, which deletes 1,903,409 and inserts 1,883,817 rows per full pass with no tail; (d) `external_relationships_review_queue` (709 MB, `autovacuum_count` **0** — never autovacuumed in its life, no `reloptions` at all, 82,682 inserts since its last vacuum) needs tuning at minimum, and FIX-943 explicitly left it alone as "pipeline-only" when it was smaller. **Methodological note worth keeping:** `relallvisible` is a *lagging* proxy — it is only refreshed by `VACUUM`, so a table dirtied since its last vacuum reads better than it is (`entity_connections` shows 98.4% all-visible yet 26.5% real heap fetches). `Heap Fetches` in `EXPLAIN` is ground truth; `relallvisible` is the early warning. Playbook B1 says watch both — this pass confirms they disagree by a wide margin and in which direction. Measurement conditions: prod, 04:29–04:48 UTC 2026-08-07, box NOT idle (an `INSERT INTO financial_relationships` ran throughout), clear of the nightly and of the 09:00/12:00 firings. - [x] 🟠 S — **refresh_treemap_individuals_global writes its chunk cursor with NOW() inside the per-chunk COMMIT loop — the byte-identical twin of the FIX-972 defect, in a sibling procedure FIX-972 never enumerated** — **Found by the 2026-08-07 site-wide efficiency audit (`docs/audits/2026-08-07-efficiency-audit.md`), class 5 — lying timestamps; SURVIVED adversarial verification.** This is playbook **E5** in its purest form: [[FIX-972]] diagnosed the defect, fixed the one site it was standing on, and nobody grepped for the mechanism. **The defect, verbatim FIX-972's.** `public.refresh_treemap_individuals_global` (live `prosrc:145-148`) writes its chunk cursor's `updated_at` with `NOW()` from inside the per-chunk `COMMIT` loop. `NOW()` is `transaction_timestamp()`; every chunk runs in its own transaction that BEGINs immediately after the previous chunk's `COMMIT`, so the stamp records when chunk N *started* — **one whole chunk early**. The cursor VALUE is never wrong; only its timestamp. FIX-972's proof was exact — a run's last cursor write read 13:31:23 against a 15:20:29 end, a phantom **1h49m** of apparent stall equal to that run's `slowest_chunk_seconds` (6,546 s) to the second — and it cost a full diagnostic pass to chase. **Measured here:** prod `data_sync_log` run 2026-08-06 02:23:09 → 03:09:28 UTC, `status=complete`, span 2,779 s, `metadata->>'slowest_chunk_seconds' = 59`. So today's lie is bounded at **59 s** — small, because this procedure's chunks are currently fast. That is precisely why it should be fixed now rather than after it bites: [[FIX-965]] chunked this refresh at 64 windows against a 2400 s budget, [[FIX-964]] records it already blowing that budget mid-tail once, and the same procedure appears in [[FIX-969]]'s over-ceiling set at **21,615.9 s**. Cross-ref [[FIX-972]], [[FIX-965]], [[FIX-964]], [[FIX-969]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-974]]. <!--id:FIX-981-->

The nightly enrichment job *does* fire, but `runLittleSisPipeline` short-circuits at the SHA256 freshness gate (`littlesis/index.ts:94-98`, `skipSync('dumps_unchanged')`) **before** the preload runs. CONCURRENTLY` requires a unique index**, so the missing index is the *cause* and the `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock is the *consequence* — for the whole duration of the refresh, on a materialized view the **homepage reads**. **Why this is not hypothetical.** This exact object is the receipt behind playbook **C4** (*"runtime measurements are floors — design to survive the miss"*): `refresh_homepage_stats_mv()` takes **0.7 s on local** and ran **22 minutes** against an otherwise-idle prod on 2026-07-31, pushing the homepage to **18.5 s**. That is a one-line migration plus a one-word change in the procedure body. **Sequence:** add the unique index first (it must exist before `CONCURRENTLY` will run), then flip the refresh; verify the homepage stays served during a refresh rather than blocking. Note `CONCURRENTLY` trades the lock for a longer refresh and needs the MV to be populated, so confirm the first post-change run on local before prod. The rest of the class is untreated. Honest scoping: the direct cost of bloat on a 1-5 page relation is near zero, so this is a hygiene/consistency item, not a performance one — the value is that these are the relations where the [[FIX-884]] all-visible mechanism is invisible in monitoring precisely because the absolute numbers look harmless. Fix shape: a threshold-led override on the enumerated set, no new framework and no per-table cron jobs (autovacuum genuinely suffices once the trigger is reachable). So **there is no confirmed reader of the 438,094 frozen rows**, and if they were deleted that same hypothetical call returns EMPTY rather than STALE — from the route's perspective the two states are indistinguishable. **(2) The 08-16 deadline pressure is gone.** It came from treating frozen rows as actively-wrong output; they are unread output. **(3) Recommendation stands at option (a)** — DELETE the 438,094 non-official rows, accept that a financial-entity focus always takes the raw fallback (which is what every other arm already does), and add the matching assertion to `donor_rollup_bulk_assert_invariants()` ([[FIX-974]]) so the two regimes cannot diverge silently again. **(4) Execution deliberately DEFERRED pending Craig's sign-off** — it is a 438k-row delete on a live MV and the FIX-943 vacuum tail applies, so it wants a supervised off-peak window, not an autonomous one. **⏳ PROGRESS 2026-08-13 (cc-prompt-60): the DURABLE half shipped, the DELETE did NOT — FIX STAYS OPEN.** Migration `20260813020000_fix1023_arm_official_only_invariant.sql` extends `donor_rollup_bulk_assert_invariants()` ([[FIX-974]]) with a per-arm no-non-official assertion covering **all six** arms, so the incremental and bulk regimes cannot diverge silently again. The 438k-row prod DELETE was deliberately NOT executed: the supervised [[FIX-1021]] firing that shared this window ended with a **prod postgres restart at 01:45:27 UTC** (see the restart FIX), and a 438k-row delete plus its [[FIX-943]] vacuum tail on a just-restarted cold-cache box is not a supervised-window operation — it is now the first item for the next off-peak session. **Consequence to know before then: the bulk regime is GATED.** The assertion is live on prod and prod still holds the non-official rows, so `donor_rollup_rebuild_bulk()` will now REFUSE with the FIX-1023 message until the delete runs. That is the intended behaviour and it is safe — no scheduled job calls the bulk regime (verified prod 2026-08-13: cron 24 = `refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental`, cron 15 = `reconcile_donor_rollup_orphans`, cron 32 = a vacuum; nothing CALLs the bulk procedure) — but a manual break-glass bulk run will hit it. **Two premises corrected by measurement.** (1) **The bullet's 'treemap_individuals_rollup 928,064/0' is wrong.** That arm keys on `scope_id`, not `official_id`, and carries a legitimate GLOBAL scope row-set under the all-zeros sentinel uuid — 3,034 rows on prod, maintained by `refresh_treemap_individuals_global()` / cron 26. The assertion therefore exempts the all-zeros uuid **by value** rather than skipping the arm, so the one arm with a non-official-keyed scope still gets guarded. An assertion written from the bullet as stated would have fired on every bulk run. (2) The delete was rehearsed end-to-end on the local prod clone: pre 1,018,455 rows / 442,421 non-official / 8,483 ids → `DELETE 442421` (1.7 s) → `VACUUM (ANALYZE)` (0.7 s) → post 576,034 / 0 → assertion passes. Local's counts run slightly above the 2026-08-11 prod measurement (438,094 / 8,369), so **re-count live on prod before deleting** rather than reusing either figure. Note the assertion costs ~32 s (six anti-join scans) — fine as a pre-flight for a multi-hour bulk rebuild, but it is not free. Cross-ref [[FIX-1018]], [[FIX-974]], [[FIX-704]], [[FIX-943]], [[FIX-1021]]. <!--id:FIX-1023-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **The burn-rate RPC scanned every snapshot payload — 427ms and ~12k buffer blocks per tick** — Self-inflicted by [[FIX-1044]] and caught within hours because Craig noticed a Supabase spike and asked. **MEASURED ON PROD from pg_stat_statements 2026-08-16:** get_platform_daily_cost_deltas — calls 9, mean 427.4 ms, max 966.7 ms, 109,087 buffer blocks total, i.e. **~12,000 blocks (~95 MB of buffer traffic) PER CALL** — against 115 calls of everything else touching that table at 18.1 ms mean. It runs on EVERY snapshot tick, forever. **THE CAUSE:** the function read every platform_usage_snapshot row in a 14-day window (measured: 276 rows, 4.6 MB of payload, 17 kB average, so nearly all TOASTed) and ran jsonb_array_elements over the metrics array of each one, purely to take max() per MTD day at the end. On an instance with 256 MB shared_buffers and a ~54 pct cache hit rate ([[project_prod_buffer_churn_baseline]]) that is exactly the churn packages/db/CLAUDE.md warns about under "Cost note: profile the COMPUTE, not just the read" — the read path was considered and the cron-side compute was not. **THE FIX:** Vercel counters are cumulative and step ONCE PER DAY, and consecutive snapshots inside a day are byte-identical to 16 decimal places (established by the 2026-08-15 audit). So ~19 of every 20 rows carry information already present in another, and the whole series is recoverable from a couple of rows per Vercel billing day. Bucket by Pacific day using ONLY fetched_at — no payload is detoasted to make the selection — take the first and last row of each bucket via DISTINCT ON, and only THEN do the jsonb extraction, on ~28 rows instead of ~276. Same output; if anything more correct than max(), since the last snapshot of a day is the settled end-of-day value whereas max() would have preferred a larger mid-day reading had one occurred. **WHY BOTH ENDS AND NOT JUST THE LAST:** insurance against boundary jitter, not a fix for an observed skip. The audit dates the step at "~06:00-07:00 UTC" and the bucket boundary is Pacific midnight = 07:00 UTC. Measured on the clone the step lands cleanly (last row with an old window_days is 03:45-06:29 UTC, first with the new one is 07:07-09:32), but a step at 06:00 — the early end of the audit own range — would put a row bearing the NEW window_days into the OLD bucket where, being last, it would become that bucket sole representative and silently drop a whole MTD day. Bracketing costs one extra detoast per day and removes the failure mode. **METHOD NOTE worth keeping:** during this fix MTD day 1 appeared to vanish from the local series and was briefly misdiagnosed as bucket masking. The real cause was the rolling 14-day window moving past it in the two hours between runs. Verified by widening p_days to 16, which returned days 28-31 and 2-9 all consecutive — no skip. Check the window before blaming the query. Cross-ref [[FIX-1044]], [[FIX-281]]. <!--id:FIX-1049-->

The mechanism is a stale size assumption. On this box hash_mem_multiplier is 2, so that node is permitted 512MB, and max_parallel_workers_per_gather is 1, so leader plus one worker is up to 1GB for that single node, against a commit limit of roughly 2.18GB with shared_buffers already at 256MB and max_connections 60. Note the prod GLOBAL work_mem is also 262144kB (256MB), and refresh_derived_mvs sets 128MB for its own session but rebuild_entity_search_index overrides it back up to 256MB. Candidate fixes to measure before choosing: lower the SET LOCAL work_mem to a value sized against the current table, replace the UNION ALL degree count with a precomputed source (entity_connection_stats_mv already holds per-entity connection counts), or SET LOCAL max_parallel_workers_per_gather 0 for this statement so the worker copy is not doubled. pg_stat_statements cannot be consulted for the incident window because it reset at the crash; absence of pgss data is not absence of cost. - [x] 🟠 M — **An ad-hoc VACUUM of financial_relationships is a front-door incident, and its scheduled-job history is the wrong way to size it** — MEASURED THE HARD WAY on prod 2026-09-01, in a supervised window, by causing it. A VACUUM (ANALYZE) of financial_relationships was run ad-hoc at 23:09 UTC as a prerequisite for [[FIX-1118]] (an index-only scan needs a fresh visibility map). It was sized at about 4 minutes from jobid 38 fr-vacuum-analyze's last three firings — 227.2 s, 20.3 s, 97.8 s. It was cancelled at 675.5 s, still inside its FIRST pass over the indexes, after putting 8 statement timeouts (SQLSTATE 57014) through the front door between 23:03 and 23:19 UTC, peaking at 4 per minute, which Craig observed live. Errors stopped at 23:20 the moment it was cancelled. TWO SEPARATE LESSONS, both worth encoding. FIRST, the sizing error: a scheduled vacuum's history measures the STEADY STATE, not a catch-up. jobid 38 is cheap precisely because it is weekly and runs 01:00 UTC, so it never has much to do; the ad-hoc run had two days and 187,000 updates behind it. Never size an ad-hoc vacuum from the cron job's runtimes. Size it from n_dead_tup and the index footprint. SECOND, and the more useful finding: the heap was never the cost. The heap phase finished 631,265 blocks in about 115 seconds. The remaining 560 s was the INDEX phase, because financial_relationships carries EIGHTEEN indexes totalling 6,926 MB, all of which a vacuum must sweep in full to remove 187,854 dead item IDs, on a box with 256 MB of shared_buffers (see [[project_prod_buffer_churn_baseline]]). So FR's vacuum cost is dominated by its index count, which also means every FR write pays 18-index maintenance. An index census on this table — which of the 18 are actually used, per pg_stat_user_indexes idx_scan — is probably the highest-leverage thing available here, and would cut vacuum cost, write amplification and disk together. THIRD, a corollary that bit us the same evening: a cancelled VACUUM banks NOTHING. vacuum_count stayed 1, last_vacuum stayed 2026-08-31 01:03, n_dead_tup stayed 187,854, so the 675 s bought zero progress and the next attempt restarts from the top. That is the same cancel-discards-the-work property documented for the ec-crawl stats windows in docs/audits/front-door-degradation-2026-09-01.md. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE STANDING RULE: the FIX-943 convention (any script that bulk-rewrites a table ends by vacuuming what it rewrote) is still right, but on this table the tail is a front-door risk, not a formality. Bulk-rewrite scripts touching FR must be scheduled off-peak and budgeted in the tens of minutes, per the no-heavy-prod-ops-during-active-hours rule. Cross-ref [[FIX-943]] [[FIX-884]] [[FIX-1118]] [[FIX-1107]] [[FIX-1034]]. <!--id:FIX-1133-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **official_homepage_stats_mv scans financial_relationships THREE times per refresh — collapse to one pass with FILTER** — MEASURED ON PROD 2026-09-02, surfaced by the jobid-9 unit_seconds regression. official_homepage_stats_mv is the second-largest unit in refresh-derived-mvs-daily and it went 253.9 s (08-31 06:00) to 252.8 s (08-31 23:36) to 800.5 s (09-01 06:00). THE STRUCTURE: its defining query has four CTEs, and THREE of them scan public.financial_relationships independently — donor_counts (to_type=official AND relationship_type=donation), fin_counts (to_type=official), donation_sums (to_type=official AND relationship_type=donation AND amount_cents IS NOT NULL) — each GROUP BY to_id. FR is 4,932 MB of heap and 14.5M rows, so one refresh reads it three times, roughly 15 GB of I/O against a box with shared_buffers 256 MB. All three share the SAME to_type=official predicate and the SAME grouping key, so they collapse to a single scan with conditional aggregates: count(*) FILTER (WHERE relationship_type=donation), count(*), sum(amount_cents) FILTER (WHERE relationship_type=donation AND amount_cents IS NOT NULL), all GROUP BY to_id. Expected saving is about two thirds of the FR work in this unit. VERDICT STRUCTURAL, NOT TRANSIENT, and the instrument matters: EXPLAIN on prod shows the three FR nodes are Parallel Bitmap Heap Scan, Parallel Seq Scan, Parallel Bitmap Heap Scan — ZERO Index Only Scans over FR — and neither a bitmap heap scan nor a seq scan consults the visibility map, so visibility-map decay CANNOT be the mechanism here no matter what the surrounding tables look like. That rules out the tempting VM-decay story and it is why this needs a query change rather than a vacuum. The 3.2x excursion on 09-01 06:00 is a separate same-morning contention event (homepage_stats_mv also went 11.8 to 64.5 s and rebuild_entity_search_index went 383.9 to 490.7 s on that same run, three unrelated units regressing together); the 253 s baseline is the structural part and it grows linearly with FR. WHY IT ESCAPED FIX-1123: that census filtered on functions setting work_mem >= 128MB, and a REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY sets no work_mem at all, so an unbounded refresh over a growing source was invisible to it. Note this unit lives in jobid 9, the job that has now twice taken prod down. Cross-ref [[FIX-1123]] [[FIX-1125]] [[FIX-1129]] [[FIX-775]]. <!--id:FIX-1134-->

- [x] 🔴 M — **A manifest-scoped remediation must not carry a platform-scoped tail — --defer-tails still runs two global rebuilds, and one of them cost the front door 70 statement cancellations in 28 minutes** — MEASURED ON PROD 2026-09-07 during the FIX-954 set-2 apply (Alan Armstrong, a 28-row manifest). The delete and the three manifest-scoped rollups took 78 seconds combined — donor_rollup_rebuild_recipients 28.8s for 2 officials, financial_entity_donation_totals_rebuild 15.3s for 28 donors, donor_party_rollup_rebuild_donors 33.8s. The script then entered rebuild_financial_entity_ie_totals(), a PLATFORM-scoped rebuild whose cost is independent of the manifest, and was cancelled by hand 28 minutes in. Front-door damage over that step, from the Supabase Logs API by SQLSTATE: 70 x 57014 (statement cancellation) plus 13 x 08006 and 6 x 08P01 connection failures, against a BASELINE of 1 x 57014 in the equivalent 28-minute window at 18:00 the same day — roughly 70x. The preceding conservation phase took another 132 x 57014 over 81 minutes. Total 202 cancellations the front door would not otherwise have served, and the rate was HIGHEST during the global rebuild (2.50/min vs 1.63/min). With every script stopped the next 15-minute window measured ZERO. THE DEFECT: --defer-tails (shipped earlier the same day) defers the VACUUM, the search index, the treemap and — after a same-day follow-up — the six MV refreshes, on the principle that each has a scheduled owner. It does NOT defer or scope the two remaining global steps in runRollups: rebuild_financial_entity_ie_totals() and refresh_group_donor_rollup(). Both rebuild the whole platform for a manifest-sized change. OWNERSHIP IS SPLIT AND WAS NEVER CHECKED: rebuild_financial_entity_ie_totals IS owned — the fec_bulk pipeline calls it at packages/data/src/pipelines/fec-bulk/index.ts:2418 and it ran on prod 2026-09-06 06:58 and 2026-09-07 07:12, both complete — so running it from a remediation script is pure duplication. refresh_group_donor_rollup has NO scheduled owner at all: no cron.job command names it, no SQL function or procedure calls it (checked via pg_proc.prosrc on prod), and its only non-script caller is scripts/rebuild-entity-connections.ts, whose workflow became workflow_dispatch-only when FIX-688 moved the EC rebuild schedule to pg_cron. So the group rollup silently lost its cadence and is currently re-derived ONLY as a side effect of a remediation script's tail. FIX SHAPE: (a) rebuild_financial_entity_ie_totals — defer it under --defer-tails and name fec_bulk as the owner, or scope it to the affected financial_entities; (b) refresh_group_donor_rollup — either give it a real scheduled owner (its own pg_cron job, off-peak) and defer it here, or scope it to the affected groups; (c) the dry run must PRINT each tail step's cost class — manifest-scoped, platform-scoped-with-owner, or platform-scoped-orphan — so the trade is visible before the go-ahead rather than discovered at minute 28. THE STANDING RULE THIS EARNS, and it generalises past these scripts: a manifest-scoped remediation must not carry a platform-scoped tail. Every tail step either SCALES WITH THE MANIFEST or HAS A SCHEDULED OWNER; anything that is neither is a bug in the script, not a cost of the change. Corollary: a step's presence in a tail is not evidence it has an owner — check cron.job by name, pg_proc.prosrc, and the GHA workflows, because FIX-688-style schedule migrations orphan callers silently. Cross-ref [[FIX-1153]], [[FIX-943]], [[FIX-964]], [[FIX-965]], [[FIX-688]], [[FIX-1129]], [[FIX-1144]]. New shared module packages/data/src/scripts/remediation-manifest.ts holds the manifest reader, the clone-vs-here diff (match/shrunk/grown/gone; GROWN is reported and SKIPPED because the manifest is an authorisation, not a description) and the tail cost table. THREE PLATFORM-SCOPED READS FOUND, not one: besides rebuild_financial_entity_ie_totals() and refresh_group_donor_rollup(), the CONSERVATION check (PLATFORM_SQL, a full aggregate over every official donation row) and the CLOSING NUMBER were both platform-scoped -- PLATFORM_SQL is the conservation phase that cost the other 132 cancellations. - [x] 🟡 S — **Missing set_updated_at trigger on public.financial_entities (lost in shadow→public promotion)** — `public.financial_entities` has **no `updated_at` trigger** on prod. Migration 0004 created `CREATE TRIGGER financial_entities_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON financial_entities ... EXECUTE FUNCTION set_updated_at()`, but the shadow→public promotion (migration 20260422000000) promoted/recreated `public.financial_entities` WITHOUT re-creating the trigger. Confirmed on prod 2026-06-30: `pg_trigger` shows zero non-internal triggers on `public.financial_entities`. `set_updated_at()` is unconditional (`NEW.updated_at = NOW()`), so with the trigger gone, `updated_at` is set only on INSERT (column DEFAULT NOW()) and is **never bumped on UPDATE** — it has been stale on every updated row since the 2026-04-22 cutover. The `financial_entities_updated_at` index consequently points at insert-time, not last-modified, so any freshness/recency consumer of `financial_entities.updated_at` is wrong. **Scope (verified prod 2026-06-30):** only `financial_entities` lost the trigger — `financial_relationships`, `votes`, `proposals`, `officials`, `agencies`, `career_history` all RETAIN their `set_updated_at` trigger, so the incremental `entity_connections` rebuild (keys on `financial_relationships.updated_at` / `votes.updated_at` dirty sets) is NOT affected (the worst case checked for). `entity_connections` also lacks the trigger but is TRUNCATE-rebuilt wholesale, so `updated_at` is cosmetic there. **How found:** FIX-677 backfill monitoring — the donor-entity upsert was mostly UPDATEs yet `count(updated_at >= run_start)` tracked only `n_tup_ins` (~37k) while `n_tup_upd` was ~1.5M. **Fix:** migration recreating `CREATE TRIGGER financial_entities_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON public.financial_entities FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION public.set_updated_at();` (optionally also on `public.entity_connections`); apply local + prod; audit promotion migration 20260422000000 for any other dropped triggers. Optional one-time `updated_at` backfill is low priority. Cross-ref [[FIX-677]]. <!--id:FIX-699-->

- [x] 🟠 M — **Expand the donor-industry vocabulary to 16 keys; consolidate four duplicate label maps into one** — A full dollar-weighted audit of all twelve donor-industry tags (2026-07-27, read-only on the local prod-clone; docs/audits/) found **not one tag above 79% accuracy by dollars, seven below 50%, median 41%**. Root cause is NOT dirty keywords: ai-classifier.ts forced a **12-way choice made from the donor name alone**, and the vocabulary had no bucket at all for electric utilities, industrial manufacturing, chemicals, autos, steel, mining or media. A model asked to place *Duke Energy PAC* into those twelve answers oil_gas and is not wrong to — it is the nearest available label. That single gap is the largest error mass in eight of the twelve tags. **Adds four keys** (utilities, manufacturing, mining, media; VALID_INDUSTRIES 12 to 16) and **renames pharma to health** — a blanket key rename, correct for the unaudited tail too, because the entire keyword list feeding the tag is health-sector and the tag measured **20.4% pharmaceutical but 91.2% health-sector** (hospital/physician assocs 32.0%, health trade assocs 20.7%, health insurers 11.6%). manufacturing already existed as a 1-donor out-of-vocabulary tag (NAM-PAC) and is PROMOTED, not deleted. **oil_gas keeps its key AND stays narrow** — widening it to Energy and Utilities would take it 40.7% to 91.8% honest but would destroy the money_vote_influence HR 26 measure, which needs fossil-fuel money specifically; the fossil core is coherent (upstream 18.0% + refining 9.1% + pipeline 6.0% + trade assoc 3.7% + fuel marketing 2.8% + oilfield svcs 1.0%) and the honest fix is moving the utilities OUT. Labels widen where contents justify (tech to Technology and Communications, legal to Legal and Professional Services, retail to Consumer Goods and Services, real_estate to Real Estate and Construction, defense to Defense and Aerospace, agriculture to Agriculture and Food, lobby to Advocacy and Lobbying, finance to Finance and Insurance). **Consolidation:** INDUSTRY_LABELS was duplicated in four places (tags/rules.ts, tags/ai-classifier.ts — which additionally carried an 'other' key never in VALID_INDUSTRIES — enrichment/queue.ts INDUSTRY_DISPLAY, and app-side CANONICAL_INDUSTRY_TOKENS); all now resolve to ONE exported constant beside VALID_INDUSTRIES in tags/topics.ts, which is already the FIX-890 drain write-boundary source. UI keeps its own key-to-lucide registry (different type, no dep edge from apps/civitics to @civitics/data) mirrored by packages/graph/src/industries.ts, pinned by a test that reads that file off disk. **No donor is re-assigned by this change** — the curated override list that actually moves donors into the new buckets is a separate follow-up. Cross-ref [[FIX-890]] [[FIX-889]] [[FIX-897]] [[FIX-896]]. Explicitly NOT bundled: [[FIX-873]]/[[FIX-875]] industry-tag dedup, and the DISTINCT ON alphabet-gradient tie-break. <!--id:FIX-908-->
