- [x] 🟡 S — **ai-classifier writes 'other' as a real industry tag — out-of-vocabulary rows that bypass the write-boundary guard** — Documented at the call site by [[FIX-908]], filed here rather than fixed there because changing it changes what gets written. buildPrompt() in packages/data/src/pipelines/tags/ai-classifier.ts offers 'other' as an answer for 'if unclear', and classifyPac() ALSO coerces any unrecognised or unparseable model answer to 'other'. That value is then upserted into entity_tags as a real industry tag with display_label 'Other' — but 'other' is NOT a member of VALID_INDUSTRIES. Three consequences. (1) **It bypasses the guard**: the [[FIX-890]] write-boundary check lives in drain/vocabulary.ts and only covers the drain path; ai-classifier upserts straight over PostgREST, so the one vocabulary enforcement point in the codebase never sees it. (2) **An abstention is indistinguishable from a parse failure** — both collapse to the same string, so 'the model declined to classify this PAC' and 'the model returned malformed JSON' are the same row, and neither is visible in the skipped count. (3) **It renders a meaningless pill**: a donor labelled 'Other' is worse than an unlabelled donor, because it looks like a classification. Measured 2026-07-27: **8 rows on prod, 0 on local** — small, but it is the same out-of-vocabulary class as the energy/pharmaceutical singletons [[FIX-909]] deleted, still being actively written. The [[FIX-909]] migration's vocabulary assertion explicitly TOLERATES 'other' for exactly this reason (asserting it away would fail the migration on prod today, and would fail again on the next classifier run even after a cleanup) — that tolerance should be removed as part of this fix. **Suggested shape:** stop writing the row at all when the model abstains, record the abstention in the sync-log counters as its own category distinct from parse failures, and clean up the 8 existing prod rows in the same change. Consider also routing this upsert through checkTagVocabulary so the guard covers every writer, not just the drain. Cross-ref [[FIX-908]] [[FIX-909]] [[FIX-890]]. <!--id:FIX-911-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **Curated industry overrides — 742 hand-audited donors re-assigned or de-tagged** — Follow-up to [[FIX-908]]/[[FIX-909]], which added the four missing vocabulary keys but deliberately moved no donor into them. The 2026-07-27 dollar-weighted audit hand-classified 1,438 donors covering 90-100% of each industry tag's donation dollars and produced a **742-donor override list** committed at `docs/audits/2026-07-27-industry-tag-overrides.tsv`: **380 donors carrying the wrong industry** and **362 that are not industries at all** (leadership PACs, party committees, abstract vanity PACs — WinRed, NRSC, Save America, Huck PAC, AmeriPAC were all tagged `lobby`). Decision was explicitly hand-curation, NOT an AI re-run. **New table `public.financial_entity_industry_overrides`** keyed on `fec_committee_id` (text PK), not `financial_entities.id` — UUIDs are not portable across a re-seed and FEC committee IDs are the stable external key (`financial_entities.fec_committee_id` is already UNIQUE); all 742 audited donors have one and all 742 are distinct. `industry IS NULL` is a POSITIVE ASSERTION — 'this donor carries no industry, ever' — not 'unknown', and it SUPPRESSES tagging rather than merely omitting it. **The override is applied INSIDE `tagFinancialEntities()`** in packages/data/src/pipelines/tags/rules.ts, as the last word after the keyword and NAICS passes. It cannot live anywhere else: that function calls `clear_financial_entity_rule_tags(['industry'])`, which DELETEs every `entity_type='financial_entity' AND generated_by='rule' AND tag_category='industry'` row and re-inserts from the keyword list, so an override written by any other job would be shadowed by a freshly re-inserted keyword tag on the very next nightly — the same authoritative-rebuild trap [[FIX-897]] hit with the official industry pills and the co-owned-rows class of [[FIX-808]]. Override rows are written `generated_by='curated'`, confidence 1.0, visibility 'primary', with `metadata` carrying `source`, `audited_sector` and `fec_committee_id` so the number behind the label stays auditable. Because the nightly clear is scoped to `generated_by='rule'`, curated rows SURVIVE it — so the producer owns them with its own authoritative delete-then-insert over the same direct-pg connection as the upsert, making a re-run a no-op rather than an accumulation. **Exactly one industry per overridden donor**, which has a second payoff: it collapses 96.4% of the multi-tag donation dollar mass ($328.4M of $340.8M across 478 multi-tag donating donors) to a single tag at the source, leaving the alphabetical `DISTINCT ON` tie-break ([[FIX-918]]) almost nothing to arbitrate. The migration also does a **one-time delete of the surviving `generated_by='ai'` industry rows for overridden donors only** — the nightly clear never touched them, so the AI-derived tags carrying most of the dollars (93.7% of `lobby`, 71.5% of `oil_gas`, 66.4% of `defense`) would otherwise persist forever and shadow the curation. AI rows for NON-overridden donors are left alone. **KNOWN, ACCEPTED LIMITATION:** 742 rows is the audited set at 90-100% dollar coverage per tag; the unaudited tail keeps its current tag. In particular `oil_gas` retains a tail of small utility PACs (~8% of its dollars) the audit did not reach. Depends on [[FIX-910]] (the producer must actually complete) and pairs with [[FIX-917]] (without which the AI classifier re-tags the 362 de-tagged committees on its next run). Cross-ref [[FIX-908]] [[FIX-909]] [[FIX-897]] [[FIX-890]] [[FIX-873]] [[FIX-875]]. <!--id:FIX-916-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **AI classifier must exclude curated-override donors — else it re-tags exactly what was de-tagged** — The fail-open trap paired with [[FIX-916]], filed separately because it is a distinct guard with its own test. `runAiClassifier()` in packages/data/src/pipelines/tags/ai-classifier.ts builds its candidate set as 'PACs over the donation threshold that have **no** industry tag' — `allPacs.filter(r => !alreadyTagged.has(r.id))`. Fix is to subtract every entity present in `financial_entity_industry_overrides` from the candidate set — INCLUDING, and especially, the NULL-industry rows — so a positive 'no industry, ever' assertion is honoured rather than read as a gap. Pinned by a test that puts a NULL-override entity in the tagged/PAC fixtures and asserts it is absent from the candidate set, so deleting the guard fails the suite. - [x] 🟡 S — **Drain vocabulary guard's documented fail-open warn was never implementable — verdict type cannot express it** — `packages/data/src/drain/vocabulary.ts`'s module header promises that an unregistered `entity_type` degrades to 'write it and warn' rather than silently discarding every tag. Only the first half existed. `VocabularyVerdict` was `{allowed: true} | {allowed: false; reason}`, so a fail-open allow (nothing was checked — no vocabulary is registered for this entity type) was byte-identical to an enforced allow (the tag really is in the vocabulary). The caller could not tell them apart, so `drain/apply.ts` wrote both in silence. NO allow/reject outcome changed — fail-open stays fail-open, which is exactly what the FIX-896 `official: {}` reasoning depends on, and `agency` is deliberately NOT registered in `TAG_VOCABULARY`. Observability only. `allowed` stays the discriminant so every existing call site and test compiles and passes untouched; `vocabulary-official-retired.test.ts` now pins both halves (unregistered → unenforced + reason naming the type; `proposal`/`topic` → enforced) so the two allows can never be conflated again. <!--id:FIX-925-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **A donor industry-tag change never triggers a sector-affinity rebuild — content-signature gate + targeted rebuild** — The FIX-704/832 incremental refresh of official_sector_affinity_rollup keys its dirty set off financial_relationships.updated_at, and a tag-only change never touches a financial relationship — so a donor industry re-tag (FIX-916, FIX-921, FIX-923, and every future audit cohort) leaves the officials-side pills frozen with no error. That is exactly the 2026-07-16→07-29 drift: the last full backfill predated FIX-916 by eleven days and 1,607 of 1,779 override-touched officials still showed pre-audit pills while every non-freshness check passed. The only remedy was a human remembering backfill_official_sector_affinity_rollup() (943.8s / 19,869 rows measured on prod 2026-07-29). **The change signal must be content-derived, never time-derived**: entity_tags has created_at and NO updated_at, and tagFinancialEntities() does an authoritative DELETE-then-reinsert of every rule industry row nightly, so max(created_at) resets to ~now on every successful run — a rollup-older-than-last-write check would fire every night forever, and a signal that always fires is a signal nobody reads. Fix: (1) an md5 **content signature** over the (entity_id, tag) set for entity_type=financial_entity AND tag_category=industry (count + hash, computed by compute_fe_industry_tag_signature()), stored in pipeline_state under sector_affinity:industry_tag_signature — the FIX-652/716 count+signature gate shape; identical content → identical signature → zero work. (2) A per-donor shadow table public.donor_industry_tag_state (~24k rows: donor_id, md5 of its ordered tag set, tag count) that the refresh procedure diffs via FULL OUTER JOIN — the diff yields exactly the donors whose industry assignment changed, including donors whose tags were REMOVED. (3) refresh_sector_affinity_from_tag_changes(): affected recipients = officials who received a donation from a changed donor (an index probe on financial_relationships (from_id) via financial_relationships_donation_size_rollup), rebuilt in 500-official chunks with per-chunk COMMIT through the existing sector_affinity_rebuild_officials() — NOT the 16-minute full backfill, which is reserved for a cold start / signature-store miss; data_sync_log rows under sector_affinity_tag_refresh name which path ran (noop / targeted / full_backfill) and why. Signature + shadow advance only on a clean run, so a failed chunk retries next night. Donor-side dirty set unchanged — the gap was officials-only. Cross-ref [[FIX-704]] [[FIX-777]] [[FIX-832]] [[FIX-916]] [[FIX-921]] [[FIX-923]] [[FIX-652]] [[FIX-716]]. <!--id:FIX-958-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **Rule-tagger phase order lagged official industry pills a full night — reorder around the affinity refresh + content-keyed staleness alarm** — Companion to [[FIX-958]], split out because the order fix is independently verifiable and would otherwise hide inside the trigger diff. runRuleBasedTagger() ran tagProposals → tagOfficials → tagFinancialEntities, so tagOfficials — which reads official_sector_affinity_rollup to write the FIX-897 industry pills — executed BEFORE that night's donor tag changes existed, and any rollup rebuild came later still. **Even with a perfect trigger, pills would lag a full night.** Fix half 1 (order): the phases now run proposals → financialEntities → refresh_sector_affinity_from_tag_changes() → officials, so the targeted rebuild completes before tagOfficials reads the rollup; proven by the single-run test (flip one donor's industry via the override table, run the tagger ONCE, the receiving official's pill reflects it — not on the second run). The refresh call is deliberately NON-fatal to the tagger (a stale rollup is the pre-existing condition and a dead nightly is worse — the FIX-920 direction); the alarm below is what makes a silent strand loud. Fix half 2 (alarm): check_sector_affinity_tag_staleness() compares the LIVE content signature against the stored sector_affinity:industry_tag_signature — keyed on signature-CHANGE, never write time, so the nightly DELETE-then-reinsert of identical content can never false-fire (decision-1 discipline). A mismatch is only escalated when the STORED signature has been stuck unchanged for >26h (probe state in pipeline_state sector_affinity:staleness_probe records first_mismatch_at + the stored sig it saw; a stored sig that advanced since the probe means the refresh is alive and the mismatch is a new change in flight — probe resets). Wired into canary-check.ts beside the FIX-885/943/944 detectors: recorded in the meta row every run, escalates (email + non-zero exit → red workflow) on stale=true. This is the FIX-884/885 silent-strand class: the guard exists so the next eleven-day drift is loud. Cross-ref [[FIX-958]] [[FIX-897]] [[FIX-920]] [[FIX-885]] [[FIX-944]] [[FIX-916]]. <!--id:FIX-959-->

### HOMEPAGE

- [x] 🟠 S — **Homepage hero stats render 0 when the DB is saturated — carry null through all four** — During the 2026-08-19 saturation the homepage rendered zeros rather than degrading. Line-anchored trace in apps/civitics/app/page.tsx: the MV read at L144-151 has no withDbTimeout label, and L186 / L226-231 / L481-484 coerce a failed read to 0 with a null-coalescing default. FIX-431 fixed exactly this for the DONOR stat only; the other three hero stats still fabricate a zero. A zero is not a smaller truth, it is a false one — it reads as an authoritative measurement of nothing, which is the opposite of the apps CLAUDE.md real-data-or-empty-state rule. THE FIX: carry null (meaning not measured) through HomeStats for all four hero stats and render a degraded state — last-known value with an as-of stamp, or omit the tile — never a fabricated 0. Add the missing withDbTimeout label on the MV read. Also skip the fallback queries entirely when the primary read timed out: firing two more expensive queries at an already-saturated DB is anti-help and lengthens the outage it is reacting to. Fails open already (withDbTimeout 3000 + console.error + empty Map; EngagementBadges returns null when there is nothing to show), so a stale or missing MV never breaks the profile. Surfaced by the [[FIX-859]] backfill, which resolves 5180 of 5240 unlinked state legislators; the residual is exactly these 58 plus 2 Maine tribal seats (Passamaquoddy Tribe, Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians — non-geographic representation, correctly unlinked forever). Do NOT invent rows in the backfill script; this needs a real seeding pass against an authoritative NH floterial boundary source, after which the existing name-match tier picks them up with no code change. Until then NH is the only state whose SLD choropleth has visible holes. **SOURCE CANDIDATES named 2026-09-05 (cc-prompt-113) so the next session starts from a URL, not a sentence.** Nothing seeded; this is orientation only. (2) NH GRANIT, the state GIS clearinghouse at the University of New Hampshire (https://www.granit.unh.edu/) — NH's authoritative publisher of political/administrative boundary layers, the first place to look for a floterial polygon set. (3) NH Secretary of State / NH General Court redistricting materials (https://www.sos.nh.gov/ and https://gencourt.state.nh.us/) — the 2022 House redistricting plan is STATUTORY (RSA 662:5) and enumerates every floterial district by name together with the towns and wards it spans. (4) THE CHEAPEST PATH IS PROBABLY DERIVATION, NOT DOWNLOAD: a floterial is defined as the union of named base districts, all of which we already hold as jurisdiction rows. Given the statutory membership table from (3), the 58 floterial jurisdictions can be minted as unions of existing base-district geometries with no external shapefile — which also keeps the provenance auditable. Whichever path is taken, the existing name-match tier picks the rows up with no code change once they exist. Still do NOT invent rows in the backfill script. Seeded as ST_Union of the base rows via derive_nh_floterials(); 39 valid geometries, centroid inside all 39, area equal to the sum of base areas to 0 (exactly), 3 multipart (818, 907, 908). GRANIT cross-check: 39/39 matched by code; land-clipped IoU min 0.9532 / median 0.9995 / max 0.9999. Raw IoU flagged one row, 738 Rockingham 38 at 0.7078 — investigated and cleared: GRANIT\ours is 0.31 km2 (nothing missing) and ours\GRANIT is a single 43.11 km2 polygon in the Atlantic off Rye, coastal water TIGER already carries in untouched base row 724 (111.05 km2 against ~64 km2 of land). - [x] 🟠 S — **Officials 'Total raised' and 'Donors on record' both describe numbers the page does not have** — Three surfaces render the same two mislabelled figures: apps/civitics/app/officials/[id]/page.tsx StatCells 'Total raised' + 'Donors on record', apps/civitics/app/officials/components/OfficialCard.tsx, and the prompt string in apps/civitics/app/api/officials/[id]/summary/route.ts. **'Total raised' is not total raised.** It is the ALL-CYCLE sum (2020+2022+2024+2026) of ITEMIZED donation financial_relationships only — it excludes unitemized individual contributions entirely (51% of Ossoff's receipts, and FEC never discloses them at any grain so that is not a closeable coverage gap), joint-fundraising transfers, independent expenditures, loans and other receipts. For Jon Ossoff it renders $14.6M against $77.3M of FEC receipts for the 2025–26 cycle ALONE. **'Donors on record' is not a donor count.** It sums official_donor_rollup_mv.tx_count, which counts financial_relationships ROWS — i.e. donor×cycle pairs, since the table is unique on (relationship_type, from_id, to_id, cycle_year). Measured for Ossoff: 16,646 rows vs 15,761 distinct donors vs 26,520 underlying FEC transactions — so the label overstates donors by 5.6% and is not a transaction count either. official_homepage_stats_mv.donor_count (which OfficialCard and the summary route read) is the same COUNT(*) over the same rows. Neither MV can produce a distinct-donor count without a grain change, so this is a RELABEL, not a recompute: 'Itemized donations' and 'Donor records', with the coverage caveat given a placement that survives the note slot already being contended by the IE support/oppose totals. Cycle-scoping the money figure is a schema change tracked separately as [[FIX-932]]. Cross-ref [[FIX-518]], [[FIX-836]]. <!--id:FIX-931-->
- [x] 🟢 S — **$0 candidate stubs left behind by the FIX-933 merge — cosmetic duplicates, but 16 of them hold real Senate votes** — **File only.** [[FIX-933]] deliberately does NOT delete any `officials` row — "neutralise the duplicate" means it ends up holding zero `financial_relationships` rows, which keeps the merge fully reversible, keeps every FK intact, and keeps that PR out of the officials-dedup design question. The residue is 47 candidate-tier rows carrying $0, a retired `merged_fec_candidate_id` for provenance, and their original `metadata.cand_status/cand_ici/fec_election_yr`. They are same-person duplicates of a sitting member (`T Ossoff` alongside `Jon Ossoff`) and will surface in search, browse facets and any same-name cluster audit. **Not purely cosmetic though:** 16 of the 83 candidate rows [[FIX-933]]'s CAND_ID reconciliation touched hold **real Senate votes** — that is [[FIX-940]], a separate live bug, and those rows must NOT be deleted until it is fixed or the votes would go with them. So the ordering is [[FIX-940]] first, then this. (c) is the cheapest thing that makes the state legible. Cross-ref [[FIX-933]], [[FIX-940]], [[FIX-375]], [[FIX-325]], [[FIX-248]]. <!--id:FIX-939-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **Two SAME-PERSON duplicates hide inside the CROSS-PERSON branch — Shontel Brown and Al Green hold their own money twice** — Surfaced by the [[FIX-934]] phase-1 manifest, which classifies each (suspect, owner) pair SAME-vs-CROSS instead of classifying the suspect once against its single best-overlap twin. **[[FIX-933]] could not see these because cross-person contamination dominated the overlap ranking.** Two sitting House members in the [[FIX-934]] cross-person population hold money that is duplicated onto **their own** `tier='candidate'` row: **Shontel M. Brown** (`f29bbd4e-944f-4840-adbd-16a4706a3c02`, Representative OH-11) has **$2,984,275 / 881 rows** duplicated onto `M Brown` [`H2OH11169`] — *Candidate for Representative, OH, district 11*, i.e. her own seat, holding $2,261,183; her elected row's overlap ranking is dominated by **Sherrod** Brown's $47.3M, which is why [[FIX-933]] never surfaced it. **Al Green** (`e9015ab5-913e-4f2c-a917-190ebd0dde22`, Representative TX-9) has **$941,978 / 596 rows** duplicated onto `Alexander Green` [`H4TX09095`] — *Candidate for Representative, TX, district 09*, his own seat (FEC files his legal name, so the first names disagree on the surface and only the seat signal decides it), holding $1,195,809; his best twin is **Mark** Green [`H8TN07076`], a different person. Total $3,926,253. **These are [[FIX-933]] merges, not [[FIX-934]] deletes — the direction is opposite.** The elected row survives and the candidate row is neutralised; deleting the suspect's side (which [[FIX-934]]'s originally-specified 'high collision rate → DUPLICATED → delete from the suspect' rule would have done, at 97.1% and 45.0% collision respectively) would have deleted a sitting member's own donors from their own page. Both pairs fail [[FIX-933]]'s own manifest gates as written (its survivor must be an attribution orphan whose twin is the sole `fec_candidate_id` holder, and it requires `stateOk` on the classifier's single best twin), so re-running that script unchanged will NOT pick them up — the merge needs the per-owner relation from `ownerRelation()` in `packages/data/src/scripts/fec-orphan-classify.ts`. Note both officials ALSO hold cross-person money that [[FIX-934]] phase 2 removes, and 2020/2022 residue blocked by [[FIX-952]]; sequence this AFTER [[FIX-934]] phase 2 so the merge operates on a cleaned row. - [x] 🟠 S — **merged_fec_candidate_id is single-valued, so a House→Senate member's stub can only retire ONE id (4 pairs, $3.0M re-split)** — Surfaced by the [[FIX-955]] repair pass. [[FIX-933]] records a retired claim in `officials.source_ids->>'merged_fec_candidate_id'`, a single scalar. That is sufficient for a member who only ever held one seat, but **4 sitting Senators who previously served in the House have a candidate stub carrying TWO of their CAND_IDs**: the stub retired the Senate id and has since re-claimed the House one. Measured on the local clone: **Jim Banks** (elected `S4IN00196`; stub live `H6IN03229`, retired `S4IN00196`, 414 rows / $1,516,488), **Ted Budd** (`S2NC00505` / live `H6NC13129`, 269 rows / $1,368,057), **Jon Ossoff** (`S8GA00180` / live `H8GA06195`, 1 row / $91,883), **Tom Cotton** (`S4AR00103` / live `H2AR04083`, 7 rows / $27,198). Total $3,003,625 across 691 rows, all of it the member's own House-era money now double-held with their elected row. The [[FIX-955]] repair **deliberately excludes these four** and its post-merge assertion refuses them by design: merging while a LIVE second claim remains on the stub means the next FEC run re-binds the House id and re-splits the same money, so the merge would undo itself exactly as [[FIX-955]] describes. Note [[FIX-955]]'s pipeline guard is keyed on the single retired value too, so it does not cover the second id either. Options: (a) make the marker an ARRAY (`merged_fec_candidate_ids`) and have `hasRetiredClaim()` test membership — cleanest, but touches the [[FIX-933]] write path, the [[FIX-955]] guard and `persistNewFecIds`; (b) retire only the id whose seat the SURVIVOR does not currently hold, keeping one scalar — works for this population (a Senator's House id is always the stale one) but breaks the moment someone holds three; (c) leave them and accept a bounded $3.0M double-count. (a) is the durable answer and is small. Ordering: this is only reachable once [[FIX-955]] has landed, and it should be applied to prod in the same pass. Cross-ref [[FIX-955]], [[FIX-933]], [[FIX-941]], [[FIX-939]]. <!--id:FIX-956-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **/api/officials/[id]/summary fails open — a DB error returns 200 with summary:null, indistinguishable from an official with no record** — Noticed while choosing a probe target for the FIX-1021 supervised firing (cc-prompt-60); the route was rejected as a liveness probe BECAUSE of this, and the probe now routes around it via `/responsiveness`. The route never returns a non-200 for an infrastructure failure. Four separate paths all emit the same `200 {"summary": null}` body: (1) the `officials` read at route.ts:79-86 — supabase-js returns `{data: null, error}` rather than throwing, so a DB outage lands on `if (!official) return NextResponse.json({ summary: null })` and is reported as 'this official does not exist'; (2) the genuine no-data case at route.ts:109-111 (`voteCount === 0 && donorCount === 0`); (3) an empty model response at route.ts:163; (4) the catch-all at route.ts:197-200, which console.errors the exception and then returns the same null body. `getMonthlySpendCents` compounds it at route.ts:38-40 by swallowing its own error and returning 0, so a failed spend-cap read silently reads as '$0 spent this month' and the cap is not enforced for that request. **Why this is wrong on its own terms, independent of the probe use:** a caller cannot distinguish 'we have nothing to say about this official' from 'the database is down', so the surface is structurally incapable of reporting an outage — the same class of signal-laundering as [[FIX-1027]], where an outage was reported as health. The CDN discipline is already correct and should be preserved: FIX-796 deliberately stamps cache headers ONLY on the two summary-bearing 200s (route.ts:64, 196), leaving every null variant unstamped so a transient null is never pinned at the edge — so this fix must not start caching an error. **Fix shape:** distinguish the cases. Return 503 (uncached) when the `officials` read or the spend-cap read errors, keep 200 `{summary: null}` for the genuine no-data and kill-switch cases, and let `getMonthlySpendCents` propagate rather than defaulting to 0 so the cap fails CLOSED. Cross-ref [[FIX-1027]], [[FIX-796]], [[FIX-311]], [[FIX-893]]. <!--id:FIX-1029-->

- [x] 🟠 S — **Graph treemap click-for-more dead (tooltip identity churn)** — useTooltip returned fresh show/hide closures every render, so any viz listing showTip/hideTip in a d3-render dep array (TreemapGraph) rebuilt the whole SVG on every mousemove — a real-mouse click died because the cell was torn down and rebuilt between mousedown and mouseup (motionless automated clicks worked). - [x] 🟡 S — **Graph treemap labels aggregate individual donors as 'Other'** — Every named individual donor has industry_label NULL in official_donor_rollup_mv (675k/675k local), so they and the small-dollar tail all landed in a treemap cell literally named 'Other'. - [x] 🟢 M — **Split treemap 'Individual donors' cell into size brackets** — Follow-up to [[FIX-845]]: split the aggregated 'Individual donors' treemap block into size-bracket cells ($200–1k / $1k–10k / etc.). Needs a new/parameterized RPC that restricts to financial_entities.entity_type='individual' (and correctly attributes the small-dollar tail by bracket), then TreemapGraph renders the bracket children under the Individual donors group. <!--id:FIX-848-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **Canonical graph node-id scheme + shared helper** — Graph used THREE un-normalized node-id conventions — connections route emits type-prefixed `official:{uuid}` / `financial_entity:{uuid}`, group route emitted `donor-{uuid}` + raw official uuids, FocusEntity ids are raw uuids. Raw-vs-prefixed `===` made the same real-world entity render as 2-3 distinct nodes by path. Fix: one shared `packages/graph/src/nodeId.ts` (makeNodeId/extractUuid/matchesFocus/isFocusNode), canonical scheme = `type:{uuid}` everywhere; migrate group route (donor-/raw-official/raw-agency/raw-gb ids) + GraphPage repNodes + all ForceGraph ad-hoc `fe.id===n.id || n.id.endsWith(':'+fe.id)` sites to the helper. FocusEntity ids stay raw (saved-view back-compat). Post-G5 wave 2. <!--id:FIX-849-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **Graph per-focus ownership tracking: prune + SharedConnectionsBar** — Two removal defects rooted in raw-vs-prefixed id drift [[FIX-849]]. (1) Entity removal was a state NO-OP — deleting a second focus entity left the graph unchanged. (2) Group removal OVER-pruned — it dropped every edge incident to a member, killing surviving focuses' edges to shared nodes. (3) SharedConnectionsBar was permanently empty (`focusIds.has(e.fromId)` compared raw uuid set vs `official:{uuid}` endpoints). Fix: record {addedNodeIds,addedEdgeKeys} per focus id at fetch time (mirror FIX-827 expansions machinery); on removal drop edges owned solely by the removed focus, then prune nodes with no surviving edge and no surviving owner; SharedConnectionsBar matches via the helper. Post-G5 wave 2. <!--id:FIX-850-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **Graph field-wise node merge (focus-set-invariant donation identity) + live depth chip** — Adding a second focus entity clobbered the first's node payloads via last-write-wins `Map.set` merge — e.g. add Kamala (FFPAC $498M donor), then add Trump (FFPAC opposition-scoped, NO donationTotal) and FFPAC visually lost its Kamala identity. Fix: field-wise merge — derive donationTotal/connectionCount in one post-merge pass over the edge set so they're invariant to fetch order; collapsed = prev && incoming. Also: the depth chip [1|2] in FocusTree was inert — `updateEntity(id,{depth})` changed state but fetchedIds skipped the already-fetched entity, so nothing refetched. Fix: a depth change evicts that entity from fetchedIds + its owned nodes/edges [[FIX-850]] and refetches it surgically. Post-G5 wave 2. <!--id:FIX-851-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **Graph depth-2 connector invariant + edge-guard + client zero-edge drop + truncation badge** — Depth 2 on most officials scattered dozens of tiny 2-node islands. Root cause: the individual-donor bracket loop keyed buckets per-recipient (`c.to_id`) and suppressed donor nodes/edges GLOBALLY, so a hop-2 connector donor (gave to focus A AND neighbor B) got deleted and replaced by an unlinked `bracket:{B}:{tier}` island — B lost its only tie to the focus component. Fix (server): restore the connector invariant — an individual whose donation rows reach >=2 distinct recipients IN THE RESPONSE passes through as a real node (reuse individualMode==='connector' logic); only add a donor to skipEntityKeys when ALL its rows were aggregated (fixes the edge-guard dropping non-donation rows whose endpoint was bracketed). Fix (client): drop non-focus/non-user/non-group nodes with zero incident edges after merge; consume meta.depth2Truncated / partial as a canvas truncation badge (read by nothing today). Post-G5 wave 2 [[FIX-849]]. <!--id:FIX-852-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **Treemap group scoping ignores governingBody (silent global fallback)** — Treemap group mode forwarded only chamber/party/state, but every built-in congress preset (Full Senate/House, chamber+party) filters on governingBody, so nothing was forwarded and the route fell through to the GLOBAL top-500 officials (House + state legislators included). Fix: treemap route learns a governingBody param resolving the cohort via officials.governing_body_id (currentGoverningBodyMembers, the FIX-495/FIX-470 non-polluted path — role_title counts Arizona state rep David Marshall as the 437th US House member); chamber=senate|house aliases to the federal gb slugs. Client maps federal gb slugs to chamber, other gb slugs to governingBody, and shows an explicit unsupported empty state (committee/official_role/empty filter) instead of the silent global request. Cross-ref [[FIX-849]]. <!--id:FIX-853-->

Cross-ref [[FIX-839]]. <!--id:FIX-854-->

- [x] 🟠 S — **Choropleth black map — resolveToken rgb() form unparseable by d3-color** — Choropleth painted an all-black map. `resolveToken` (packages/graph/src/tokens.ts) returned space-separated `rgb(R G B)`; browsers parse it but d3-color does not (`d3.color('rgb(43 74 139)')` -> null -> `interpolateRgb` emits `rgb(0,0,0)`). Prod census: all 369 valued districts painted black, the 67 null districts got the direct .attr fill. Fixed at the tokens layer to emit comma-separated `rgb(R, G, B)` — valid CSS everywhere AND d3-parseable — which also un-blackens every other d3-interpolated fill (treemap blend, sunburst darken). Consumer sweep: withAlpha/toHexColor already tolerant (split on [\\s,/]+). Unit test pins d3.color(formatRgbTriplet(...)) !== null. Rider: scatter Y-axis displays dollars not raw cents. <!--id:FIX-860-->

Donor cells now map entity_type to a real NodeType (individual/pac/corporation); bracket/tail/IE aggregates use bracket:/tail: pseudo ids and the individual_bracket type; PAC cells without a real id use a pseudo id (never a display name); and NodePopup suppresses the profile button for ANY id lacking a uuid. - [x] 🟡 M — **Donation-side industry-tag fan-out: multi-tag donors double-counted across sectors on graph money surfaces** — Sweep rider from the FIX-873 session (which fixed the contract-RECIPIENT-side multi-industry-tag fan-out). The DONATION/donor side has the same class unfixed on 5 surfaces that JOIN entity_tags(industry) on the DONOR and aggregate money WITHOUT a single-tag-per-entity pick, so a donor carrying more than one industry tag has its dollars counted under EVERY tag (or emitted as N duplicate donor rows). Measured multi-tag financial_entities: 1058 local / 1654 prod; of those, 478 local are donation donors (from_id). Sites, all donation donor-side: (1) official_sector_dollars_mv (FIX-506) INNER JOIN entity_tags, GROUP BY (official, et.tag) counts a multi-tag donor under each tag AND drops untagged donors entirely (INNER JOIN); consumers get_group_sector_totals + chord_sector_vote_for_officials. (2) chord_industry_flows_mv (FIX-207/222, nightly) LEFT JOIN, GROUP BY (COALESCE(et.tag,untagged), party_chamber) double-counts multi-tag donors in the platform-wide industry-party chord. (3) chord_industry_flows_for_official(uuid) (FIX-854) GROUP BY COALESCE(et.tag,untagged): FIX-854 only collapsed SAME-tag display-metadata splits, a donor with genuinely DIFFERENT tags still fans out. (4) chord_top_pacs_for_official(uuid,int) GROUP BY fe.id + tag: a multi-tag PAC emitted as N duplicate rows each with full total, LIMIT can be consumed by dups. (5) get_official_donors(uuid) GROUP BY fe.id + tag: multi-tag donor emitted as N duplicate donor rows. Do NOT bundle one fix: each surface has its own display semantics (per-donor row list vs per-sector aggregate vs an INNER-JOIN MV that also drops untagged) and needs its own equality analysis + before/after delta, exactly as FIX-873 did for the contract side. The deterministic fix per site is the FIX-836/777/873 smallest-tag DISTINCT ON pick (or the refresh_group_donor_rollup _gdr_ind MIN() pick, already the SAFE pattern). Verified SAFE this sweep (already single-tag): refresh_group_donor_rollup (_gdr_ind MIN(display_label) per donor), sector_affinity_rebuild_officials (FIX-777/872 DISTINCT ON), and the FIX-704/518/836 donor-rollup machinery. Cross-ref [[FIX-873]] [[FIX-506]] [[FIX-854]] [[FIX-780]] [[FIX-839]] [[FIX-777]]. <!--id:FIX-875-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **Group route live donor fallback pages full entity_connections fan-out — budget-blown on whale cohorts; swap to a cohort-aggregation RPC** — Any official cohort that is NOT gb-materialized (`rollupGbId` null — ad-hoc/custom groups, state-narrowed gb groups per [[FIX-495]], legacy state/party groups, and any gb whose `group_donor_rollup` row is a miss) falls through [[FIX-500]]'s rollup-first read to the live path in `apps/civitics/app/api/graph/group/route.ts`. That path (1) pages EVERY `entity_connections` donation row for the members — including the individual-donor long tail — through `fetchPagedConnections` under `DONOR_FETCH_BUDGET_MS = 8000` with a `maxRows: 50000` ceiling, then (2) resolves every distinct donor's name/entity_type/sector via 100-id `financial_entities` chunks + `fetchIndustryTagsByEntityId`, and only then (3) discards individuals JS-side and takes top-N institutional. Individuals are ~87% of the rows fetched and are thrown away. Local floors (stale clone — prod is larger): senators average ~1,433 donation edges each, p50 79, p90 3,140, max 38,617 — so a random 4-senator cohort has roughly a 1-in-3 chance of containing a top-decile member, one whale alone means 30–50+ sequential pages inside the 8s budget, and stage 2 for thousands of distinct donors is dozens-to-hundreds of concurrent PostgREST chunk queries. `raceWithBudget` also abandons rather than aborts the losing fetch, so it keeps burning pool connections after the flagged response ships. Reproduced 2026-07-24 on `governingBody=senate&state=TX` (2 members, 34,285 edges, Ted Cruz 31,219): LOCAL `donorFetchError: true` / `donorFetchErrorCode: null` at 15.8s, PROD same flag at 8.97s; a repeat local run surfaced the stage-2 failure mode directly (`financial_entities chunk error: TypeError: fetch failed`, 20.7s). This is the [[FIX-497]] fail-open doing its job over a request-path live aggregation that should never have been on the request path. Fix: replace stages 1+2 of the official-branch live path with ONE server-side aggregation RPC over `entity_connections` — same source, same filters, so donorCount / totalDonatedUsd / the top-N list stay byte-identical to a successful live run; uses the existing `entity_connections_donation_to_official_idx` partial covering index. Same caller-swap pattern as [[FIX-774]], same request-path-materialization class the [[FIX-775]] audit closed elsewhere. NOT `official_donor_rollup_mv` ([[FIX-518]]/[[FIX-704]]/[[FIX-809]]/[[FIX-832]]), which was the first candidate: its `rank` is computed over ALL donors including individuals, so `rank <= 200 AND entity_type <> 'individual'` keeps only the institutional donors that outrank the individual long tail — measured on the TX cohort, 196 donors / $1.09M top-25 vs the live path's 1,126 / $16.9M (a 94% understatement, 9 of 25 donors overlapping; Ted Cruz alone has 174 individuals in his top-200, leaving 26 institutional slots). Independently, the MV is built from `financial_relationships` ($32.0M for Cruz) while the route reads `entity_connections` ($41.1M), a 28% source gap. Documented here so the MV is not proposed again for cohort donor display. <!--id:FIX-883-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **BUNDLE AS GROUP discards the row selection — bare-officials handoff aggregates the whole platform; add officialIds mode end-to-end** — The /search explorer's BUNDLE AS GROUP button (`ExplorerActionBar.handleBundleConfirm`) derives only a "dominant kind" from the checked rows and hands off `/graph?groupType=official&groupName=…` — **the selected row ids are discarded**. The dialog says "N items will be sent to the graph as a group", then sends none of them. GraphPage's handoff decode turns that into a bare `{entity_type:'official'}` filter; the group route's legacy no-gb path resolves up to 1,000 active officials (`.limit(1000)`) and calls `get_cohort_top_donors()` at whole-platform scale, which blows the statement timeout (57014) and surfaces as the [[FIX-497]] fail-open donor popup with a member count in the hundreds/thousands. This is the root cause of Craig's 2026-07-24 "4 random senators time out" sighting — NOT the filter-cohort perf class closed by [[FIX-883]]/[[FIX-884]]/[[FIX-885]]. ADD TO GRAPH (the `addEntityIds` path) is unaffected; the lossiness is specific to the bundle path, and predates the Browse redesign — [[FIX-751]] explicitly preserved "exact pre-W1 handoff semantics". Fix: `GroupFilter.officialIds?: string[]` serialized by `graphGroupParams`, decoded by the GraphPage handoff, and honored by the group route's official branch (validate/dedup/cap 50, skip cohort resolution, straight into `get_cohort_top_donors()` — the [[FIX-883]] RPC already takes `uuid[]`, nothing UI-side ever fed it ids). BUNDLE AS GROUP enabled only when every selected row is an official. Ids-groups are in-session only (BrowseState cannot express hand-picked ids, so no saved-view persistence). Client-only shift-click selection groups ([[FIX-826]]) are untouched. <!--id:FIX-886-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **Group route: refuse degenerate/oversized live cohorts (422) instead of aggregate-and-timeout** — Guard the /api/graph/group official branch's NON-materialized (live `get_cohort_top_donors()`) path against cohorts no legitimate UI affordance produces. Two refusals, both structured 422 so [[FIX-490]]'s client error path surfaces a visible notice rather than a blank bubble: (1) a legacy no-gb cohort with NO narrowing at all (no party, no state, no officialIds) — "all active officials" is never a legitimate group, and today it is reachable only via the [[FIX-886]] bug and hand-built URLs — returns `filter_too_broad`; (2) a resolved cohort larger than a measured `MAX_LIVE_COHORT` returns `cohort_too_large` with the memberCount in the body. The gb rollup-first path ([[FIX-500]]) is untouched — materialized cohorts read a single indexed top-N regardless of size, so the guard applies only where the request-path aggregation actually runs. Cap chosen from measured RPC latency across cohort sizes on prod (warm), with clear headroom above the largest legitimate live cohort (House-class ~436 must pass). Complements [[FIX-883]], which made the aggregation server-side but left it unbounded in cohort size. <!--id:FIX-887-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **tag-groups route silently truncates at the PostgREST 1000-row cap** — `/api/graph/tag-groups` aggregates proposal topic counts in JS over an unbounded `.select()`, on the stated assumption that 'the row volume is bounded (~1.4k topic rows total)'. That assumption expired: local now has 5,600 qualifying rows and prod ~7,500 after [[FIX-889]]. PostgREST caps a plain select at `max_rows=1000`, so the route sees ~1,000 arbitrary rows and reports counts that are wrong by roughly 6x — measured local sum of returned counts was 986 against 5,600 real rows. Every displayed tag-group count is therefore understated, and low-volume topics can fall below the `count >= 10` floor and vanish from the browse list entirely. Discovered while verifying [[FIX-889]]; pre-existing and independent of it. Fix is a server-side GROUP BY (an RPC returning one jsonb aggregate, per the standing `reference_postgrest_rpc_row_cap` rule that set-returning RPCs must not be `.range()`-paginated), not a bigger `.limit()`. <!--id:FIX-892-->

The count therefore returned 0 from day one and the tile has always read 'queue idle'. Consequence: 44 abandoned `processing` claims (all `task_type='tag'`, claimed 2026-04-29, orphaned by an interrupted drain wave) sat invisible for three months — invisible to `pending_tag`/`pending_summary` (not pending) and to `in_progress` (never existed). Fixed: `getPipelines()` now reports `processing` and `stale_processing` (claim older than `ENRICHMENT_STALE_CLAIM_MINUTES` = 60, a deliberately looser threshold than `data:drain:status`'s 10-minute reclaim default — the script answers 'what can I reclaim now', the dashboard answers 'does this look abandoned'). The threshold governs only the warn; `processing` is reported unconditionally. `backlogTotal`/`backlogTone` stay pending-driven. Note the persisted `status_snapshot` payload also carries this shape, so `/api/claude/status/core` serves the old key until the next 10-min cron write — self-healing, renders 'queue idle' in the interim. Not fixed here and deliberately out of scope: surfacing permanently-`failed` rows (148), and whether a scheduled reclaim sweep deserves a cron. <!--id:FIX-924-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **Vercel billing math was wrong: Pro includes $20 of usage, so the dashboard showed $31.38 on a $0.00-overage month** — Craig-stated 2026-08-16: Vercel Pro is \$20/month AND THAT \$20 BUYS \$20 OF INCLUDED USAGE, so the bill is \$20 base + max(0, metered usage - \$20). The snapshot and the dashboard both treated the ENTIRE EffectiveCost sum as money owed. EffectiveCost is the LIST VALUE of all consumption PLUS the prorated Pro subscription line, so the headline was the gross list price of everything — and every dollar of it sat below the included credit. **Measured on prod 2026-08-16 (platform_usage_snapshot, fetched_at 03:13 UTC): the card read \$31.38/mo when the actual projected billable overage was \$0.00 with \$8.62 of the credit still unspent.** BEFORE: gross MTD \$15.1852, projected \$31.3828, displayed as the Vercel cost. AFTER: usage MTD \$5.5078 (gross minus the \$9.6774 Pro line), credit remaining \$14.49, projected usage \$11.38, projected billable overage \$0.00, projected total bill \$20.00. **This is a DETECTION defect, not a cosmetic one.** A headline that reads \$31 on a perfectly normal month cannot alarm — there is no band you can put on it that separates healthy from burning, which is part of why the 08-15 burn had nowhere to show up. **The Pro line must come out FIRST.** The FOCUS charge export carries the subscription as its own ServiceName (Pro), accruing \$20/31 = \$0.6452/day — verified against prod where day 15 read exactly \$9.6774. That line is the SUBSCRIPTION, not consumption, so it does not draw down the credit the subscription buys; counting it would peg the account at 100 pct of credit from the first of every month. Added plan_base_usd as a first-class field on VercelUsage rather than deriving it downstream from cost_breakdown, which is sliced to top-8 before persistence ([[FIX-1041]]). Matching is anchored /^(hobby|pro|enterprise)\$/i, not a substring — a substring test on pro swallows Fluid Provisioned Memory and silently inflates remaining credit by a real consumption line. **New pure module packages/db/src/vercel-billing.ts** (no clock, no network, no DB) with table-driven tests whose first row is the live prod reading, so the old interpretation cannot be reintroduced silently. **Two new platform_limits rows:** included_usage_usd (consumption vs the \$20 credit — finally a percentage bar that means something, warns at 80 pct) and billable_overage_usd (THE headline). monthly_spend_usd is KEPT unchanged as the gross list value because it is the leading indicator and the only figure that reconciles against the Vercel dashboard. The \$20 lives in platform_limits.included_limit and is READ BY the collector, so retuning the credit is an UPDATE and not a deploy. **CYCLE-BASIS CAVEAT, stated rather than hidden:** getVercelUsage queries charges from the first of the CALENDAR month and the Pro line prorates over 31, so the projection is calendar-month; the Vercel usage page separately describes an Aug 14 - Sep 14 cycle and nothing in the charges API discriminates between the two. daysInCycle is an argument, not a hard-coded 31, so correcting the basis is a one-line call-site change. **USER ITEM (open):** is there a hard page-me-at-\$X number for true overage? billable_overage_usd.included_limit is provisionally 20 (page when the bill doubles) with warning at 50 pct = \$10/mo; answering the question is an UPDATE. Cross-ref [[FIX-648]], [[FIX-1041]], [[FIX-1044]]. <!--id:FIX-1046-->

- [x] 🟡 M — **Per-metric rates + self-counted labeling + companion-row display flag consumed** — The R4b half of the [[FIX-1089]] rate work: every payload field the data plane added is now READ by the card. - [x] 🟠 M — **Supabase disk denominator flaps across snapshot ticks: Disk row wobbles 58 to 87 percent; stabilize the Prometheus source and settle capacity_pct** — Prod evidence (2026-08-24 read of platform_usage_snapshot, 30-day retention): the /data provisioned-disk figure the Costs card divides by has exactly TWO values in history, 37,930,876,928 and 56,950,861,824. The step from the first to the second at 2026-08-19 08:56 UTC is a genuine Supabase disk grow (40 GB to 60 GB nominal; the 1.5x step is the auto-scale ratio). Since that step, 160 of 161 ticks carried the new value and exactly ONE did not: 2026-08-23 01:20:27 UTC reported the PRE-resize size, which put supabase.disk_used_bytes.included_limit at 37.93 GB and db_size_bytes.display_limit at the same, so the public Disk Utilization row read 87.26 percent instead of 58.12 and capacity_pct read 83.88 instead of 55.87. It stayed wrong for 81 minutes until the 02:41 tick overwrote it. Root shape: getSupabasePrometheusMetrics writes whatever a single scrape says straight into platform_limits, which is DURABLE config, so one divergent scrape poisons a public row until the next tick and poisons the persisted snapshot forever. Two defects behind it. (1) parsePrometheusText SUMS every row matching mountpoint /data, so if the endpoint ever exposed two /data filesystems the denominator would silently become their sum with nothing to say so; the live endpoint today has exactly one row (device /dev/nvme1n1) so the sum is currently a no-op, but it is an unguarded fabrication path. (2) there is no corroboration on a SHRINK: a provisioned disk grows on auto-scale and effectively never shrinks, yet a lone scrape reporting a smaller disk is applied immediately. Fix: require exactly one matching filesystem row (refuse 0 or 2+ rather than sum), and gate a shrink on two consecutive agreeing scrapes so a single divergent reading is a no-op. Also settle capacity_pct, which cc-83 left computed and rendered nowhere. <!--id:FIX-1104-->

- [x] 🔴 S — **status/core + /quality return 500 whenever the snapshot read times out — withDbTimeout's timeout sentinel is truthy, so every !snapshot guard takes the wrong branch** — LIVE ON PROD, observed 2026-08-29 06:20 UTC while verifying [[FIX-090]]: GET /api/claude/status/core returned 500 with an empty body, four times in 45 seconds. Pre-existing since fd233013 (2026-05-18, [[FIX-297]]); nothing in FIX-090 touched the failing block, which added only a daily_counts field to the response object. ROOT CAUSE: withDbTimeout resolves its timeout branch to the literal { data: null, error: Error } cast 'as unknown as T' (apps/civitics/src/lib/supabase-check.ts:61,77). That envelope is the correct shape for a PostgREST builder, but readStatusSnapshot is a PLAIN promise that resolves to a StatusSnapshotRow or null -- it has already unwrapped the envelope. So on timeout the caller does not get null, it gets a TRUTHY object with no fetched_at and no payload, while the type annotation says StatusSnapshotRow | null and hides it completely. The failure then cascades through three guards in a row, each of which reads correct: (1) fresh = Date.now() - new Date(undefined).getTime() < STALE evaluates NaN < n = false, so a perfectly good cache decision becomes 'stale' and the route falls through to live recompute; (2) the live recompute is capped at SNAPSHOT_FALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS = 5000 but genuinely costs 10.1-17.8s on prod (measured, status_snapshot.query_time_ms over the last five rows), so on this path it ALWAYS times out -- the fallback is not a safety net, it is a guaranteed miss; (3) the last-resort branch 'if (!snapshot) return 503' does not fire, because the sentinel is truthy, so the route assigns payload = snapshot.payload = undefined and dies on payload.version with TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined. A 503 that was deliberately written for exactly this case is unreachable. Observed log line proves the truthy branch: '[status/core] live-compute fallback timed out after 5000 ms { fetched_at: undefined, served_stale: true }'. THREE CALL SITES share the misuse -- core/route.ts:49, quality/route.ts:46, dashboard/page.tsx:123. The two API routes 500. dashboard/page.tsx does NOT, but only by luck: its whole body sits in a try/catch that returns null, so /dashboard degrades to a client-fetch render and still serves 200, which is why this has been invisible. TRIGGER is DB slowness, not traffic: the 2s snapshot read only times out when the box is under load, which is why it surfaced during the 06:00 UTC nightly window with refresh_derived_mvs and entity_connections_rebuild both running, the same window where the pooler was refusing connections outright with ECHECKOUTTIMEOUT. So this fires precisely when the dashboard is most needed -- during an incident. FIX SHAPE: make withDbTimeout's timeout value distinguishable rather than adding defensive checks at each call site. Either return a unique sentinel the caller must narrow, or add a withDbTimeoutValue variant for already-unwrapped promises that resolves to null on timeout. Then the existing !snapshot guards are correct as written. Also worth reconsidering: a 5s cap in front of a 10-17s operation is not a timeout, it is an unconditional failure -- either raise it above the measured cost or drop the live-recompute fallback and serve stale. Same class as project_withdbtimeout_any_infers_unknown but a different mechanism: there the generic inferred unknown, here the 'as unknown as T' cast makes a structurally wrong value type-compatible. Cross-ref [[FIX-297]], [[FIX-327]], [[FIX-1094]], [[FIX-090]]. <!--id:FIX-1120-->
- [x] 🔴 S — **Transparency stat cards render as blank skeletons on most prod ticks — getDatabase's votes exact count loses to the snapshot's own concurrency, and one partial count blanks all four cards** — MEASURED ON PROD 2026-08-29 while verifying [[FIX-090]]: 6 of 7 retained status_snapshot ticks carry database.error = 'count failed for: votes' (one also failed proposals). Consequence is NOT a missing number, it is FOUR MISSING CARDS. getDatabase sets partial:true on the whole database object when ANY of its 11 counts fails; DashboardClient does 'const db = isPartial(database) ? null : database' and passes loading={!db} to every StatCard; StatCard returns its animate-pulse skeleton when loading. So a single failed count on one of eleven blanks Officials, Open Proposals, Votes and Donation Flow simultaneously. Confirmed by headless render against the live vercel.app origin, cache-disabled: 5 skeletons, 0 stat-card labels, 0 hero numbers, 0 sparklines. THE COUNT IS NOT SLOW AND THAT IS THE WHOLE POINT. Measured on prod the same minute: SELECT count(*) FROM votes = 261 ms via psql; the same count through PostgREST as the app issues it = 555 ms; and a faithful replay of getDatabase's entire 11-way fan-out from outside the lambda completed in 559 ms WALL CLOCK with all 11 returning 206 and correct values. Against an 8s statement_timeout on the authenticator role, that is a 14x margin. The failure only appears INSIDE computeStatusPayload, whose total is 8.9-17.8s (avg 11.4s over the retained ticks), because that function fans out ELEVEN SECTIONS in parallel and getDatabase's eleven counts are only a fraction of the concurrent PostgREST requests in flight. So this is self-inflicted contention on a Small instance, not query cost, which is why it is INTERMITTENT: a manually dispatched tick at 08:09:32 came back clean (votes 969302, database.error NULL) four minutes after the 08:05:18 tick failed. Same code, same data, different luck. NOTE THE INTERACTION WITH [[FIX-1095]]: switching votes/officials/proposals to count exact was correct (reltuples was 31 percent wrong) and the fix is NOT to revert it -- an exact count that costs 261 ms is affordable by any measure. The defect is that the payload computes eleven sections at once with no concurrency bound, and that a single count failure is escalated to a whole-section partial that a consumer then escalates again to a whole-ROW blackout. FIX SHAPE, three independent levers, any one of which helps: (a) bound the fan-out in computeStatusPayload (the counts do not need to race each other); (b) make getDatabase report per-count failure instead of poisoning the section, so a failed votes count blanks the Votes card and nothing else; (c) make StatCard's loading state per-metric rather than per-section in DashboardClient, so a card with a good number renders it. (b) is the smallest and most valuable -- it converts a four-card blackout into one honest missing figure. Also worth noting the retention interaction: status_snapshot prunes at 24h, so there is no history to tell how long this has been happening; it has been invisible since [[FIX-1095]] landed 2026-08-22 precisely because nothing retains the evidence. Cross-ref [[FIX-1095]], [[FIX-297]], [[FIX-1120]], [[FIX-090]], [[FIX-1077]]. <!--id:FIX-1121-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **daily_platform_counts row is labelled source=observed even when the tick only wrote some of its metrics** — Found immediately after [[FIX-090]] shipped, by the [[FIX-1121]] partial tick. recordDailyCounts correctly OMITS officials and votes from the upsert when the database section came back partial -- that guard works and is what preserved the good reconstructed values on prod 2026-08-29 08:05. But the upsert still sends source: 'observed' unconditionally, so the row ends up labelled observed while two of its four metrics are still the reconstructed backfill values. Verified on prod: the 08-29 row read source=observed with officials 37242 / votes 969302 carried over from the migration backfill, not from that tick. Nothing reads source today, so there is no user-visible wrong number -- but this is a PROVENANCE label on a feature whose entire design rationale is refusing to present reconstructed data as observed, so a label that lies is worse here than in most places. Fix is to send source only when the metrics that define it were actually observed this tick (i.e. gate it on the same dbOk the metric writes are gated on), letting the existing value stand otherwise. Consider also whether one row-level source can honestly describe a row whose four metrics have different provenances -- a per-metric provenance, or simply dropping the column in favour of inferring 'reconstructed' from the backfill's day range, may be more truthful than a single flag. Cross-ref [[FIX-090]], [[FIX-1121]]. <!--id:FIX-1122-->

- [x] 🟡 S — **session:worktree:done strands merged branch when the dir removal loses to a Windows lock** — When `git worktree remove` + the FIX-876 backoff loop + the contained `fs.rm` fallback all lose to a transient AV/indexer lock on the freshly-hardlinked node_modules, `done()` used to `die()` inside the fs.rm catch — BEFORE the branch-deletion block. Result: a fully-MERGED `feature/fix-*` branch pointer was left behind alongside the stranded dir (observed on fix-447), and the failure message only said 'fs.rm fallback failed … left intact' without telling the operator the git side could still be finished or that a re-run clears it. Fix (this FIX): branch deletion now runs regardless of the dir outcome — a branch confirmed an ancestor of origin/main is force-deleted (`-D`, a stronger guarantee than `-d`'s local-only merge check which wrongly refuses when the primary checkout's main is behind origin/main); the registry is pruned; and on a stranded dir the script prints a clear 'DIR is LOCKED / git side is otherwise clean / re-run `session:worktree:done <id>` once the lock clears or delete <path> manually' message and exits non-zero. Directory deletion itself stays gated on the removal actually succeeding (no fake success). Backoff retry was already added by [[FIX-876]]; this closes the residual half-succeed + orphaned-merged-branch gap. <!--id:FIX-877-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **session:worktree:done recovery re-run fails-closed on a de-registered orphan dir** — Follow-up to [[FIX-877]], surfaced by its own live teardown test. When the first teardown strands the dir on a Windows lock, git has ALREADY de-registered the worktree (git worktree remove succeeds at the admin level before the fs.rm loses to the lock), so the dir is a de-registered ORPHAN still on disk. The FIX-877 stranded-dir message says 're-run pnpm session:worktree:done <id>' — but that plain re-run FAILS: done()'s porcelain safety check runs 'git -C <dir> status --porcelain', which errors 'not a working tree' on the orphan, so cleanIgnoringArtifacts is false and it refuses without --force ('could not read git status / refusing to remove a dirty worktree'). The working recovery is --force (per the FIX-876 memo), which the message did NOT mention. Also, on that path the backoff loop wastes ~34s pointlessly retrying 'git worktree remove' against a permanent 'not a working tree' error. Fix: detect the de-registered-orphan case (path absent from 'git worktree list') and, for it, skip the git-worktree-remove retries and go straight to the containment-guarded fs.rm (no --force needed) — making the plain recovery re-run in FIX-877's message actually work. Confirmed live: the FIX-877 teardown of fix-sweep-0722 stranded, plain re-run refused, --force succeeded. <!--id:FIX-879-->

- [x] 🟠 M — **Shared chunked-by-ids fetch helper (fetchChunkedByIds); migrate three call sites** — `.in()` over an unbounded id list is the most-repeated bug in this codebase — four independent instances ([[FIX-509]], [[FIX-514]], [[FIX-774]], [[FIX-899]]). Mechanism is always the same and always silent: a large id list builds a request URL past the gateway's header limit, Kong 414s (`URI too long`) before PostgREST sees it, `withDbTimeout` returns `{data:null}`, and a `?? []` fallback turns the failure into an empty result. **The bound is URL LENGTH at roughly 200 ids, not the 1,000-row PostgREST cap.** [[FIX-899]] is the case that forced a structural fix: `app/officials/page.tsx` fetched tags with one `.in()` over ~1,000 officials (~40 KB URL) and every official card rendered zero tag pills, silently, for months — surfacing only because [[FIX-897]] added industry pills to that exact surface and they did not appear. Two facts set the shape: (a) a warning comment 15 lines ABOVE the bug already described this precise trap for a different fetch, and the fetch below it did it anyway — comments do not enforce; (b) the pattern had already been hand-written three times locally ([[FIX-732]] `ID_CHUNK` + local helper in `api/graph/connections/route.ts`, [[FIX-778]] in `api/graph/agency-staffing/route.ts`, [[FIX-899]] inline in `officials/page.tsx`) — not a knowledge problem. **Deliverable:** one shared `fetchChunkedByIds` in `apps/civitics/src/lib/paginate.ts`, beside `fetchAllRows`, so 'how do I read a lot of rows' and 'how do I read by a lot of ids' are found together. Contract: default chunk size 200 via an exported named constant (`ID_CHUNK_SIZE`); **returns a result OBJECT carrying rows AND failed-chunk info, never a bare array** — a helper that returns `T[]` and swallows a failed chunk reproduces the bug class one layer down; does NOT throw by default (some surfaces legitimately prefer partial data) but offers opt-in `strict` for callers where partial is worse than nothing; dedupes and drops empty/nullish ids before chunking; short-circuits an empty list to zero requests rather than issuing `.in("id", [])`; optional per-chunk timeout label so it composes with `withDbTimeout`. **Three migrations only** — the three sites above, where correct behaviour is already known and verified so migration is provably behaviour-preserving. The remaining id-list surface is a separate audit. <!--id:FIX-901-->

The result contract is unchanged for any input: rows in chunk order, `failed` in chunk-index order, `chunkCount` unaffected, and `strict` still issues EVERY chunk before throwing (a pool that cancelled the queue on first error would change failure semantics, not just pacing; `paginate.test.ts` pins it). KNOWN LIMIT, documented in the JSDoc rather than fixed: the cap is per CALL, so a route issuing N concurrent `fetchChunkedByIds` calls can have N × maxConcurrency in flight — `app/api/graph/connections/route.ts` does exactly that with seven concurrent calls. A shared module-level limiter was considered and left out of scope. Measured: all three existing call sites are at or under 6 chunks on their heaviest local inputs (officials index ≤ 1,000 ids = 5; agency-staffing 124 active federal agencies = 1; connections at depth 2 on the top-degree official = 5 raw-financial / 3 official / 3 proposal), so none of their timing changes. <!--id:FIX-926-->

- [x] 🟡 M — **No launcher-side runtime record for GHA-launched pipelines — reaped data_sync_log spans are read as runtimes and there is no second source to correct them** — **Found while correcting [[FIX-944]]'s runtimes during [[FIX-968]] (2026-08-06).** There is an asymmetry in how we can know when a pipeline actually stopped. For anything **pg_cron** launched, `cron.job_run_details` records `start_time` / `end_time` / `status` / `return_message` **from the launcher's side, independently of anything the job wrote about itself** — so a job that died without closing its own log row can still be timed exactly. For anything **GitHub-Actions** launched (`nightly.yml`, `rebuild-entity-connections.yml`, `usaspending-bulk.yml`, `fec-backfill.yml`, …) there is **no equivalent**: the only record is `data_sync_log`, which is *self-reported*. When the process is SIGTERM'd at the GHA cap, OOMs, or the runner is evicted, it never writes a terminal row, the row stays `status='running'`, and the only thing that ever touches it again is the reaper. **And the reaper stamps its own clock** — `packages/data/src/scripts/mark-killed.ts` writes `completed_at: now` (line ~146) — so the resulting `started_at`..`completed_at` span is bounded by **when the reaper ran**, not by when the work stopped. **This has already produced a materially wrong diagnosis.** [[FIX-944]]'s bullet reported its failing runs as 20h15m / 20h22m / 20h09m and concluded "the nightly's startup reaps the still-running rollup … the job can never win: it needs longer than the gap to the next nightly" — a causal story that shaped [[FIX-950]]'s framing too. `cron.job_run_details` (runids 105/116/123/129) shows those runs were **6h08m / 6h00m / 6h00m / 6h00m**, every one starting 09:00 and dying at ~15:00 on the `postgres` role's 6h `statement_timeout` — already dead ~14 hours before the nightly that supposedly reaped them. The nightly never killed that job. **That was correctable ONLY because `donor-rollup-refresh` happens to be a pg_cron job.** Had the same reap landed on a GHA-launched pipeline — which is where the reaper primarily operates, on `nightly_cron` / `fec_bulk` rows — there would have been **no second source and the wrong duration would be permanently uncorrectable**. Note `data_sync_log` already carries several `reaped` / `reaped_orphan` GHA rows in exactly this shape (e.g. `fec_bulk` on 08-02/08-03/08-05, `nightly_cron` 08-03), whose spans are being read as runtimes today. **The truth does exist externally** — the GHA API returns `run_started_at`, `updated_at` and `conclusion` per run (`gh api /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/{id}`, plus per-job timings via `/jobs`) — it is simply never joined to `data_sync_log`, and cannot be joined after the fact because **no run identifier is recorded**: neither `packages/data/src/pipelines/sync-log.ts` nor `mark-killed.ts` reads `GITHUB_RUN_ID`, `GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT` or `GITHUB_WORKFLOW`. **Fix shape, cheapest first:** (1) record `GITHUB_RUN_ID` / `GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT` / `GITHUB_WORKFLOW` into `data_sync_log.metadata` at `startSync()` — a few lines in `sync-log.ts`, no migration, and it makes every future row joinable to the authoritative external record forever; (2) stop overloading `completed_at` for reaped rows — either a distinct `reaped_at` column or a `metadata.reaped=true` marker plus leaving `completed_at` NULL, so a span can never again be mistaken for a runtime (note `check_rollup_freshness()` and the [[FIX-234]] canary both read these columns, so change them together); (3) optionally a `metadata.last_progress_at` heartbeat written per chunk/phase, which bounds the true stop time to one heartbeat interval even with no external source. **Rule worth encoding wherever these get read:** a `reaped_orphan` row's `started_at`..`completed_at` span is an upper bound on *reaper latency*, never a runtime — `cron.job_run_details` is authoritative for pg_cron work and the GHA API for workflow work. See `docs/audits/2026-08-06-fix968-cron-window-envelopes.md` §6b for the corrected FIX-944 run table and the full derivation. Cross-ref [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-950]], [[FIX-290]], [[FIX-462]], [[FIX-234]], [[FIX-969]]. <!--id:FIX-971-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **donor-rollup drain stops at exactly 600 recipients per window with 27–32% of its budget unspent, and its cursor timestamp reports the chunk's START not its end** — **Found auditing the first day of the [[FIX-968]] `0 9,12 * * *` schedule (prod runids 181/182, 2026-08-06).** Two defects, unrelated causes. **(1) The 600 ceiling.** Both windows cleared EXACTLY 600 recipients and stopped at 601. Not a `LIMIT`, not an array cap, not a dirty-set fetch that is never re-fetched — the fetch is uncapped and correctly built sets of 10,286 and 9,686. 600 is `3 × c_chunk_size`, produced by the [[FIX-944]] predictive budget guard `v_elapsed + (v_max_chunk × 1.25) > c_budget` doing exactly what it was designed to do at a quantum that no longer fits: runid 181 `11,770 + 1.25×4,247 = 17,079 > 16,200`; runid 182 `11,054 + 1.25×6,546 = 19,236 > 16,200`. It repeats at exactly 600 because it is arithmetic, not coincidence — for any roughly uniform per-chunk cost `c`, three chunks complete and the fourth is refused whenever `3,812 s < c < 4,985 s`, and prod sits at `c ≈ 3,900 s`. The cost is **quantization**: the guard can only stop BETWEEN chunks, so the least budget it can leave unspent is one reservation (`1.25 × slowest chunk`), which at a 65-min chunk is **27–32% of the window**. Those constants were correct when FIX-944 set them — the 07-31 sweep (runid 135) ran 42 chunks with a slowest chunk of 749 s, where the same reservation costs 936 s, under 6%. **(2) The phantom 1h49m tail.** runid 182's last cursor write is stamped 13:31:23 while the run ended 15:20:29, reading as 1h49m of stall after the final commit. It is **chunk 3 running**. Proof by exact equality: `15:20:29 − 13:31:23 = 6,546 s`, precisely the run's recorded `slowest_chunk_seconds`. The cursor UPDATE wrote `updated_at = NOW()`, and `NOW()` is `transaction_timestamp()`; in this procedure every chunk runs in its own transaction that BEGINS immediately after the previous chunk's COMMIT, so `NOW()` inside chunk N's cursor write returns the moment chunk N *started* — one whole chunk early. The cursor VALUE was never wrong; only its timestamp, by up to one chunk. That is a live observability defect, not cosmetics: `pipeline_state.updated_at` is the natural thing for an operator or a future stall detector to read, and during a slow chunk it reports a working sweep as idle for over an hour. It cost a full diagnostic pass. **Fix (migration `20260806230000_fix972_donor_rollup_chunk_quantum.sql`):** `c_chunk_size` 200 → 50 so the quantum is ~7% of the budget instead of ~24%; chunk size becomes overridable via a `civitics.donor_rollup_chunk_size` SESSION GUC mirroring the existing `civitics.donor_rollup_budget_seconds` contract (session-scoped so it can never strand a widened setting into the scheduled job, and clamped to [1,1000] because 0 would make the loop never advance while holding an advisory lock); `NOW()` → `clock_timestamp()` on both cursor-write paths; `chunk_size` + `recipients_done` added to run metadata so a future rate detector has something to read. Smaller chunks also shrink the blast radius of the outer 6h role-level `statement_timeout` backstop — a run cancelled mid-chunk discards that chunk's uncommitted work, which was up to 109 min and is now ~27 min. Body rebuilt from the CURRENT live prod definition (`pg_get_functiondef` md5 `b21f8f65452415e4dcd55d725691e6ef`, verified byte-identical to the FIX-944 migration text and to local) so the FIX-776/777/779/836/868 layering is preserved rather than reverted. **Deliberately NOT changed: `c_budget` stays 4h30m.** The 5,400 s between it and the 6h `statement_timeout` is real and unused, but spending it is a SCHEDULING decision, not a defect fix — prod runs **chain back-to-back** (runid 182 began 1 s after 181 ended; the 12:00 firing was deferred while 181 held the job, so the FIX-968 backstop does NOT log `status='skipped'` as its migration predicted, it runs a second full window), so a longer window pushes the second run deep into US active hours. Left for a human call. Cross-ref [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-951]], [[FIX-965]], [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-973]], [[FIX-589]]. <!--id:FIX-972-->
- [x] 🔴 L — **donor-rollup per-chunk cost regressed ~9× per FR row between 07-31 and 08-06 with FR vacuum-clean — this, not the chunk ceiling, sets the drain ETA** — **Found while diagnosing the [[FIX-972]] 600-recipient ceiling (2026-08-06). This is the finding that contradicts the premise that removing that ceiling would give 2–3× throughput.** Measured on prod: the **07-31** sweep (runid 135, `complete`) cleared **8,381 recipients in 42 chunks in 3h08m** = **1.35 s/recipient**; the **08-06** sweeps (runids 181+182, both `partial`) cleared **1,200 recipients in 6 chunks in 6h20m** = **19.0 s/recipient**. **Density is not the explanation** — counted as they actually were at the time, the 07-31 dirty set carried 3,127,537 rows over 7,402 recipients (**422 rows/recipient**) and today's carries **584**, a 1.38× difference against a 14× wall-clock difference. Normalizing for it still leaves **~9× per FR row (3.6 ms → 33.0 ms)**. The documented playbook for "this job went slow again" ([[FIX-943]], recorded in the header of `packages/data/src/scripts/donor-rollup-sweep.ts`) is `financial_relationships` dead tuples / visibility-map decay — **checked and clean**: FR is 0.72% dead, 94.1% all-visible, last `VACUUM (ANALYZE)` 2026-08-06 00:56. **So this is not FIX-943 recurring, and the existing playbook has no next step.** Leading hypothesis is **working set vs cache**: FR donation rows grew **+52% in six days** (4,253,944 → 6,457,535; 2,203,591 created since 07-31, from the 08-03/08-04 FEC bulk loads of ~1.1M rows each). The table is now 10.27M rows / 448,249 pages / ~3.5 GB with a 616 MB `financial_relationships_donor_rollup_idx`, against **256 MB `shared_buffers`** on the Pro Small ([[FIX-589]]). `donor_rollup_rebuild_recipients()` has six arms that each re-scan the same recipients' rows, so one 200-recipient chunk moves on the order of GBs of buffer traffic through a 256 MB cache — consistent with the FIX-968 audit finding the backend pinned on `IO/DataFileRead` for 64+ min. **Explicitly NOT yet proven:** an `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` of arm 1 over 25 real remaining recipients returned in **47 ms** with `shared hit=11674 read=2` — but against a cache warmed by the preceding density query, so it measures only the warm path and does not settle the cold-cache question. Proving it needs per-arm cold-cache profiling, which cannot be done read-only on prod; local Docker (4.37M FR donation rows) can host it. **Why it matters:** at 19.0 s/recipient the 9,086 remaining recipients need ~48 h of pure compute. Daily throughput is `wall-clock spent × rate`, and prod runs chain (see [[FIX-972]]), so the box works continuously 09:00→15:20 and clears ~1,200/day — meaning **~1,200/day is close to what the current window genuinely allows, and the 600-per-window ceiling was costing ~33%, not 50–66%.** At the 07-31 rate the entire remaining set would clear in a single ~3.4 h run. So the cost regression, not the chunk quantum, is the lever worth the next unit of effort, and it is the strongest concrete evidence yet for the [[FIX-589]] instance-size conversation. Sequence: profile per-arm cost under a cold cache, attribute it, then choose between (a) more `shared_buffers` / a larger instance, (b) [[FIX-970]]'s dirty-set scoping (~30% of row work), (c) [[FIX-969]]'s delta-apply. **⚠ MEASUREMENT 2026-08-07, from the [[FIX-974]] bulk run — the regression is ACCESS PATTERN, not the box, so option (a) is NOT indicated by this evidence.** The same work in a `to_id`-RANGE, set-based regime ran on the SAME instance the SAME night at **0.060 s/recipient** (all 15,316 recipients in 926 s, one CALL) against the 19.0 s/recipient measured here — **~314×** — and the per-chunk `EXPLAIN` is an `Index Only Scan` at **0.118 ms/FR row vs the 33.0 ms/row above**. Two causes, both properties of the per-recipient regime rather than of the hardware: (1) `to_id = ANY(uuid[])` over scattered uuids is N independent index descents plus scattered heap access, where a range predicate on the same index is one dense walk; (2) `fr.to_type='official'` is not in `financial_relationships_donor_rollup_idx`, so arms 2–6 forced a heap visit per row — and that predicate turns out to be **exactly** `to_id IN (SELECT id FROM officials)` (measured: 0 exceptions in either direction across all 6,457,535 rows in the index scope), so resolving it off the index keeps the whole scan index-only. Cache warming was visible in-run (62.5 s/chunk over the first 10, **13.7 s/chunk** over the last 22), which is corroborating evidence for the working-set hypothesis in this bullet but *not* evidence that the box is undersized for this work. **This bullet stays OPEN**: FIX-974 routes around the regression without explaining why the per-recipient path went 3.6 ms → 33.0 ms per row in six days, and that path is still what the daily trickle uses. The per-arm cold-cache profiling asked for above is still unwritten. Cross-ref [[FIX-974]], [[FIX-972]], [[FIX-943]], [[FIX-951]], [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-969]], [[FIX-970]], [[FIX-589]], [[FIX-884]]. - [x] 🟠 M — **fec_bulk indiv resume cursor is an array offset, so a FEC republish laps all in-flight progress** — [[FIX-754]]'s cursor is an OFFSET into a rebuilt rows array (`StageProgress.cursor` + `total_rows`, resolved by `resolveResumeCursor`), not a content key. Row order is not stable across a republish, so `planCycleResume` correctly returns 'stale' and `clearRunState` discards the cursor whenever FEC republishes the cycle's indiv file — which it does WEEKLY, Sundays ~15:20 UTC. That makes the loop structurally non-convergent for any stage whose remaining work exceeds one night's budget: the republish always laps the progress. MEASURED 2026-08-08: prod `fec_bulk_run_state` holds cycle 2026 donor-entities at cursor 484,000/840,338 (started 08-06T06:42, updated 08-08T04:30) at a measured 52.3-67.7 s per 4,000-row chunk — ~237 min for the full stage against a 150-min nightly job budget, i.e. ~2 nights for stage 1 of 4 — and the 2026-08-09 republish resets it to 0. Committed work is NOT invalidated by a republish: the republished file is cumulative for the cycle and every write is an idempotent upsert on a stable arbiter (`donor_fingerprint` / `financial_relationships_relcycle_unique`). Only the OFFSET is invalidated. Direction: checkpoint the last-committed CONTENT KEY (donor fingerprint under a stable sort order) and resume by key, which survives a superset file; `bulkUpsert` would sort rows by that key and binary-search the resume point rather than slicing at an integer. Same family as [[FIX-991]]'s watermark ratchet — progress must be durable against the INVALIDATION cadence, not merely against process death. Note this also removes the `total_rows` mismatch reset, which fires on any night when DB churn changes the rebuilt array length. Cross-ref [[FIX-995]], [[FIX-754]], [[FIX-991]], [[FIX-903]], [[FIX-998]]. <!--id:FIX-999-->
