- [x] 🔴 M — **The donor-rollup budget guard is structurally incapable of firing on the run that takes the site down** — On 2026-08-08 jobid 24 run 195 ran 12:28:39 to 18:28:46 (6h00m06s), was killed by the 6h role statement_timeout, and committed ZERO chunks: pipeline_state.donor_rollup_watermark.updated_at is still 12:28:38 holding the cursor written by the PREVIOUS run. Six hours of flat-out I/O, no durable progress, and the public site served statement timeouts and 503s throughout; by 18:00 the Supabase SQL editor could not open a connection at all. This is a different and more severe failure than the job-vs-job starvation [[FIX-969]] describes, and rescheduling cron jobs does nothing for it. Cause: the FIX-944 predictive guard reads IF v_chunk_no is greater than 0 AND v_elapsed + v_max_chunk * 1.25 is greater than c_budget THEN EXIT. It is skipped entirely before chunk 1 and can only be evaluated BETWEEN chunks, so a run whose FIRST chunk exceeds the whole window never evaluates it even once. Run 195's chunk 1 was 50 recipients and ran past 21,600s against a slowest-ever chunk of 5,447s recorded three hours earlier. The guard is not broken; it cannot fire in the case it exists for (rule C3 -- cf. [[FIX-972]] which retuned the same guard's quantum, [[FIX-965]] and [[FIX-944]] which built it). Underlying defect: the chunk is quantised by RECIPIENT COUNT while the real cost driver is per-recipient financial_relationships fan-out, which varies by orders of magnitude across the uuid-ordered dirty set, so a fixed 50-recipient quantum has unbounded cost. Second finding, which falsifies a stated FIX-968 premise: pg_cron QUEUES the 12:00 firing behind a still-running 09:00 one rather than letting it hit the advisory lock and log skipped -- measured on 08-06, 08-07 and 08-08, the second run starts within ~1s of the first ending, chaining two full budget windows into one continuous 9.5h block. Fix shape: chunk by estimated FR-row weight (official_donor_totals.donor_count is already maintained by this same procedure and costs 117 pages to read) instead of by count; arm the guard from chunk 1 with a durable cross-run slowest-chunk seed; cut c_budget from 4h30m to 2h so a firing cannot still be running when the next is due; yield between chunks. Cross-ref [[FIX-969]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-965]], [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-972]], [[FIX-943]]. <!--id:FIX-1002-->

- [x] 🔴 M — **FEC bulk writers rewrite ~95% unchanged rows every Sunday — skip no-op upserts** — The weekly FEC file is a cumulative SUPERSET, so every Sunday run re-upserts the WHOLE cycle, but MEASURED on prod 2026-08-09 only 0.5-6.3% of the rows written are new (`created_at` histogram, cycle 2026 `financial_relationships`: 6,841-86,818 new rows per weekly run against 1,375,438 total; individual donor entities 15k-45k new against 3.42M). The other ~95% were byte-identical re-upserts that still cost a FULL write. WHY THAT IS EXPENSIVE: `financial_relationships` takes **exactly zero** HOT updates (`n_tup_upd` 4,911,666 / `n_tup_hot_upd` **0**), because the unpredicated `financial_relationships_updated_at` btree (159 MB) indexes a column the `set_updated_at()` BEFORE UPDATE trigger changes on EVERY update — so HOT is impossible by construction and every upsert rewrites all 16 indexes (4,855 MB) and leaves a dead tuple. `financial_entities` carries the SAME trigger but does NOT index `updated_at`, which is exactly why it gets 27.06% HOT and FR gets 0.00%. Fix: `BulkUpsertSpec.skipUnchangedRows` in `packages/data/src/lib/direct-pg-upsert.ts` emits `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE SET ... WHERE (any SET column IS DISTINCT FROM EXCLUDED)`, so an unchanged conflict row is left completely alone — no heap write, no index maintenance, no dead tuple, no WAL, no `updated_at` bump. The predicate always covers EXACTLY the SET list (never a caller-chosen subset: a SET column outside the predicate could change silently). Wired into all four fec-bulk writers; the donor writer additionally re-reads the ids that RETURNING no longer emits (an unchanged row returns no row) on the same direct-pg connection, which also closes a pre-existing gap where [[FIX-754]]'s mid-stage resume never got RETURNING rows for chunks committed by an earlier run. MEASURED before/after, local prod-clone, same table, same 4,000-row chunk, 4 alternating slices per variant, source rows pre-materialised so only the upsert is timed: `financial_relationships` 6,941 ms -> 1,289 ms per chunk (1.735 -> 0.322 ms/row, **5.39x**), `financial_entities` 1,377 ms -> 433 ms (0.344 -> 0.108 ms/row, **3.18x**), with `rows_written = 0` on every skip slice confirming the no-op. Gate impact: a from-zero cycle-2026 indiv run costs 348.9 min of writer work at the prod pg_stat_statements means (840,338 FE rows @ 11.246 ms + 1,375,438 FR rows @ 8.349 ms, both from 4,000-row chunk samples) against `fec-backfill.yml`'s 350-min cap — it does NOT fit. With this fix it is ~123 min (65% headroom), and even assuming the donor stage gets ZERO benefit it is ~200 min (43% headroom), so the FR half alone clears the 25%-headroom bar. Cross-ref [[FIX-995]], [[FIX-999]], [[FIX-943]]. <!--id:FIX-1008-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **fec_bulk donor writer overwrites the authoritative all-cycle total_donated_cents with a cycle-only value every run** — Surfaced by [[FIX-1008]]'s skip-unchanged measurement, and it directly caps that fix's payoff on the donor stage. `upsertIndividualDonorsBatch` writes `total_donated_cents` = the donor's aggregate FOR THE CYCLE BEING INGESTED. The post-cycle `rebuild_financial_entity_donation_totals()` ([[FIX-269]]) then overwrites it with the live SUM across ALL cycles — which is the authoritative value, and the reason that rebuild exists at all ('replaces the lossy per-cycle overwrite that left multi-cycle individuals with only the latest cycle's total'). So for every multi-cycle donor the pipeline writes a value it KNOWS is wrong, and repairs it minutes later. Two costs. (1) It is pure write thrash on the platform's hottest table. (2) It defeats [[FIX-1008]]'s predicate: the stored all-cycle value never equals the cycle-only value being written, so those donors are rewritten every single week no matter what. MEASURED on prod 2026-08-09 (sample of 2,576 individual donors with donation rows): **75.8% are single-cycle**, so ~24% of donors are permanently un-skippable for this reason alone — [[FIX-1008]]'s donor-stage skip rate is bounded at ~72% (0.758 x ~0.95 unchanged) instead of ~95%. The machinery to fix it already exists and is already correct: [[FIX-700]]'s `skipAggregateOverwrite` drops `total_donated_cents`/`total_received_cents` from the INSERT column list entirely, so an existing donor keeps their current aggregate and a new donor takes the `BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`; it is currently applied only to SCOPED runs. Direction: apply it to unscoped runs too and let the totals rebuild be the single writer of that column. Care needed on one point before doing it — confirm the rebuild covers every donor an unscoped run can introduce, including donors whose only rows are in a cycle the rebuild's predicate does not reach, otherwise a brand-new donor could sit at 0 until the next full rebuild. Cross-ref [[FIX-1008]], [[FIX-700]], [[FIX-269]]. <!--id:FIX-1009-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **FIX-999's below-cursor-count invariant does not converge — re-scope now that FIX-1008 makes the re-pass cheap** — Correction to the design sketched in [[FIX-999]], found while sizing it 2026-08-09. The proposed completeness guard was: store the count of rows at or below the content-key cursor, and on resume re-run that slice if the count differs. That guard is correct but, on this data, it is equivalent to no cursor at all. The sort key must be the conflict arbiter (`donor_fingerprint`, or `(from_id, to_id)`) to be stable across a republish, and those key spaces are effectively RANDOM with respect to newness — a donor who first appears this week gets a fingerprint uniformly distributed over the whole range. So a republished superset almost always adds rows BELOW the cursor, the below-count always differs, the slice is always re-run, and the re-run slice IS all the progress the cursor bought. Net saving on a mid-file cursor: zero. Nor can the hole be closed by probing the DB for which below-cursor keys already exist — that finds rows that are ABSENT but is blind to rows that are PRESENT WITH A CHANGED VALUE (a donor who gave again), so it would silently drop real updates. What actually closes it is [[FIX-1008]]: with `skipUnchangedRows`, re-running the below-cursor slice costs an arbiter probe plus a predicate evaluation and writes nothing, MEASURED at 5.39x cheaper on `financial_relationships` and 3.18x on `financial_entities`. That removes the need for the below-count bookkeeping, the existence probe, and the sweep ordering entirely — the correct resume becomes 'replay the whole file, let the DB skip the no-ops'. It also removes the ORIGINAL motivation: with [[FIX-1008]] a from-zero cycle-2026 indiv run fits one dispatch (~123 min of writer work, 65% headroom, vs 348.9 min before), so the cursor no longer has to survive a republish for the cycle to converge. Recommendation: leave [[FIX-999]] OPEN but re-scope it to 'confirm from a completed post-FIX-1008 dispatch whether a content-keyed cursor is still needed at all' rather than building the offset-to-key conversion on spec. Do not build the below-count guard as originally specified. Cross-ref [[FIX-999]], [[FIX-1008]], [[FIX-754]]. <!--id:FIX-1010-->

- [x] 🟠 S — **R2 cache freshness compares our upload time to FEC's publish time — a republish mid-run can pin stale bytes for a full ingest cycle** — `downloadWithR2Cache` in `packages/data/src/pipelines/fec-bulk/util.ts` decides cache freshness with `r2Fresh = r2Lm >= fecLm`, where `r2Lm` is the R2 OBJECT's own LastModified — i.e. when WE finished uploading — and `fecLm` is FEC's publish time. Those answer different questions, and the object timestamp answers the wrong one. The race: HEAD FEC at T0 and get the old Last-Modified; download the old bytes; FEC republishes at T1; our upload of the OLD bytes completes at T2 > T1. R2 now holds superseded content stamped NEWER than FEC's current file, so `r2Fresh` is true and every subsequent run is served the stale copy without ever re-reading FEC. NEAR-MISS MEASURED 2026-08-09 — the sequence happened, only the upload did not. `fec-backfill.yml` dispatch (GHA run 31322394244) HEADed indiv26.zip at 15:57:17Z and got `Sun, 02 Aug 2026 15:45:35 GMT` / etag `...-238`; FEC republished at **16:03:26 GMT** (live HEAD: `Last-Modified: Sun, 09 Aug 2026 16:03:26 GMT`, etag `"9167f97b6dfbd1c58e4f4f50997b8c2f-246"`, Content-Length **2,061,619,898**); the run's R2 uploads drained 16:54:40-16:55:32Z, comfortably after T1. It did not fire only because indiv26 took the CACHE branch that run (R2 `fec/2026/indiv26.zip` LastModified 2026-08-06T06:41:27Z, 1,995,728,131 bytes) and a cache hit returns `r2UploadPromise: null`, so nothing was re-uploaded. Had the sizing gone the other way — indiv26 fetched from FEC and uploaded at ~16:55 — the bucket would now hold the Aug 2 bytes stamped 16:55, newer than FEC's 16:03, and every run until the next publish would be served them. Four of the six cycle-2026 files DID re-upload with today's timestamps (cm26 15:55:54, weball26 15:55:53, cn26 15:55:54, ccl26 15:57:17), so the upload path is live and routinely lands inside the window. BLAST RADIUS IS ONE INGEST CYCLE, NOT PERMANENT — and that is the right way to size it. A cache HIT does not re-upload, so `r2Lm` stays frozen at T2 rather than ratcheting forward; FEC's next weekly publish (Sundays ~15:20 UTC) produces a Last-Modified later than T2 and freshness resolves itself with no intervention. So the cost is bounded at one full ingest cycle of silently-stale donor data — which is EXACTLY the outcome [[FIX-903]] exists to prevent (prod donor data a full week behind FEC, one real ingest per two weeks), arriving through the cache layer instead of the watermark. Same failure, different door, and unlike FIX-903 this one leaves no signal: the run logs `complete`, the row counts look plausible, and only the `fec_bulk_run_state` lm value betrays it. FIX SHAPE — compare like with like, and add size. Store FEC's OWN reported headers as R2 object metadata at upload time (`x-amz-meta-fec-last-modified`, `x-amz-meta-fec-content-length`, `x-amz-meta-fec-etag`) and make freshness `stored_fec_* == live_fec_*`, so the comparison is FEC-reported-then vs FEC-reported-now and the R2 object's own timestamp drops out of the decision entirely. Content-Length is the cheap belt-and-braces and should NOT be omitted as redundant: today's two files are 1,995,728,131 vs 2,061,619,898 bytes — **65,891,767 apart, 3.3%** — so a size check alone would have caught this instance, and it costs one integer compare. CAUTION on ETag: R2's object ETag is NOT comparable to FEC's, because multipart chunk sizes differ between our uploader and theirs — our cached indiv26 reads `"44e6967bdbad3e73b09964f1e7677b28-119"` against FEC's `-238`/`-246` for the same class of file. That is precisely why the stored value must be FEC's etag as a metadata string, never the object's own. Cross-ref [[FIX-903]], [[FIX-192]], [[FIX-1010]], [[FIX-995]]. <!--id:FIX-1014-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **fixes-sync.mjs carries a literal NUL byte, so every repo-wide grep treats the FIXES-workflow script as binary** — `scripts/fixes-sync.mjs` builds a cache key as ``${trunk}<U+0000>${sha}`` where the source was meant to carry the two-character escape `\0`. What is actually stored in the file at **byte offset 8362 is a literal U+0000 control character**. Node parses it fine — it is a legal character inside a template literal and the cache key behaves exactly as intended — so nothing fails and nothing has ever surfaced it at runtime. **The entire cost is in search.** ripgrep, `git grep` and the Claude Code Grep tool all sniff for NUL to classify a file as binary, so any repo-wide content search that would match this file returns a binary-file notice instead of the matching lines. Measured 2026-08-09: `grep -n 'closes-as' scripts/fixes-sync.mjs` returns `Binary file scripts/fixes-sync.mjs matches`, and the same query through the Grep tool returns `binary file matches (found \0 byte around offset 8362)`. Reading the file with `node -e` or the Read tool works normally, so it is not corrupt — it is simply invisible to the one access pattern people actually use on it. **Why this is worth more than its size suggests:** this is the script that owns the whole FIXES workflow — the `Fixes:` / `Closes:` / `Verified[FIX-NNN]:` trailer grammar, the closure vocabulary, the [[FIX-461]] trunk-ancestry guard, the done.log column format. It is the single most likely file in the repo to be grepped for 'how does trailer X actually work', and it is the single file in the repo that silently refuses to answer. Every future session of this workflow pays the toll: the real behaviour has to be recovered by reading the file whole or decoding it through node, and a session that greps, gets a binary-file notice and moves on may reasonably conclude the pattern is absent. Encountered exactly that way twice in the 2026-08-09 closure session. **Fix:** replace the literal control character with the escape sequence `\0`; or, cleaner and leaving no NUL in the file at all, use a separator that cannot collide with either operand — both are ref/sha-shaped, so `|` or `::` is unambiguous. One character either way. **Verify:** `node -e "console.log(require('fs').readFileSync('scripts/fixes-sync.mjs').indexOf(0))"` must print `-1`; then `grep -c 'closes-as' scripts/fixes-sync.mjs` must return a count rather than a binary-file notice; then `pnpm fixes:test` and `pnpm fixes:check` to prove the trunk-ancestry cache still behaves. Worth sweeping for the same typo elsewhere in the same breath — `grep -rlP '\x00' --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=.git .` over tracked text files. Found while auditing the trailer grammar during the FIX-1004/999/944/920 closure pass. Cross-ref [[FIX-1001]] (the four-digit regex widening, same file), [[FIX-314]], [[FIX-369]], [[FIX-461]]. <!--id:FIX-1015-->

- [x] 🔴 S — **No external request-path monitor — the 08-11 outage ran 14h undetected while GHA laundered the signal into 'cancelled'** — **Shipped in this session; filed for the record and for the residual gap it does NOT close.** The 2026-08-11 outage ran **14 hours** before a human noticed. The signal to catch it already existed and was structurally incapable of paging anyone. **Measured 2026-08-12 from this workflow's own run history:** during the outage window the five `platform-snapshot` runs at 08:28, 09:31, 10:27, 11:17 and 12:00 UTC all hung against the unreachable site and were cut off by their `timeout-minutes: 5`. **GitHub reports a timeout-expired job as `cancelled`, not `failed`, and sends no notification for a cancelled run** — verified on run 31478090511, which started 09:31:46 and ended 09:36:49 (5m03s) with conclusion `cancelled`. Five consecutive cancelled runs spanning exactly the degraded window, zero emails. That is the whole finding: this is **alerting on an existing signal, not new monitoring**. **What shipped:** a `request-path-probe` job added to `.github/workflows/platform-snapshot.yml` (Craig's call — no new scheduled workflow; GHA cron is unreliable at tight cadences). It runs independently of the snapshot job, curls three surfaces verified 200 + `X-Vercel-Cache: MISS` on 2026-08-12 so none can answer from the CDN while the DB is unreachable (`/`, `/officials`, `/api/officials/<id>/responsiveness`), retries 3 x 20s with `--max-time 25`, and **exits non-zero itself** rather than hanging into a timeout. **The API endpoint is `/responsiveness` and NOT `/summary` deliberately: `/summary` FAILS OPEN** — its own header documents that the `summary: null` variants (kill switch, spend cap, no data, **DB error**) return unstamped 200s, so it is blind to exactly the outage this job catches; `/responsiveness` returns 500 on a DB error (route.ts:36, :111). Both verified against prod. Probe verified end-to-end in both directions before commit: 3/3 200s exit 0, unreachable host exits 1 with the `::error::` annotation. **Known limit:** the two page routes are not proven to fail closed on a DB-down-but-Vercel-up partial outage; on the 08-11 failure mode (Cloudflare 522, origin unreachable) every endpoint fails, but a partial outage rests on `/responsiveness` alone. Three properties are load-bearing and must survive future edits: (1) `concurrency` was moved from workflow level onto the `trigger` job only — a workflow-level `cancel-in-progress` makes the whole RUN `cancelled` and re-launders the signal; (2) the probe carries no concurrency group at all; (3) its worst case (~3.5 min) sits far inside `timeout-minutes: 10`, so it can only ever conclude `success` or `failure`. **The residual gap, stated plainly:** GHA cron does not honour its own schedule. Configured `*/10`, the **observed** gaps on 2026-08-11..12 were 38, 50, 56, 63, 87, 107 and 153 minutes (playbook D2 applied to GHA — read observed starts, never cron expressions). So detection latency is about **one hour, not minutes** — a ~10x improvement on 14 hours at zero new cost, and **not** minutes-scale monitoring. True minutes-scale detection means an external uptime service (e.g. UptimeRobot's free 5-minute checks): zero repo code, entirely in that service's dashboard, Craig can set it up whenever he wants. **Also unresolved:** GitHub routes scheduled-workflow failure mail to the account that last committed the workflow file, currently `Civitics Platform <civitics.platform@gmail.com>` (96c2204c). If that inbox is not watched the alert is decorative. Cross-ref [[FIX-281]], [[FIX-1021]], [[FIX-1022]], [[FIX-969]]. <!--id:FIX-1026-->

And the weekly job sits at the **furthest possible point from a vacuum**: `fe-vacuum-analyze` (jobid 30) ran `0 2 * * 0,3`, so it fired **Sun 08-09 02:00 and not again until Wed 08-12 02:00** — while the Sunday FEC ingest (observed **15:55-16:55 and 22:28-23:43**) and the Mon 08-10 [[FIX-953]] merge both landed *inside* that gap. **The Sunday firing precedes the ingest it exists to clean up by ~14 hours.** [[FIX-884]] is this instance's measured precedent for exactly this access shape, and the same night [[FIX-1013]]'s one-shot vacuum of `financial_relationships` reproduced the mechanism at full strength on a sibling table: **7,952 ms -> 365 ms, Heap Fetches 129,415 -> 0, buffer reads 60,883 -> 439** (21.8x / 139x). **The self-reinforcing part.** Unit 6, `refresh_spending_totals()`, is an unbounded whole-table UPDATE of `financial_entities` — **127,728 rows rewritten every week, of which ZERO would change** (measured), across **19 indexes / 1,403 MB**. So the weekly job bloats the very table its own MVs index-only-scan, and its vacuum owner never covers the window. **What shipped:** (1) `refresh_spending_totals()` gains the [[FIX-1008]] skip-unchanged predicate — same rows read, no-op rows no longer written; (2) jobid 30 altered in place by name (playbook D3, preserving its run history) to `0 2 * * 0,1,3`, adding a Monday firing **after** the observed Sunday window while keeping Sunday for Saturday's `fec-backfill` dispatches. **What this does NOT establish, and the test that would.** The stats collector was reset by the 08-11 23:26 restart and `financial_entities` has since been vacuumed, so the degraded state **cannot be reproduced** — `pg_stat_statements` holds zero REFRESH rows and every `last_vacuum` reads NULL. The visibility mechanism is therefore a strong inference from plan shape + schedule receipts + the FIX-884/FIX-1013 precedents, **not a before/after of the incident itself**. **Falsifiable prediction:** with jobid 30 now firing Monday 02:00, the next Tuesday 07:00 weekly should complete in **~15-45 min**; if it blows up again with `financial_entities` freshly vacuumed, this diagnosis is wrong and the remaining suspect is unit-level cost under cold cache (`shared_buffers` = 256MB against a 3.5GB FR heap). - [x] 🟠 M — **14 of 15 procedures cannot close their own data_sync_log row on cancel — WHEN OTHERS does not match query_canceled** — **Found while fixing [[FIX-1021]]; the census is catalog-derived, not a hand-kept list.** PL/pgSQL's `EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS` **matches every error type EXCEPT `query_canceled` and `assert_failure`**, and `statement_timeout` raises `query_canceled` (57014). So a procedure that opens a `data_sync_log` row with `status='running'`, COMMITs it, and relies on a trailing `UPDATE` to close it will have that `UPDATE` skipped entirely when the 6h axe (or any `pg_cancel_backend`, or a client disconnect) lands — the error blows through the handler and out of the procedure, leaving the row stranded `running` until the nightly reaper finds it. **This is not hypothetical and it is not one procedure.** It is exactly what happened to the 2026-08-11 07:00 `refresh_derived_mvs('weekly')` row, which sat `running` for **15 hours** until `reap_stale_sync_log` closed it at 08-12 04:08:28. **Census, prod 2026-08-13:** of the **15** procedures that write a `running` row AND use transaction control, **14 cannot close it on cancel** — `donor_rollup_rebuild_bulk`, `rebuild_entity_connection_stats`, `reconcile_donation_edge_orphans`, `reconcile_donor_party_rollup_orphans`, `reconcile_donor_rollup_orphans`, `reconcile_entity_connection_stats_orphans`, `reconcile_financial_entity_totals`, `refresh_donor_party_rollup_incremental`, `refresh_financial_entity_totals_incremental`, `refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental`, `refresh_sector_affinity_from_tag_changes`, `refresh_treemap_individuals_global`, `run_entity_connections_rebuild`, `run_rule_taggers`. Only `refresh_derived_mvs` handles it, as of [[FIX-1021]]. Reproduce the census with `pg_get_functiondef(p.oid) LIKE '%WHEN query_canceled%'` over that set. **This is very likely the shared root cause of the stranded-`running` population** that [[FIX-990]] keeps re-discovering (two EC rows stranded from 08-10 alone), the stranded `treemap_individuals_global_refresh` row, and the recurring `fec_bulk` `reaped` rows — every one of those is a job that was cancelled or killed, not one that crashed. **Consequences beyond tidiness:** (1) a stranded `running` row makes the pipeline look alive to anything reading `data_sync_log`, which is what `list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines()` and `check_cron_job_health()` ([[FIX-968]], [[FIX-977]]) read for freshness — so a killed job masks itself as an in-flight one for up to the reaper's 60-minute stale window; (2) the reaper's own note is explicit that elapsed-since-`started_at` is an **upper bound, not a measurement**, so every reaped row permanently loses its true runtime; (3) advisory locks taken with `pg_try_advisory_lock` are released by session teardown so stampede guards still hold — that part is fine. **Fix shape, mirroring what [[FIX-1021]] shipped:** add `WHEN query_canceled THEN` **by name** to each per-unit/per-chunk handler, record the cancel, `EXIT` the loop rather than continuing (the box has just proven it cannot finish one unit), and let the existing trailing `UPDATE` close the row as `partial`. **Verified locally in FIX-1021 that this works:** the `statement_timeout` timer is disarmed once it has thrown, so the bookkeeping `UPDATE` after the catch does run — the repro closed the row with `canceled=true` and 4 units named as skipped. Note the handler CANNOT be an outer block wrapping the loop: PL/pgSQL forbids `COMMIT` inside a block that has an `EXCEPTION` clause, so it must go on the existing inner per-iteration block. Do these in priority order by blast radius — `refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental` and `run_entity_connections_rebuild` are the two that actually get cancelled in practice. **⏳ PROGRESS 2026-08-13 (cc-prompt-60): 2 of 14 done — FIX STAYS OPEN.** Migration `20260813010000_fix1028_query_canceled_handlers.sql` fixed the two named above as highest blast radius: `refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental()` and `run_entity_connections_rebuild()`. Both bodies were taken from prod `pg_get_functiondef()` and edited in place, so the migration cannot silently revert an intermediate definition. **Verified locally by repro, not by inspection:** with `SET statement_timeout='4s'` the EC procedure logged `[chunk] rebuild_entity_connections_donations — CANCELED`, the `CALL` returned normally instead of raising 57014, and its row closed itself `status=partial, canceled=true, elapsed_seconds=4`; with `'8s'` the donor procedure logged `chunk 2 CANCELED` / `PARTIAL (canceled) — 32 of 6995 recipients, resumable at chunk 3` and closed `stop_reason=canceled`. **Two things found while doing it that the bullet did not anticipate.** (1) The EC procedure's existing per-window handler carried the comment *'WHEN OTHERS catches a statement_timeout cancel too'* — the exact inversion of the trapping rule, now corrected in place; a future census should grep for that claim as well as for its absence. (2) **A cancelled `mode='full'` EC rebuild was leaving autovacuum STRANDED OFF on `entity_connections`**: the procedure COMMITs `autovacuum_enabled=false` before the chunk loop and re-enables it after, and the un-caught cancel jumped straight over the re-enable. That is precisely the [[FIX-884]] mechanism (2026-06-28 run cancelled at its cap → flag off ~4 weeks → 9.5M dead tuples, all-visible 0.9%, index-only scans degraded to per-row heap fetches); [[FIX-885]]'s startup reconcile heals it on the NEXT run, but the cancelling run now cleans up after itself. This makes the EXIT-and-fall-through shape load-bearing rather than merely tidy. (3) The donor procedure needed one extra invariant the generic idiom does not imply: its resume cursor must NOT advance past a CANCELLED chunk. A FAILED chunk may advance it (sweep_failures then blocks the watermark and the whole set is retried), but a cancel routes to the `partial` branch which does not set sweep_failures, so an advanced cursor there would permanently SKIP the recipients whose work had just rolled back — the cursor write is now gated on `v_canceled IS NULL`, and the repro confirms the cursor stopped at chunk 1's end while chunk 2 (recipients 33..239) was the cancelled one. **Remaining 12, unchanged:** `donor_rollup_rebuild_bulk`, `rebuild_entity_connection_stats`, `reconcile_donation_edge_orphans`, `reconcile_donor_party_rollup_orphans`, `reconcile_donor_rollup_orphans`, `reconcile_entity_connection_stats_orphans`, `reconcile_financial_entity_totals`, `refresh_donor_party_rollup_incremental`, `refresh_financial_entity_totals_incremental`, `refresh_sector_affinity_from_tag_changes`, `refresh_treemap_individuals_global`, `run_rule_taggers`. full writeup `docs/audits/2026-08-13-fix1030-chord-donor-state-plan-flip.md`.** **It is a PLAN FLIP, and fix direction (b) above was aimed at the wrong thing** — the four chord MVs do not share a problem, and per-unit `work_mem` / `max_parallel_workers_per_gather` would not have helped. Prod's plan for unit 3 is a `Nested Loop` whose inner side is `Memoize → Index Scan using financial_entities_pkey`, driven by ~950k outer rows; its siblings use `Parallel Hash Join`. It wins on cost by 19% (613,522 vs 756,100 with `enable_nestloop=off`), and that win is manufactured by three compounding defects: **(1) a 298.5× underestimate** of the `financial_entities` filter — `LENGTH(metadata->>'state')=2` is an expression no index or statistics object covers, so it gets the hardcoded `DEFAULT_EQ_SEL` 0.005; prod estimates **10,714** rows of 3,679,374 where the measured truth is **3,198,178 (87.13%)**; **(2) a 41× underestimate** of `n_distinct(financial_relationships.from_id)` — pg_stats says **42,267**, measured truth **1,745,921** distinct donors across 4,183,604 rows, which is what makes Memoize look ~99%-effective; **(3) `random_page_cost = 1.1`** (prod's Supabase default; local Docker and stock postgres are 4) — **isolated one-at-a-time on the clone, this is the SINGLE setting that flips the plan**, and with prod's GUCs replayed the clone reproduces prod's plan node-for-node (602,475 vs 607,984). **The TRIGGER is confirmed as candidate (a), [[FIX-1018]]'s `financial_relationships_donor_rollup_dirty_idx`, built ~03:00 UTC 08-11 — four hours before the first death.** Its predicate covers unit 3's WHERE almost exactly, so it handed the nested loop a cheaper outer path than it had ever had (bitmap startup 17,539 vs 41,217; 953,828 est rows vs 1,519,884), dropping the total below the hash join. Dropping the index in a rolled-back transaction on the clone restores the hash join. **The index is not at fault and is not touched** — it made a pre-existing misestimate reachable. Candidates (b) FIX-1013 vacuum, (c) 08-09 ingest cardinality and (d) definition drift are all excluded (prod's live MV definitions match the migration; siblings got faster after the vacuum). **Measured execution** (`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on the clone): `Memoize Hits: 2,328,993 Misses: 1,854,611 Evictions: 869,096 Memory Usage: 262,145 kB` — a **44.3% miss rate** against a model assuming ~99%, and **256 MB in ONE node**, because Memoize sizes at `work_mem × hash_mem_multiplier` (128MB×2) — i.e. a single plan node may allocate the entire size of prod's `shared_buffers`. **That is the OOM-consistent shape** answering direction (a)'s remaining question as far as it can be answered in-database; no server memory parameter is tuned. The clone reproduces the PLAN and the I/O DEMAND exactly and the WALL CLOCK never — which is why the evidence is buffer counts, not seconds. Standing caveat for future perf repro on this clone. **THE FIX, two parts.** **(i)** The FE filter and state extraction are hoisted into a CTE `AS MATERIALIZED` fence, so FE is scanned once and projected narrow (width 48 vs 163) before the join; with no index on a CTE there is no parameterised inner path, so the nested loop is not merely unattractive but **unavailable** — the fix deliberately does not depend on the planner estimating anything correctly. Output identical (`LENGTH(x)=2` subsumes the `IS NOT NULL` and `<> ''` quals): full symmetric-difference parity, **325 rows before and after, 0 either direction, identical SUM 2,197,387,010.00**. **(ii)** `enforce_derived_mvs_unit_budget()` on a 2-minute pg_cron job (`derived-mvs-unit-watchdog`) cancels a unit outliving **900 s** (GUC `civitics.derived_mvs_unit_budget_seconds`; the procedure now publishes the in-flight unit + pid + start + budget, COMMITted before each unit). **The prompt's prescribed `SET LOCAL statement_timeout` is NOT implementable and this was re-verified, not assumed** — both `SET LOCAL` and plain `SET` report the new value while `pg_sleep(8)` completes under a nominal 2 s cap, because `statement_timeout` is armed once in `start_xact_command()` and a procedure's `SPI` COMMIT never re-arms it ([[FIX-703]]'s finding, still true on PG 17); `SET …; CALL …` from pg_cron fails with *invalid transaction termination*. **A cancel from outside the backend is the only mechanism that can interrupt a running unit**, and it lands in FIX-1021's existing `query_canceled` handler, so nothing about that path is new. **Local proof, both paths.** Post-fix weekly cadence **6/6 `complete`, 85 s**, with units 4-6 measured for the FIRST time (FIX-1021's instrumentation shipped 08-13 and the run that would have recorded them died): industry 26.5 s / donor_type 20.0 s / **donor_state 18.7 s (was unbounded, now 3rd fastest)** / subject 1.2 s / sector_dollars 3.2 s / spending_totals 15.7 s — so **no weekly unit comes within an order of magnitude of 900 s**, which is why that budget is chosen rather than guessed. The fence works regardless. **🚀 PROD APPLIED 2026-08-13 03:55:29-04:03:15 UTC — and the apply itself caused ~5.5 min of request-path timeouts. See [[FIX-1032]].** Gate was clean at 03:55 (0 non-idle backends, 0 running data_sync_log rows, last cron 03:30 succeeded in 13s, jobid 10 paused, daily cadence 2h away). But an MV definition cannot be replaced in place, so the migration does DROP + CREATE ... AS (which populates), and prod logged `duration: 442115.812 ms` for that CREATE plus `process 13991 still waiting for AccessShareLock on relation 127653 ... after 1000.090 ms`, dozens of 57014 `canceling statement due to statement timeout`, and 08006 `connection to client lost`, from 03:57:43 to 04:03:12 — stopping dead at the apply's end. - [x] 🟠 S — **Swapping a materialized view definition via DROP+CREATE holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the whole rebuild — 442s of prod request-path timeouts on 08-13** — Caused a real user-visible incident during the [[FIX-1030]] prod apply, 2026-08-13 03:57:43-04:03:12 UTC. A materialized view's definition cannot be replaced in place, so the FIX-1030 migration did DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW + CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... AS (which populates). Postgres logs: 'duration: 442115.812 ms plan: Query Text: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW public.chord_donor_state_party_flows_mv AS WITH donor_states AS MATERIALIZED (...)', alongside 'process 13991 still waiting for AccessShareLock on relation 127653 of database 5 after 1000.090 ms', dozens of 57014 'canceling statement due to statement timeout', and 08006 'connection to client lost'. TWO compounding mechanisms, and the second is the one that made it a whole-site event rather than a chord-page event. (1) LOCK: the DROP+CREATE pair holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the MV name for the ENTIRE 442s rebuild, so every reader of that MV blocks on AccessShareLock and then dies at the 8s service_role statement_timeout. (2) I/O: the CREATE's sequential scan of the 1.6GB financial_entities heap ran on a box that had been up only 2h10m since the 01:45:27 crash, so shared_buffers (256MB) was cold and the scan paid full physical-read cost — which starved the request path generally, not just the blocked readers. This is why the timeouts were not confined to /graph chord callers. ESTIMATE MISS WORTH RECORDING: the same statement measured 18.7s on the warm prod-scale clone. The session extrapolated a ~7x clone-to-prod factor from steady-state weekly unit timings and predicted 2-3 min; the real cold-box factor was ~24x. A warm-cache clone timing is NOT a safe basis for predicting a cold-prod DDL window. DURABLE FIX SHAPE: build the replacement out of line and make the exclusive window milliseconds instead of minutes. CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW x_new AS <def> WITH NO DATA (instant, no lock on x); REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW x_new (populates, still no lock on x, so readers keep being served the old data throughout); then one short transaction that does DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW x and ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW x_new RENAME TO x. Remember the things a DROP discards and the swap must re-apply: the unique index required for REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY (rename it too), the GRANTs, the COMMENT, and any per-relation autovacuum reloptions ([[FIX-1003b]] sets these on all four chord MVs — FIX-1030 did re-apply them, but only because it was checked for deliberately). SECONDARY RULE: schedule MV-definition swaps against a WARM box. A box within a few hours of a restart has a cold 256MB shared_buffers against multi-GB heaps and will pay worst-case I/O for any full scan. Cross-ref [[FIX-1030]], [[FIX-1003b]], [[FIX-1021]], [[FIX-884]]. <!--id:FIX-1032-->

- [x] 🟠 M — **Two live planner statistics defects on financial_entities / financial_relationships — FIX-1030's fence protects ONE query, nothing protects the next** — Split out of [[FIX-1030]], where both were measured but deliberately not corrected. They are the loaded gun that FIX-1018's index merely pulled the trigger on, and they are still loaded. DEFECT 1 — expression selectivity. The predicate LENGTH(metadata->>'state') = 2 on financial_entities is an expression that no index and no statistics object covers, so the planner falls back to its hardcoded DEFAULT_EQ_SEL of 0.005: prod estimates 10,714 rows of 3,679,374 where the measured truth is 3,198,178, i.e. 87.13 percent. That is a 298.5x underestimate and it is what makes a nested loop's inner side look ~300x smaller than it is. DEFECT 2 — n_distinct. pg_stats reports n_distinct = 42,267 for financial_relationships.from_id (42,600 on the clone, so this is not a clone artifact); the measured distinct-donor count is 1,745,921 across the 4,183,604 qualifying donation rows alone. That is at least a 41x underestimate, and it is what makes Memoize look ~99 percent effective when its real miss rate is 44.3 percent with 869,096 evictions. WHY THIS IS ITS OWN FIX. Together, at prod's random_page_cost of 1.1, these two made a Memoize-backed nested loop price 19 percent BELOW the hash join, and that plan wedged prod for 14h22m on 2026-08-11 and crashed it on 2026-08-13. FIX-1030 fixed the symptom the only way that was safe in one session: a CTE AS MATERIALIZED optimiser fence on chord_donor_state_party_flows_mv, which makes THAT query structurally immune because a CTE has no index and therefore no parameterised inner path. The statistics themselves were left wrong. So any OTHER query joining financial_relationships to financial_entities, or filtering on a metadata expression, can still flip the same way — and the trigger does not have to be exotic: FIX-1018 flipped it by adding one perfectly reasonable partial index whose predicate happened to offer a cheaper outer path. The next such index is not predictable. FIX SHAPE, three steps. (1) CREATE STATISTICS on the expression, PG14+ expression statistics, for LENGTH(metadata->>'state') and probably also for the bare metadata->>'state' on financial_entities, since the two are separate expressions and stats on one do not help the other. (2) Correct n_distinct on financial_relationships.from_id with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN from_id SET (n_distinct = ...). Measure count(DISTINCT from_id) over the WHOLE table first, not just the donation subset, then express it as a NEGATIVE value, which postgres reads as a fraction of reltuples and therefore stays correct as the table grows; a positive absolute would go stale the same way the sampled one did. (3) ANALYZE both tables — neither change does anything until the stats are rebuilt. GATE BEFORE LANDING. This changes plan choice prod-wide for every consumer of these two tables, which is precisely why it was excluded from FIX-1030's bounded scope. Take before/after EXPLAIN diffs on the main FR/FE consumers and land only if none regresses: the six donor-rollup arms, run_entity_connections_rebuild, the treemap RPCs including the resumable individuals sweep, the get_*_page consolidating RPCs, get_cohort_top_donors, and the chord cohort paths. Note that making an estimate HONEST usually improves plans, but 'usually' is not a standard this particular code path has earned. OPERATIONAL NOTE. The ANALYZE itself is a full-scan-class cost against a 1,632MB and a 3,502MB heap, so schedule it per [[FIX-1032]]'s warm-box rule and off-peak, not within a few hours of a restart. Cross-ref [[FIX-1030]], [[FIX-1018]], [[FIX-1032]], [[FIX-884]], [[FIX-443]]. <!--id:FIX-1034-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **Unit watchdog cannot tell a long-running unit from a dead backend until the 900s budget elapses — add per-poll pid liveness** — Demonstrated live on prod 2026-08-13 during the first (aborted) [[FIX-1033]] supervised firing. enforce_derived_mvs_unit_budget() ([[FIX-1030]]) checks whether the published backend_pid is still a live refresh_derived_mvs backend ONLY on the branch it reaches AFTER unit_age exceeds the budget. Every earlier poll short-circuits at 'within budget' using nothing but arithmetic on metadata.current_unit_started_at — a timestamp that is FROZEN once the backend dies, so it keeps growing forever and looks exactly like healthy long-running work. Observed: the backend was terminated at ~04:35:56 mid unit 2, and at 04:44 the watchdog still returned {action: none, reason: within budget, unit_age_seconds: 702.5} for a process that had been gone eleven minutes. It also fooled the operator — this session reported to Craig that unit 2 was 'running long at 486s then 638s, heading for the fence' when unit 2 had in fact only ever accrued ~149s of real work. WHAT IS NOT BROKEN, so nobody re-opens it: the post-budget guard itself is CORRECT and was verified — it refuses to cancel when the pid is absent or is not running this procedure, which is the safe direction and protects against pid reuse. Separately verified the same day that a pg_cron worker IS visible to that guard: application_name pg_cron, backend_type client backend, state active (NOT null), query CALL public.refresh_derived_mvs('weekly'), and the guard's full predicate evaluates TRUE against it — so the 900s fence is live for pg_cron-launched runs, which was an open worry and is now closed. THE GAP is purely detection latency for the dead-backend case: today such a run stays 'running' until unit_age crosses the budget (up to 900s of nothing), at which point the watchdog correctly declines to cancel, and the row then waits for reap_stale_sync_log's window (up to 60 min) before anything closes it. A stranded non-terminal row is not cosmetic — it is what poisoned connections_pipeline_healthy in [[FIX-833]], because health checks that order by completed_at see a NULL and sort it first. FIX SHAPE: hoist the pg_stat_activity liveness probe ABOVE the budget comparison so it runs on every poll. If the published pid is gone (or is no longer running this procedure) while the row is still 'running', do not cancel anything — there is nothing to cancel — but close the row immediately as 'reaped' with an error_message naming the last published unit and stating that started_at..close is NOT a runtime, mirroring reap_stale_sync_log's existing FIX-944 wording. That turns a 900s-plus-60-minute blind spot into a 2-minute one and makes the last-known unit durable at the moment of death, which is the same instrumentation gap [[FIX-1030]] consequence (3) was about. Keep the existing post-budget cancel path exactly as it is. Cross-ref [[FIX-1030]], [[FIX-1033]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-833]], [[FIX-1028]]. <!--id:FIX-1035-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **sync-canary-check has been red for 10 days and every failure is a TRUE POSITIVE — the gap is alert delivery, not the checker** — sync-canary-check has failed every morning since 2026-08-04 (last pass 08-03; 10 consecutive red runs through 08-13), which reads as a broken checker. It is not. **Every failure is a true positive, and the red X IS the alarm** — [[FIX-885]] made the DB-health findings exit non-zero precisely because an email alone is not escalation. Layer verdict (playbook E11): not the canary, not the checker logic, not the workflow env/secrets. Two things are actually wrong and neither is the canary. **(1) The conditions it reports are real, and they ROTATE — which is why a week of red looks stuck.** 08-04: vm_degraded on financial_entities at 47.6 pct all-visible. 08-05: donor_rollup_refresh stale 68.49h against a 48h window. 08-08: financial_entities again. 08-09 through 08-13: escalating rollups under the [[FIX-977]] derived registry, latest being entity_connections_rebuild at 356.65h against an escalate-past-210h bound. That last one is a live operational gap in its own right: prod data_sync_log shows entity_connections_rebuild status=reaped on 08-03 and 08-10 (both Monday, jobid 22) with NO row at all on the Wednesday firings (jobid 2) of 08-05 and 08-12, and last status=complete on 2026-07-29. entity_connection_stats_rebuild is reaped since 08-10, donor_party_rollup_refresh since 08-04. Those need their own FIX; they are not canary defects. **(2) A distinct checker-side failure on 08-06 that is NOT an escalation.** That run died with "canary-check failed: data_sync_log query failed: canceling statement due to statement timeout" and wrote no meta row — prod data_sync_log carries canary_check rows for 08-01 through 08-13 with 08-06 missing. This is the one run where the checker itself broke rather than reported. [[FIX-968]] built nightly_check_unavailable for this class but the failure here lands a layer above it. **The notification gap — why no alert reached Craig.** The runs wore status completed/failure, never cancelled, and metadata.alert_sent was true on every escalating run. sendAlert THROWS on a Resend error, so a true value means the Resend API ACCEPTED roughly ten sends to ADMIN_EMAIL. The gap is therefore downstream of the API accept: delivery, spam filing, a wrong ADMIN_EMAIL secret, or an unverified RESEND_FROM sender domain. None of that is checkable from the repo — it needs the Resend dashboard delivery log. Rule out at the same time: GitHub Actions scheduled-workflow failure notifications should have produced ten emails on their own and evidently did not. Feeds the [[FIX-1026]] / [[FIX-969]] residual-alerting story. **Observability defect surfaced while diagnosing (small, real, fix alongside).** The escalation verdict lives ONLY in the stdout JSON, never in the canary_check meta row: writeMetaRow runs BEFORE the failures array is computed, so escalating_rollups, alert_sent and escalated are all absent from data_sync_log.metadata. Diagnosing ten days of red therefore required pulling ten sets of GHA logs when one SQL query should have answered it. Persist the escalation reason and alert_sent into the meta row so the arc is greppable. **Not fixed in session, deliberately:** there is no S-class change available — the checker is behaving correctly, and the real work splits into an alert-delivery investigation needing external dashboards plus a separate rollup-not-completing FIX. Cross-ref [[FIX-234]], [[FIX-885]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-978]]. **RE-SCOPED 2026-08-17 (cc-prompt-63), on Craig's delivery evidence — the premise above is half wrong.** This bullet assumed the gap was alert DELIVERY. It is not: Resend delivered every one of the ten alerts, verified in Gmail. So there is no delivery investigation to run and no external-dashboard dependency, which removes the stated reason this was not S-class. **The actual failure is SALIENCE — ten identical daily emails that each say the same thing become invisible, and the eleventh, which mattered, read exactly like the ten that did not.** That is a notification-design problem, not an infrastructure one, and the fix is small and local. New fix shape, three parts: (1) **Severity tiers in the SUBJECT LINE**, so the tier is legible in a notification list without opening anything — today every alert shares one subject and the reader cannot triage without reading the body. (2) **Page on DELTA, not on STATE.** The current design re-alerts every morning for as long as the condition holds, which is what manufactured the ten identical mails; alert on the TRANSITION into a bad state, on a material worsening, and on recovery, and stay quiet while a known-bad state is merely persisting. A daily "still red, day 7" digest line is fine — a daily page is not. (3) **Split the duty between the two existing checkers by what they can actually prove:** [[FIX-1026]]'s probe owns the "site down" tier (request-path reachability, page-worthy immediately), and the canary owns the "data stale" tier (rollup freshness, digest-worthy and escalating only on delta). Conflating them is why a data-staleness signal and an outage signal arrive looking identical. The meta-row persistence item above (escalating_rollups / alert_sent / escalated absent from data_sync_log.metadata because writeMetaRow runs before the failures array is computed) SURVIVES this re-scope unchanged and is still the cheapest single improvement — it is what makes "did this alert fire, and why" a SQL query instead of ten GHA log pulls. Docs-correction style per the `5dbe3405` precedent: the original text is left standing above so the corrected premise is visible rather than silently rewritten. Cross-ref [[FIX-1026]], [[FIX-1052]]. <!--id:FIX-1036-->

Limit: 500000, Usage: 500002.' **Every crawl defense the codebase has is a no-op right now.** The FIX-637 entity_pages cap, the FIX-683 entity_leaf cap and the FIX-797 entity_prefetch bucket all route through checkRateLimit in apps/civitics/src/lib/ratelimit.ts, which catches the Upstash error and returns ALLOW. All 100 sampled requests returned HTTP 200; zero 429s. A crawler walking distinct entity UUIDs across /officials, /donors, /proposals and /jurisdictions was proceeding completely unthrottled at the time of measurement, every request a cold cache MISS and a full SSR render. **The fail-open is CORRECT and is not the defect** — it is load-bearing per the module header and it kept the site up. The defect is that it is **unobservable and un-alerted**: nothing anywhere pages when the secondary cost/volumetric layer switches itself off. **Root cause of the blindness.** packages/db/src/platform-snapshot.ts computes usage for anthropic, supabase, cloudflare (R2), github and vercel. **Upstash is absent from all of it** — there is no getUpstashUsage helper, no platform_limits rows, no metric, nothing. No new cron, no new workflow, no new alerting path. **Sizing note:** 'Usage: 500002' is only 2 over the cap because the counter freezes on crossing, so it carries NO information about WHEN exhaustion happened — the Upstash console is the only source for that, and it bounds the FIX-1040 ordering claim. **Secondary, separable:** reduce commands spent per request (skip the check on cache hits, or coarsen buckets) so the next allotment does not burn at the same rate. Software lever before compute lever — raising the Upstash tier is deliberately NOT proposed. - [x] 🟠 S — **The rate limiter's fail-open path logs once per bucketed request, and nothing durably records a 429 or a fail-open anywhere — the app cannot answer 'was the limiter firing?' after the fact** — **Found by the 2026-08-15 traffic/cost-spike triage (docs/audits/2026-08-15-traffic-cost-spike.md).** Two coupled observability gaps on the edge limiter, both surfaced by the same incident. **(1) Per-request log line on the failure path.** apps/civitics/src/lib/ratelimit.ts:168 emits console.warn('[ratelimit] Upstash error on bucket=...') inside the catch, so once Upstash is exhausted EVERY bucketed request produces a Vercel observability event. Measured in prod logs 2026-08-16 00:28-01:26 UTC: 92 of 100 sampled requests carried the warn. **Size it honestly before fixing it:** at the observed ratio this is worth roughly $0.03-0.30/day — Observability Events is a $2.87/month projected line. This is a hygiene fix, NOT a cost fix, and it should not be sold as one. Its real value is that a per-request log line makes the failure mode expensive to leave running for weeks. Fix shape: sample or rate-limit the warn (once per bucket per N seconds per instance), or replace it with a counter. **THE TENSION IS LOAD-BEARING: silencing this log without adding the [[FIX-1038]] Upstash alarm makes the fail-open MORE invisible, which is the actual defect. Ship the alarm first or together — never this alone.** **(2) No durable record of 429s or fail-opens.** rateLimitResponse in apps/civitics/middleware.ts:144 returns the status and logs nothing. public.abuse_events — the [[FIX-880]] observe-only substrate built for exactly this — holds **0 rows** for the last 12 days on prod (verified: SELECT count(*) FROM abuse_events WHERE occurred_at >= now() - interval '12 days'), so either recordAbuseEvent is not wired to the limiter path or ABUSE_EVENT_PEPPER is still absent from Vercel env (a known pending item). The consequence: the ONLY way to answer 'was the limiter firing during the incident?' is Vercel logs, which retain about an hour and cap the CLI at 100 rows. This triage had to reconstruct the whole incident from billing counters because of it. **RateLimitResult already carries the right primitive** — the `limited` boolean exists specifically to distinguish a real 429 from a fail-open allow ('so callers can log/observe quota pressure without breaking', per the type's own comment) and NOTHING reads it. Wire it: count fail-opens and 429s per bucket, and land them somewhere queryable — abuse_events is the obvious home and already exists. **Explicitly NOT in scope: the fail-open semantics do not change.** It is load-bearing, it kept the site up during this incident, and it is correct. The defect is that it is silent. Cross-ref [[FIX-570]], [[FIX-637]], [[FIX-683]], [[FIX-797]], [[FIX-880]], [[FIX-1038]], [[FIX-1039]]. <!--id:FIX-1040-->

The projection arithmetic is unaffected and still correct, but the comment misleads anyone reasoning about resolution. **The resolution limitation is worth documenting where the readers are.** Because values are cumulative MTD and step ONCE PER DAY at ~06:00-07:00 UTC (midnight Pacific — Vercel's ChargePeriodStart days are Pacific days), consecutive 10-minute snapshots are byte-identical to 16 decimal places. **The 10-minute snapshot cadence buys ZERO additional resolution for any Vercel metric.** An incident can only ever be localised to a calendar day, never to an hour. - [x] 🔴 S — **The single most-crawled route on the site has no rate-limit bucket at all — /graph is 30 pct of attack traffic and middleware never inspects it, and robots.txt Disallow /*? did not stop the crawler** — **Found by the 2026-08-15 traffic/cost-spike triage (docs/audits/2026-08-15-traffic-cost-spike.md) once the crawler was identified.** **(1) The bucket gap.** getRateLimitBucket in apps/civitics/middleware.ts matches /api/search, /api/graph/narrative, /api/graph, the write paths, then LEAF_PAGE_RE (jurisdictions|districts|officials) and ENTITY_PAGE_RE (jurisdictions|officials|proposals|institutions|agencies|districts|meetings|donors|initiatives|investigations). **The PAGE route /graph matches none of them** — the "/api/graph" test is a startsWith on the API prefix and does not cover the page — so getRateLimitBucket returns **null** and no check is ever made. Measured against Cloudflare for the 24h to 2026-08-16 01:55 UTC: **/graph accounted for 44,689 of 147,611 requests (~30 pct), the single largest path on the zone by a wide margin**, every one carrying a query string of the form "?entity=UUID". So roughly a third of a hostile crawl targeted the one route the limiter structurally cannot see — and it would STILL be unlimited after [[FIX-1038]] restores Upstash. **This is a gap in the [[FIX-637]]/[[FIX-683]]/[[FIX-797]] design, not a regression:** those FIXes enumerated the entity-detail families by name and /graph is not an entity-detail family, so it was never in scope. It is now the most-attacked surface. **Fix shape:** add /graph to the bucketed set. Choose deliberately — it is a distinct cost class from the entity pages (client-heavy, and query-string-keyed rather than path-keyed), so it likely wants its own bucket rather than being folded into entity_pages, and the identifier should probably incorporate the "entity" query param since that is what makes each request unique. Confirm the actual render cost first: /graph did NOT appear in any "vercel logs" runtime sample during the incident while the entity pages did, which suggests it may be statically served and cheap per request — **if so the correct fix may be a cheap bucket or none at all, and the real finding is that nobody knew either way.** Measure before tuning (playbook: do not tune on vibes). **(2) robots.txt Disallow /*? did not stop it.** robots.txt (apps/civitics/public/robots.txt) carries the rule "Disallow: /*?" from [[FIX-513]], written precisely to stop query-string crawling after the 2026-06-07 ClaudeBot incident (~430k invocations). The crawler here is **meta-webindexer/1.1** (ASN 32934, Facebook Inc.) and it walked "/graph?entity=UUID" anyway, having fetched /robots.txt 88 times in the same window. Two candidate causes and they need distinguishing before anything is changed: (a) the crawler ignores robots.txt, or (b) **it does not support the star mid-path wildcard** — wildcard support in robots.txt is a Google/Bing extension, NOT part of the original standard, so a conforming-but-basic parser reads "Disallow: /*?" as a literal path and matches nothing. If (b), then **the FIX-513 defense is not portable across crawlers** and the durable fix is an explicit "Disallow: /graph" (a literal prefix every parser handles) alongside the wildcard, plus a named "User-agent: meta-webindexer" block. That is a meaningfully broader conclusion than 'one bot misbehaved' and is the reason this is filed rather than folded into [[FIX-1039]]. Cross-ref [[FIX-513]], [[FIX-637]], [[FIX-683]], [[FIX-797]], [[FIX-1038]], [[FIX-1039]]. <!--id:FIX-1042-->

The alert system was healthy — the problem was structural, in what it watched. Monthly-cumulative thresholds cannot see a \$21/day burn for days; the one fast leading signal (FIX-642) watches Supabase db_connections; the FIX-648 fluid-cost signal reads Vercel data whose finest resolution is ONE DAY (consecutive 10-minute snapshots are byte-identical, so the cron cadence buys zero resolution on any Vercel metric). What actually stopped the burn was a vendor email read by a human, ~16h in. **D1 — Cloudflare becomes a first-class snapshot service.** Since FIX-1038 shipped scripts/cf-analytics.mjs we know the GraphQL Analytics API is scriptable with the token already in the env, and it is the ONLY near-real-time script-readable counter in the stack — every downstream dollar (Vercel invocations, Upstash commands, observability events) follows edge request volume. New shared module packages/db/src/cloudflare-analytics.ts (the CLI script stays as the CLI face); three platform_limits rows; one GraphQL call per snapshot tick. **THE METRIC IS ORIGIN-REACHING REQUESTS, NOT TOTAL EDGE REQUESTS.** originResponseStatus != 0 (available on this Free zone; probed 2026-08-16) means the request reached Vercel. Those are the ones that cost money (~\$1.23e-4 each, measured) and keying on them makes every layer SELF-LIMITING: while a mitigation absorbs a crawl, origin volume collapses and the alarm correctly goes quiet. Measured: 7,302 origin-reaching at 21:00 UTC on 08-15, 36 at 23:00 UTC, with edge volume unchanged at ~7,300 both hours. **THE THRESHOLD IS DERIVED, NOT PICKED.** Census of all 147 complete hours this Free zone retains before the crawl onset (2026-08-09 03:00 to 2026-08-15 05:00 UTC; retention is 1w1d = 8 days, which is why the census is a week and not longer): p50 77, p75 141, p90 283, p95 841, p99 1508, max 2218 origin req/hr. The unmitigated crawl: min 7158, p50 7233, max 7548. A 3.2x GAP separates the busiest legitimate hour ever recorded from the quietest crawl hour, so anything in [2500, 7000] classifies both sets perfectly. Chose 3000 = max-legit x 1.35: zero false positives across all 147 legitimate hours, 2.4x below the crawl floor so it also catches a crawl at 40 pct of this one rate, and ~\$8.85/day if sustained (~27x a baseline day 0.33 of consumption). NB this reads the last THREE complete hours per tick, not one: GHA cadence measured over 200 runs / 6.8 days is p50 46 min, p75 60, p90 87, max 155 — a single-hour read would silently skip hours on 26 pct of runs. **D2 — burn-rate layer.** The 08-15 audit established the spike was 3.7x baseline by hand-writing a window function over the cumulative MTD series; nothing automated it. New get_platform_daily_cost_deltas RPC (jsonb extraction stays in the DB — ~150 snapshot rows/day, large payloads) plus packages/db/src/burn-rate.ts. Fires only when BOTH conditions hold: delta >= \$1.00 absolute floor AND delta >= 3x the trailing-7-day median. Neither alone works — a pure multiple pages on every ordinary day once a quiet week drags the median down, a pure floor misses a burn starting from an elevated baseline. Differentiates CONSUMPTION (EffectiveCost minus the Pro subscription line), because the flat \$20/31 daily accrual compresses the spike day from 3.7x to 1.9x. Routed through the existing platform_alert_state edge-trigger machinery with new keys: new signals, not new substrate. Cross-ref [[FIX-1038]], [[FIX-1039]], [[FIX-1041]], [[FIX-1045]], [[FIX-1046]]. <!--id:FIX-1044-->
- [x] 🔴 M — **Closed-loop auto-mitigation: the cron raises the Cloudflare security level itself and reports what it did** — Craig explicit choice: on a sustained origin-volume spike the platform should ACT, then tell him — not ask him to act. On 2026-08-15 Under Attack mode cut origin-reaching traffic ~99 pct within one hour of enablement (21:00 UTC 7,313 x 200 / 0 x 403; 22:00 UTC 445 x 200 / 6,850 x 403), worth ~\$21/day. The mitigation works. What was missing was the detection and the hand on the switch, and both are mechanisable. New packages/db/src/cf-mitigation-loop.ts, run from the same Cloudflare reading [[FIX-1044]] collects so the decision and the number behind it can never disagree. **TRIGGER:** origin-reaching >= 3000/hr in >= 2 DISTINCT complete clock hours within a rolling 6h window. **ACTION:** PATCH security_level to under_attack. **REVERT:** automatic after 6h to the level it found, then re-trip on fresh evidence if the burn resumes (Under Attack mode is a dam, not a fix — it 403s every scripted client and challenges search crawlers, so leaving it up indefinitely has its own cost, and the revert is what makes the loop safe to leave armed). **SIX SAFETY RAILS, every one covered by tests that fail if the rail is removed.** (1) ESCALATE-ONLY: only ever raises, and only reverts an escalation IT made. If the zone is already at or above the target when the trigger fires it records NO TRIP AT ALL — claiming a level it did not set is exactly what would later make it auto-revert a human decision. (2) SUSTAINED MEANS MEASURED-SUSTAINED: the CF hourly bucket is already an hour of evidence, and the count is keyed on the BUCKET TIMESTAMP, never on tick count — at the measured p50 46-minute GHA cadence the cron re-reads the same bucket most ticks, so counting readings would let one bad hour trip it alone. Detection latency ~2-3h, ~\$1.80 of burn, accepted deliberately. (3) AUTO-REVERT WITH RE-TRIP. (4) DEBOUNCE: evidence is consumed on every transition and a fresh trip needs 2h since the last revert, so it cannot flap more than once per revert window. (5) FAIL-SAFE: any CF API error records, alerts, and takes no further action — and critically, a FAILED write records NO trip, because a phantom trip record would make the next run LOWER the zone security on the strength of a write that never landed. (6) KILL SWITCH: new cf_auto_mitigation switch plus CF_AUTO_MITIGATION_ENABLED env hard-kill disarms the WRITE while leaving detection, metrics and alerting fully live — disabling the loop can never make the platform blinder than before it shipped. Deliberately the ONLY kill switch with no auto_trip_threshold_pct: a cost metric must never be able to switch off the machinery that defends against cost. State lives in pipeline_state.cf_mitigation_loop, following the FIX-1040 precedent (durable signals are state TRANSITIONS, not per-request rows; abuse_events does not fit — it needs node:crypto and an admin client). Every transition emails via a new renderMitigationEmail template, debounced on the ACTION so a persistent condition reports once. **SHIPS ALERT-ONLY.** Measured 2026-08-16: the existing CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN does GET security_level fine (200, under_attack, modified 2026-08-15 22:03 UTC) but PATCH returns 403 code 9109, and GET /user/tokens/{id} is also refused so the scope cannot be read directly — it is inferred from the shape of the write failure. USER ITEM: mint a token with Zone Settings:Edit (keep Analytics:Read) and add CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN + optionally CLOUDFLARE_ZONE_ID to the Vercel env; the loop starts acting the moment it exists, no deploy. Documented in docs/CLOUDFLARE.md (how to tell an automatic change from a manual one) and docs/OPERATIONS.md (how to disable it). Cross-ref [[FIX-1039]], [[FIX-1040]], [[FIX-1044]]. <!--id:FIX-1045-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **The mitigation loop proves its own Cloudflare write scope instead of discovering it mid-incident** — Follow-up to [[FIX-1045]], found while confirming Craig token edit. **THE GAP:** the loop only ever learned whether its Cloudflare token could WRITE at the moment it first tried to — i.e. during a live burn. isScopeError() classifies a 9109 correctly and the loop degrades to alert-only and emails, so it fails SAFE, but the question "is this thing actually armed?" was unanswerable until the one moment the answer had to be right. A token minted without Zone Settings:Edit, later rolled, re-scoped to the wrong zone, or expired stayed invisible until the mitigation was already needed. That is the same class of silent failure that made 2026-08-15 cost what it did — a hard control switched off with no signal. **THE PROBE:** twice a day, issue a PATCH of security_level with THE VALUE THE ZONE ALREADY HAS. 200 proves Edit, 9109 proves Read-only. Cloudflare accepts it, changes nothing, and does NOT move modified_on — verified by hand across the permission change on 2026-08-16, pinned at 2026-08-15T22:03:19Z through no-op PATCHes on both sides of it. There is no safer write available; every other zone setting would be a real change. The caller contract is load-bearing and enforced by making currentLevel a REQUIRED argument rather than something the probe fetches itself: pass anything other than a value just read from that zone and the probe becomes a real mutation. **WHY TWICE A DAY AND NOT EVERY TICK:** an idempotent PATCH still writes a Cloudflare AUDIT LOG entry, and the audit log is one of the three documented ways to tell an automatic change from a manual one (docs/CLOUDFLARE.md). At the measured cron cadence, probing every tick would produce ~40 no-op entries/day and bury exactly the signal it exists to protect. Cached in pipeline_state.cf_mitigation_loop.scope_probe with a 12h interval. Staleness is harmless for CORRECTNESS — before a real trip the loop attempts the actual write regardless and that write is authoritative — so a stale cache can only make the REPORTED status lag, never cause a wrong action. A DISARMED loop never probes (a no-op write is still a write) and a THROWN probe keeps the prior verdict rather than inventing a pessimistic one that would suppress a real mitigation. **ALSO: the trip threshold is now env-overridable** via CF_TRIP_ORIGIN_REQ_THRESHOLD, mirroring LEADING_DB_CONN_THRESHOLD ([[FIX-642]]) and LEADING_FLUID_USD_THRESHOLD ([[FIX-648]]) which are overridable for exactly this reason: an alarm nobody has watched fire is an alarm nobody should trust, and before this the only way to exercise the write path end-to-end was to wait for a real crawl. Set it to 50 and the next two breached hours trip for real, email, hold 6h and auto-revert. A non-numeric or non-positive value is IGNORED rather than obeyed — an env typo must never be able to set the threshold to 0 and trip the loop on every quiet hour. The EFFECTIVE threshold rides in the snapshot payload and the card shows "threshold OVERRIDDEN to N/hr" in amber whenever it differs from the derived 3000, because a verify-run value left in place is its own incident. **Card wording now distinguishes four states** — armed+verified, ALERT-ONLY, armed (unverified, i.e. a pre-FIX-1047 snapshot or never probed), and disarmed — where before "armed" meant only that the kill switch was on. **PREMISE CORRECTED WHILE INVESTIGATING:** a vercel env pull comparison appeared to show Vercel holding a DIFFERENT Cloudflare token than the local files. That was wrong and the check was invalid — Vercel cannot read encrypted values back, and all 40+ sensitive vars returned an identical 11-character redaction placeholder. Never diff a Vercel secret against a local one this way; compare token IDs via /user/tokens/verify instead. Cross-ref [[FIX-1045]], [[FIX-1039]]. <!--id:FIX-1047-->

Inside that window: jobid 16 entity-connection-stats-rebuild FAILED at 11:00 after 10s; the 11:05 and 11:18 vacuum slots failed while 11:10-11:16 succeeded but ran 30-90x their normal duration (93s/33s/60s vs 0-2s); the 12:00 donor-rollup failed; and at 14:05-14:18 ALL SIX vacuum jobs failed. TWO FINDINGS THAT CHANGE THE FIX SHAPE. (1) Monday 08-17 was the FIRST REAL TEST of max_worker_processes=12 with jobid 16 active — the 2026-08-12 audit named exactly this test, having noted the Wednesday 08-12 run was confounded because jobids 2 and 16 were paused by hand for that day. jobid 16 failed the test. mwp=12 is live (pg_settings source=configuration file) and did NOT clear the contention. (2) THE FAILURE WINDOW OUTLASTS BOTH HEAVY JOBS BY OVER TWO HOURS: failures run 09:xx to 16:08 while the EC rebuild ended 14:00 and the donor rollup 10:50, and nothing in data_sync_log runs 14:00-16:08. So the 6h-squatter story does not close. Worker-slot arithmetic does not close either: only 3 bgworkers are baseline (pg_cron launcher, pg_net, logical replication launcher) against mwp=12, with max_parallel_workers=2. The watchdog jobid 40 fires exactly 30x/hour throughout with no backlog accumulation, so it is a victim not an amplifier. The resource actually exhausted 14:00-16:08 is NOT established from catalog evidence and needs the Supabase Analytics postgres logs. IT HAD USER-FACING IMPACT: the IRS-990 job at 15:28-15:31, inside the window, died on 'Could not query the database for the schema cache' — PostgREST was degraded, not just cron. MOVES APPLIED THIS SESSION (migration, alter_job by NAME per playbook D3 to preserve run history): entity-connection-stats-rebuild 0 11 * * 1,3 -> 0 16 * * 1,3, and the afternoon vacuum wave (odr-mv, treemap-individuals, odt, osdr, osar, odbt) 14:05-14:18 -> 17:05-17:18. Reasoning for the first is correctness as much as contention: EC-stats reads entity_connections and currently starts at 11:00 with the rebuild still three hours from its ceiling, so it is both starved AND reading a half-rebuilt table; 16:00 is after the 14:00 ceiling with margin. Reasoning for the second: 14:0x sits exactly on the rebuild's cancel-and-rollback exit, and it went 0-for-6 on Monday. NEITHER MOVE TOUCHES jobid 9/10, so the FIX-1033 constraint holds — the daily/weekly derived-MV pair still share one advisory lock and the watchdog's single-slot in-flight state stays safe; no per-run keying needed yet. THESE MOVES ARE NECESSARY BUT LIKELY NOT SUFFICIENT, because of finding (2): they cannot explain the 14:00-16:08 tail. Cross-ref [[FIX-985]], [[FIX-1022]], [[FIX-1028]], [[FIX-1033]], [[FIX-1002]], [[FIX-971]].  **PREMISE VOID 2026-08-28 (cc-prompt-91) — twice over.** (1) This bullet's fix put jobid 16 at 16:00 so it would run **after** the EC rebuild. [[FIX-1111]] dissolves that: the EC rebuild is now a continuous */15 crawl, so there is no longer an "after" to schedule against, and the burst ledger flagged the premise as spent (docs/audits/2026-08-27-io-budget-burst-ledger.md 5). (2) The move is moot regardless, because **jobid 16 is now PAUSED** — it fired twice after 08-24 and both firings ended in a postmaster restart with jobid 16 the sole process in flight; see [[FIX-1103]] for the correlation and [[FIX-1115]] for the bounded rebuild that has to ship before it runs again. Nothing about the 16:00 slot needs re-deciding until then, and when it does the right answer is probably not a slot at all but a crawl-class arm inside run_entity_connections_rebuild.   <!--id:FIX-1052-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **recipient_count_reconcile is gated behind an EC rebuild that no longer completes — the 937h staleness is a downstream symptom, not a scheduling defect** — Answers the open question in [[FIX-994]], which framed this as a correlation/cadence-detection problem. Measured on prod 2026-08-17. The chain is structural, not schedule-related. (1) The recipient_count_reconcile data_sync_log row is written by the PROCEDURE reconcile_recipient_count(). (2) That procedure has EXACTLY ONE caller anywhere in the prod catalog: run_entity_connections_rebuild(). No cron job CALLs it directly — jobid 14 financial-entity-totals-reconcile calls reconcile_financial_entity_totals(), a different procedure, and jobids 15/18/19/23 call the other orphan sweeps. (3) run_entity_connections_rebuild() is jobid 2 (Wed 08:00) and jobid 22 (Mon 08:00), and it has NOT run to completion since 2026-07-29: 08-03 failed, 08-05 failed at 43s, 08-10 failed, 08-12 was paused by hand during the incident response, 08-17 ran the full 6h and was canceled at the ceiling. So the reconcile arm sits downstream of a rebuild that no longer reaches its tail. THE RULING-OUT MATTERS: the schedule was not removed, the job was not disabled, and no migration dropped the caller — jobid 14 ran normally on 08-01 12:00 and wrote its own financial_entity_totals_reconcile row that same minute while writing NO recipient_count_reconcile row, which is the discriminating observation. This is therefore NOT an S-class reschedule and was deliberately not 'fixed' by re-enabling anything; it resolves when the EC rebuild can finish (see [[FIX-1052]] and the FIX-985 6h ceiling). OPEN SUB-QUESTION, deliberately not over-claimed: the last recipient_count_reconcile row is 2026-07-05 but the EC rebuild last SUCCEEDED 2026-07-29, so either the call was added to run_entity_connections_rebuild() after that date or it is conditional on a branch the 07-29 run did not take. Resolve by reading the procedure body's call site before treating the 07-05 date as a rebuild-completion proxy. Cross-ref [[FIX-994]], [[FIX-985]], [[FIX-978]], [[FIX-977]]. **✅ RESOLVED 2026-08-18 (cc-prompt-66) — REDIRECTED TO [[FIX-1059]]. THE OPEN SUB-QUESTION IS ANSWERED AND THE ANSWER INVERTS THE BULLET.** This bullet's premise (2) — "that procedure has EXACTLY ONE caller anywhere in the prod catalog: run_entity_connections_rebuild()" — is wrong, and the bullet was right to flag it as needing verification before the 07-05 date was treated as a rebuild-completion proxy. Read on prod 2026-08-18: run_entity_connections_rebuild() mentions reconcile_recipient_count exactly TWICE and **both are inside a comment** ("recipient_count is reconciled out-of-band (reconcile_recipient_count(), monthly post-VACUUM)"). There is no CALL. A catalog-wide search over pg_get_functiondef for every function and procedure in public returns two hits: the procedure itself, and that comment. No cron job invokes it either. THE REASON IS RECORDED AND DELIBERATE: migration 20260705000200_fix736_recipient_count_fr_derived.sql states "Its cron job (ec-recipient-count-reconcile) is unscheduled below — the routine FR orphan sweep is now owned by financial-entity-totals-reconcile", and executes SELECT cron.unschedule(jobname) FROM cron.job WHERE jobname = 'ec-recipient-count-reconcile'. [[FIX-736]] repurposed the procedure as an FR-based BREAK-GLASS full recompute and left it callerless ON PURPOSE. So the last recipient_count_reconcile row being 2026-07-05 is not a symptom of anything — it is the last firing before a deliberate retirement, and the arm is NOT gated behind the EC rebuild. Fixing the rebuild would not have made it run, and closing this on the back of a successful rebuild would have been a false close. The stale comment that caused the misreading is corrected in migration 20260818000000. THE REAL DEFECT IS THE DETECTOR, filed as [[FIX-1059]]: [[FIX-977]]'s watch registry and canary-check.ts still watch this pipeline and escalate on its staleness, with no way to mark a pipeline RETIRED — so a deliberate retirement is indistinguishable from a breakage and pages forever. Cross-ref [[FIX-1059]], [[FIX-736]], [[FIX-1056]]. <!--id:FIX-1053-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **nightly-sync rows never leave status='triggered' — 104 unclosed rows back to 2026-04-30, permanently indistinguishable from a hung dispatch** — Found 2026-08-17 while reconciling the stuck-running data_sync_log rows named in the cc-prompt-63 ledger. THE LEDGER PREMISE WAS WRONG in a useful way: there is no stuck 2026-07-27 fec_bulk 'running' row on prod. What exists instead is a much larger, older population — 104 rows with pipeline='nightly-sync' and status='triggered' and completed_at IS NULL, running continuously from 2026-04-30 to 2026-08-17, i.e. essentially every nightly dispatch ever made. These are the GHA dispatcher's own rows, opened when the workflow is triggered and never closed by anything; the actual work reports separately under nightly_cron and the per-stage pipeline names, which DO close correctly. WHY IT MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING COSMETIC: every freshness/liveness detector that scans data_sync_log for unclosed rows has to special-case or silently swallow this population, and a genuinely hung dispatch would be indistinguishable from the 104 benign ones. It also means the reaper has 104 permanent candidates it either skips or re-examines forever. Note the contrast with the reaped rows, which are correct post-[[FIX-979]]: 30 rows across fec_bulk/nightly_cron/refresh_derived_mvs/etc carry status='reaped', completed_at IS NULL and a reap_note spelling out that the span is an upper bound on reaper latency rather than a runtime — that is exactly the shape [[FIX-971]] asked for, and it is working. Fix shape, cheapest first: either have the dispatcher close its own row on workflow completion (it now has GITHUB_RUN_ID in metadata per FIX-971, so the GHA API can supply the conclusion), or stop opening a sync row for the dispatch at all and let nightly_cron be the only record, or give the dispatch a distinct terminal status so 'triggered' means 'dispatch acknowledged' rather than 'in flight'. Prefer the last if the row has diagnostic value. Cross-ref [[FIX-971]], [[FIX-979]], [[FIX-963]], [[FIX-962]]. <!--id:FIX-1054-->
