- [x] 🔴 L — **EC rebuild cannot finish inside 6h because the CONTRACTS arm's throughput collapsed 3.2x — growth alone does not explain it, and FIX-1034 did not help** — Fix-shape spec for the next rollup-lane prompt. Diagnosed 2026-08-17 (cc-prompt-63); no rework done in that session by design. THE THROUGHPUT TABLE is the whole diagnosis — edges_total and runtime are both in data_sync_log/cron.job_run_details for every run, so this is measured, not inferred: 07-15 695,640 edges in 1,077s = 646 edges/s; 07-20 1,349,007 in 2,252s = 599/s; 07-22 1,313,229 in 2,206s = 595/s; 07-29 3,184,880 in 5,350s = 595/s; 08-17 4,011,180 in 21,615s = 186 edges/s. Throughput held flat at 595-646 edges/s across a 4.6x growth in edge count, then COLLAPSED to 186/s — a 3.2x regression. GROWTH ALONE DOES NOT EXPLAIN THE FAILURE: at the old steady 595 edges/s, even 4.0M edges finishes in about 6,700s, comfortably inside the 6h ceiling. It is the rate regression that pushes it past the wall, not the size. THE COLLAPSE IS LOCALIZED AND NAMED: the 08-17 run's cancel_detail is 'rebuild_entity_connections_contracts: canceling statement due to statement timeout', so the contracts arm specifically is where the 6h is spent. chunk_failures is 0, so this is not error-retry churn — it is one arm running slow. FIX-1034 DID NOT HELP: it landed 08-14 and 08-17 was the first post-statistics Monday. Runtime 21,615s vs the pre-statistics 08-10 run's 22,380s — inside noise, both pinned at the ceiling. The FR/FE planner statistics corrected a different query family; the contracts arm needs its own EXPLAIN. THE STEP CHANGE IS DATED: 07-29 completed in 5,350s, 08-03 was already dead at the ceiling. Whatever changed sits in that window and should be the first thing looked for — a plan flip (cf. the FIX-1030 nested-loop/Memoize mechanism, same shape and the same random_page_cost=1.1 cost model), or bloat in a contracts-side table with no vacuum owner (cf. FIX-884's all-visible collapse, and note per FIX-943 that entity_connections gets a vacuum but the contracts SOURCE tables may not). THE COMPOUNDING DEFECT — it never banks progress. The 08-17 run wrote 4,011,180 edges and then closed status='partial' with no resume marker; contrast donor_rollup_refresh, which closes 'budget exhausted — resumable at recipien...' and picks up next firing (FIX-1002/1021). So every EC firing restarts from the top, burns 6h, and dies at the same place — it can never win no matter how many times it runs, which is why the rebuild has not completed since 2026-07-29 and why [[FIX-1053]]'s recipient_count_reconcile arm (called only from the tail of run_entity_connections_rebuild) has not run since. FIX SHAPE, in order: (1) EXPLAIN the contracts arm on prod and find the 3.2x — do this BEFORE any budget work, because if it is a plan flip the budget becomes unnecessary; (2) give the rebuild the FIX-1002/1021 treatment — an explicit time budget and a durable resume checkpoint per arm, so a firing that runs out of budget banks its edges and the next one continues; (3) only then consider splitting the arms into separate jobs. Do NOT simply raise the 6h statement_timeout: [[FIX-985]] set that ceiling deliberately, and a job that needs longer than the gap to its next firing is the failure mode [[FIX-971]] corrected the record on. Cross-ref [[FIX-985]], [[FIX-1002]], [[FIX-1021]], [[FIX-1034]], [[FIX-1030]], [[FIX-884]], [[FIX-943]], [[FIX-1052]], [[FIX-1053]]. **✅ RESOLVED 2026-08-18 (cc-prompt-66) — AND THE DIAGNOSIS ABOVE IS CORRECTED ON ITS CENTRAL POINT.** Step 1 was run before any budget work, as specified, and it refutes the contracts-arm attribution. MEASURED ON PROD (read-only, idle box, bounded at 300s, work_mem=256MB — exactly what the procedure sets) the contracts arm's aggregate is **128.5 seconds**, not hours: GroupAggregate (actual time=125131.882..128408.178 rows=189949 loops=1), Sort Method: external merge Disk: 359544kB, Bitmap Heap Scan on financial_relationships (actual time=768.903..95472.569 rows=3908956, Heap Blocks: exact=295464), Buffers: shared hit=9 read=301515 temp read=44943 written=44944, Execution Time: 128456.054 ms. cancel_detail names contracts because that is where the AXE FELL, not where the time went — an important general lesson about reading cancel messages as attribution. WHERE THE 6 HOURS ACTUALLY WENT, measured rather than inferred, from the per-arm clock the run leaves behind: each incremental arm stamps its watermark row with now(), which is that chunk transaction's start, so pipeline_state.entity_connections_donations updated_at=2026-08-17 08:00:00 is arm 1's start and entity_connections_votes updated_at=2026-08-17 11:17:04 is arm 2's start, i.e. arm 1's end; the cancel landed at 14:00:24. **The DONATIONS arm ran 11,824s — 3h17m, 55% of the budget** — and votes+cosponsors+appointments+oversight+holds+gifts+contracts shared the remaining 9,800s. WHY: donations is incremental on an updated_at watermark, and the FEC merge/re-split work ([[FIX-933]]/[[FIX-934]]/[[FIX-954]]/[[FIX-955]]) bulk-rewrote financial_relationships — by week of updated_at, 2026-07-27 touched 1,201,953 rows across 820,602 distinct donors and 2026-08-03 touched 2,721,613 rows across 1,358,662 donors — so the incremental arm degenerated into a near-full rebuild and wrote 4,011,180 edges against the 5,706,655 donation edges that exist, ~70% of the table, matching the ~71% of donors the dirty set covered. That IS inside the 07-29..08-03 window this bullet correctly dated; the bullet attributed it to the wrong arm. THE THROUGHPUT METRIC WAS STRUCTURALLY BLIND TO IT: the contracts arm's cost scales with its INPUT (3.9M FR rows) while its OUTPUT (189,949 edges) barely moves, so no edges-per-second reading can see contracts growth at all — and conversely the donations blow-up looked like a rate collapse because the edges were real but the work per edge was not. A SECOND, INDEPENDENT REGRESSION IS ALSO REAL BUT IS NOT THE 6h: contract+grant FR rows went 1,467,389 → 3,822,744 across the weeks of 2026-07-06 and 2026-07-13 (a USASpending ingest, EARLIER than the dated window), which pushed the contracts sort past work_mem into a 359MB external merge; and the group estimate is 2,327,285 against 189,949 actual, a 12.3x over-estimate off from_id n_distinct=-0.268211 ([[FIX-1034]]). ALSO CORRECTED: the arm functions' SET statement_timeout TO '30min' clause is DECORATIVE — statement_timeout is armed at CALL start and a nested function cannot re-arm it, which is why the run died at the 6h mark rather than 30 minutes into contracts. WHAT SHIPPED (step 2, which the spec rightly said ships regardless of step 1): migration 20260818000000 — a 5h wall-clock budget checked at ARM BOUNDARIES so the exit is orderly rather than axed mid-statement (1h under the 6h ceiling so the terminal bookkeeping and cursor write always land; the ceiling itself is NOT raised, per [[FIX-985]]), a durable per-arm resume checkpoint in pipeline_state.entity_connections_rebuild_cursor so a budget exit banks its arms and the next firing skips them, and per-arm elapsed seconds in metadata.arm_timings — that last being the observability gap that permitted the misattribution in the first place. The budget is overridable via pipeline_state.entity_connections_rebuild_budget so the repros exercise shipped code rather than a test variant. Reproduced locally against prod-clone data, both paths: budget exit banked arm 1 and closed partial with 'budget exhausted — resumable at arm rebuild_entity_connections_votes (1 of 11 arms banked)', the next firing logged 'resuming cycle ... 1 arm(s) already banked', SKIPPED donations and banked votes+cosponsors; and a forced 5s statement_timeout closed the row partial with canceled=true, elapsed_seconds=5, the cancelled arm correctly NOT banked. Step 3 (arm splitting) stays DEFERRED and is now much less obviously needed. Follow-ups filed: [[FIX-1058]] (the bgworker starvation this session's log pull named), [[FIX-1059]] (the retired-vs-broken detector gap that [[FIX-1053]] surfaced). <!--id:FIX-1056-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **The request-path probe is blind to the Cloudflare layer — it curls the Vercel origin, and cannot be repointed while Under Attack is on** — Found 2026-08-17 (cc-prompt-63) while adding the 526 note to docs/CLOUDFLARE.md. THE DEFECT: the [[FIX-1026]] request-path-probe job in .github/workflows/platform-snapshot.yml inherited the snapshot job's APP_URL default, which is the VERCEL ORIGIN (civitics-civitics.vercel.app). The probe exists to answer 'can a user load the site', but a user's request traverses Cloudflare then Vercel — so probing the origin tests only the second half and is structurally blind to every edge-layer failure. NOT THEORETICAL, TWICE OVER: on 2026-08-12 civitics.com served Cloudflare 526 for much of the day (expired ORIGIN certificate, renewals failing silently behind the proxy) while the vercel.app URL kept serving — platform-snapshot stayed GREEN through the whole outage. That is the same shape as the 2026-08-11 522 that FIX-1026 was built for; the job was pointed at the one host that cannot see it. THE OBVIOUS FIX IS BLOCKED, AND THAT IS THE REAL FINDING. Repointing at civitics.com today makes the job fail every hour forever, because the zone is still at security_level=under_attack and challenges non-browser clients. Measured against the live zone the same day: GET / -> 403, /officials -> 403, /api/officials/<id>/responsiveness -> 403, every one carrying 'Cf-Mitigated: challenge', and the 403 persists with a browser User-Agent. A permanently-red pager is a disabled pager, so this is strictly worse than the blind spot and was NOT shipped. THE UNDER ATTACK STATE IS ITSELF A CORRECTION: a planning note recorded Under Attack as turned off on 08-12, but the zone says otherwise and so does the platform's own loop — pipeline_state.cf_mitigation_loop.tripped is null, which by the CLOUDFLARE.md rule means the loop did not set the level, and the loop logged skip_already_escalated twice on 2026-08-16 ('3 breach hours, but the zone is already at security_level=under_attack and this loop did not set it'). So it is a human setting still in force, and docs/CLOUDFLARE.md has been corrected accordingly. SAME ROOT BLOCKS THE OTHER HALF OF THE MONITORING GAP: FIX-1026's header already notes that true minutes-scale detection needs an external uptime service, and Under Attack blocks those too — so the zone posture, not the repo, is the binding constraint on request-path monitoring. WHAT SHIPPED THIS SESSION: the probe env now reads a dedicated PROBE_URL secret first, falling back to CIVITICS_APP_URL then the origin default, so the eventual flip is a secret change with no code change; and the workflow carries the measured 403s plus the two conditions that unblock it. FIX SHAPE, pick one: (1) take the zone off under_attack (already the standing Pending item in CLOUDFLARE.md, and the real test of whether Common Exploit Paths holds alone), then set PROBE_URL to https://civitics.com; or (2) leave the posture and add a WAF skip rule admitting this probe specifically — a secret header is the cleanest key, since UA and IP are both weak. Prefer (1); it fixes the external-uptime gap in the same move. Whichever is chosen, verify with the three curls above BEFORE flipping the secret. ALSO CORRECTED while reading the live zone: Always Use HTTPS is On, not Off as the posture table said, and there are three custom WAF rules (Common Exploit Paths, the WAF - SSL ACME skip, Meta), not two. Cross-ref [[FIX-1026]], [[FIX-1045]], [[FIX-799]]. <!--id:FIX-1057-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **Monday/Wednesday starvation window is bgworker-slot exhaustion, not query contention — pg_cron may request 32 concurrent jobs from a 12-slot pool** — Found 2026-08-18 (cc-prompt-66) while hunting the Monday 09:xx-16:08 starvation window named in [[FIX-1052]]. THE MECHANISM IS NAMED, THE CONSUMER IS NOT. Pulled the Supabase Analytics postgres_logs for 2026-08-17 13:50-16:25 UTC. Through the entire 14:00-16:08 tail — that is, AFTER the EC rebuild was cancelled at 14:00:24 and with nothing at all in data_sync_log — the log carries three independent message classes that all mean "a process could not be started in time": (1) jobid 40 (derived-mvs-unit-watchdog, every 2 min) logs "cron job 40 starting" followed EXACTLY 10 seconds later by "cron job 40 job startup timeout", firing after firing for hours — 10s is pg_cron cron.task_start_timeout, so the bgworker never registered; (2) "autovacuum worker took too long to start; canceled" and "autovacuum worker started without a worker entry", which the autovacuum launcher emits when a requested worker does not register in time; (3) "could not accept SSL connection: EOF detected" and "Connection reset by peer" in a continuous drip, i.e. clients abandoning during the TLS handshake because the postmaster cannot complete accepts. THE DECISIVE NEGATIVE RESULT — IT IS NOT A HEAVY QUERY. auto_explain.log_min_duration is 10000 on prod, so EVERY statement over 10s in that window was logged. The only ones that appear are Supabase platform telemetry: SUM(pg_database_size(...)) at 10.4s and 17.6s, and the pg_stat_statements roll-ups at 12.7s, 13.5s, 13.9s and 16.5s. Not one pipeline query, not one user query. That is precisely why data_sync_log is silent across the tail and why FIX-1052 could not find a culprit in it: none of our work was running. The box was not busy executing — it could not START processes. THE STRUCTURAL OVER-SUBSCRIPTION, measured on prod the same night: max_worker_processes=12 (configuration file), cron.max_running_jobs=32 (default, and per the Supabase config note NOT overridable), max_parallel_workers=2, max_logical_replication_workers=4, max_connections=60, autovacuum_max_workers=3. pg_cron is permitted 32 concurrent job workers out of a 12-slot pool it shares with parallel query and logical replication, and nothing enforces the difference — the ceiling is discovered at runtime as "job startup timeout". Note this is the same mwp=12 that failed its first Monday. WHAT WAS SHIPPED, AND WHAT IT IS FOR: a self-limiting bgworker census sampler (migration 20260818002000) — an UNLOGGED bgworker_census table plus sample_bgworker_census(), scheduled every 2 minutes as jobname bgworker-census, deliberately on the SAME cadence as the jobid-40 watchdog whose startup timeout is the symptom, so a MISSING sample is itself data (this job could not get a worker either). It no-ops unless pipeline_state.bgworker_census.expires_at is in the future, armed for 48h from 2026-08-18, so it disarms itself even if the cron job outlives the investigation. - [x] 🟠 S — **nightly fec-phase and fec-backfill can run concurrently against prod and share one resume-cursor key — observed overlapping 2026-08-19** — OBSERVED, not theoretical. On 2026-08-19 the fec-backfill resume (run 32200957208, cycles=2020) was writing from 00:22 to 03:15:31, and the nightly-sync fec-phase (run 32210358973) opened its OWN fec_bulk data_sync_log row at 03:02:27 — a 13-minute overlap with two pipelines running runFecBulkPipeline() against the same prod tables at once. Mechanism: the two workflows declare DIFFERENT GitHub Actions concurrency groups (nightly.yml group: nightly-sync, fec-backfill.yml group: fec-backfill), so each is serialized only against ITSELF. Nothing serializes them against each other even though both reach the same pipeline, the same financial_relationships / financial_entities write path, and — the sharp edge — the same single pipeline_state key fec_bulk_run_state. That key holds the FIX-754 per-stage resume cursor, so two live runs read and overwrite each others progress: immediately after the backfill finished all three stages (donor-entities 1944958/1944958, indiv-to-candidate 2165106/2165106, indiv-to-committee 1149355/1149355) the key was observed back at indiv-to-committee cursor=1060000 status=in-progress, i.e. the nightly had re-established state for the same cycle and was redoing work the backfill had completed. NOT DATA DAMAGE in this instance: the writes are ON CONFLICT upserts and FIX-1008 skip-overwrite means unchanged rows are skipped, so the cost was wasted IO on a box whose write throughput is the known bottleneck ([[FIX-961]]). But the resume cursor is not idempotent state — a crash during an overlap can strand a cursor that neither run owns, and the FIX-754 accounting silently under- or over-reports. Direction: give both workflows the SAME concurrency group (e.g. group: fec-pipeline) so GHA serializes them, and/or take a DB-level advisory lock around runFecBulkPipeline() so a second invocation refuses rather than interleaves (the pg_cron procedures already use a session advisory lock for exactly this — see the reference_pgcron_procedure_pattern precedent). - [x] 🟠 M — **Census result: the Mon/Wed starvation is NOT bgworker-slot exhaustion — pg_cron with use_background_workers=off never takes a worker slot at all** — The bgworker census [[FIX-1058]] armed on 2026-08-18 has been read (2026-08-20 01:5x UTC, 1,182 samples over 08-18 01:12 to 08-20 01:10, self-disarmed on schedule). IT REFUTES THE HYPOTHESIS IT WAS BUILT TO CONFIRM. THE MEASUREMENT. Through the 2026-08-19 saturation, non-client backends peaked at EIGHT against max_worker_processes=12, and every single backend_type present was a singleton: archiver, autovacuum launcher, background writer, checkpointer, logical replication launcher, pg_cron launcher, pg_net worker, walwriter, plus an occasional autovacuum worker (max_concurrent 1 for each of the nine). There was no pool of workers competing for slots at any sampled moment. Client backends peaked at 25 against max_connections=60, so connections were not exhausted either. THE STRUCTURAL POINT THAT SETTLES IT INDEPENDENTLY OF THE CENSUS: cron.use_background_workers is OFF on prod. With that setting pg_cron does NOT request a background worker per job — it opens a libpq CLIENT CONNECTION and sends the command as one simple query, which is the same fact [[FIX-1063]] relies on for its invalid-transaction-termination finding. So FIX-1058's central arithmetic (pg_cron may request 32 concurrent job workers from a 12-slot pool) cannot be the mechanism: pg_cron never asks that pool for a job worker. cron.max_running_jobs=32 bounds concurrent libpq connections, not bgworkers, and 32 against max_connections=60 is not over-subscribed. WHAT job startup timeout ACTUALLY MEANS HERE: failure to ESTABLISH A CONNECTION within pg_cron's task-start window, not failure to acquire a worker slot. That relocates the bottleneck to the postmaster's ability to fork and complete a handshake, which is exactly what FIX-1058's own log evidence showed and mis-filed as corroboration — could not accept SSL connection EOF detected and Connection reset by peer are clients dying IN THE HANDSHAKE, the signature of a postmaster that cannot accept, not of a worker pool that is full. THE CENSUS CORROBORATES A BOX-WIDE STALL BY ITS OWN ABSENCE, which is what it was designed to do: sampling every 2 minutes it should land 15 samples per half hour, and it landed 15/15 through 08:30, then 8, 4, 10, 8, 9, 2 as the morning degraded, then ZERO samples in BOTH the 12:00 and 12:30 buckets, then 1/15 at 13:00, 14:00 and 14:30. The 12:00-13:00 blackout is precisely the window in which 91 of 91 cron firings died. The sampler could not get a connection either. POSITIVE ATTRIBUTION IS STILL INHERITED, NOT PROVEN HERE: the I/O-starvation reading (roughly 265 GB of physical reads against a 256 MB shared_buffers, confirmed here as shared_buffers=32768 8kB pages) comes from the 08-19 triage, not from this census. The census establishes the NEGATIVES (not slots, not connections) and the box-wide stall; it does not by itself prove which resource saturated. Do not record I/O starvation as census-proven. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE CANDIDATE FIXES in FIX-1058: raising max_worker_processes further is a non-remedy for cron startup timeouts and should be dropped from the list; thinning the job population and staggering the every-2-minute watchdogs off boundary minutes remain live but now target connection-accept pressure rather than slot contention. TEARDOWN performed with this bullet per FIX-1058's own instruction. **MEASURED EVIDENCE FOR THE CONNECTION-ACCEPT MECHANISM — AND ITS BOUND (appended 2026-08-24, cc-prompt-76; append-only, nothing above is rewritten).** Three prod windows, all counted from `cron.job_run_details`, isolate the variable this bullet relocated the problem to. **(1) One long statement — 2026-08-19 12:00–13:30 UTC, the unwindowed single-statement EC donations arm: 136 firings, 5 succeeded, 131 failed, all 131 `job startup timeout` — 96.3 percent dead.** **(2) Windowed writes on an otherwise IDLE box — 2026-08-21, drain 2: 1,457 firings across the full 24h, 0 failures, 0 startup timeouts** (the 144/0/0 figure quoted from that session's 2h15m slice holds for the entire day, not just the slice). **(3) Windowed writes with CONCURRENT load — 2026-08-24 08:00–13:16 UTC, jobid 22's first scheduled firing under [[FIX-1069]]: 327 firings, 128 succeeded, 199 failed, all 199 `job startup timeout` — 60.9 percent dead.** Window (2) is the first direct evidence for this bullet's mechanism: short committed transactions do leave the postmaster able to accept connections, where one long statement does not. **Window (3) is the bound on that finding, and the bullet must be read carrying both halves — windowing alone does NOT keep the box accepting connections when other writers share it.** THE CORRECTED STATEMENT: what tracks the failure rate is **the duration of the longest single uninterrupted statement**, not the number of statements and not the total write volume. Drain 2's windows were all short and cost 0 percent; 08-24's donations window 5 ran 3h49m as one statement (see [[FIX-1101]]) and its hours cost 42–49 failures each; 08-19's single statement ran ~6h and cost 96 percent. On 08-24 the starvation is visible from 08:00 — the EC job's own start, not from 11:00 when it was noticed — and the per-hour failed counts rise with it (08:00 34, 09:00 23, 10:00 35, 11:00 42, 12:00 49 of 61) then fall to 0 by 14:00, 45 minutes after the job was cancelled. The self-amplification is explicit and measured: jobid 44, the watchdog holding the [[FIX-1071]] 18,000 s budget row, lost 24 of its 30 firings in the 12:00 hour and therefore cancelled the offending run 976 s late. **So this bullet's §9.2-style claim that windowed writes do not starve the box is TRUE ONLY ON AN IDLE BOX** — it is a property of the measurement conditions, not of windowing. Windowing made the writer bounded and resumable, which is what FIX-1069 claimed and delivered; it did not make the box available. Cross-ref [[FIX-1058]], [[FIX-1052]], [[FIX-1063]], [[FIX-1022]], [[FIX-1069]], [[FIX-1071]], [[FIX-1101]], [[FIX-969]]. <!--id:FIX-1072-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **A pg_cron job startup timeout is a SILENT SKIP — the firing is lost with no retry, no alert, and no gap in any log a human reads** — FILE-ONLY (design options below; do NOT build from this bullet without picking one first). Surfaced by the 2026-08-19 saturation triage. When pg_cron cannot start a job it records status=failed with return_message job startup timeout in cron.job_run_details and MOVES ON. There is no retry and no backoff: the firing is simply gone, and the next occurrence is one full cadence away. For a daily job that is 24h of skipped work; for the weekly arms it is a week. THE SCALE IS NOT MARGINAL. On 2026-08-19 between 12:00 and 13:29 UTC, 91 of 91 firings across all jobs died this way. Lifetime, the class has killed hundreds of firings (see [[FIX-1022]] for 29 as of 08-11, [[FIX-1052]] for 191 over 08-10..08-17). WHY IT IS INVISIBLE RATHER THAN MERELY BAD: a job that never STARTS writes nothing to data_sync_log, so the pipeline-health surfaces that operators and the canary actually read cannot see it — a skipped firing and a job that was never scheduled look identical from data_sync_log. [[FIX-968]]'s check_cron_job_health() does read cron.job_run_details, but it deliberately treats this class as REPORT-ONLY, because escalating on it would fire the canary most weeks and train the alert to be ignored (the FIX-943 cause-vs-consequence rule). That reasoning was right for a noisy symptom and is now hiding a real one. TWO DESIGN OPTIONS, deliberately NOT chosen here. (A) RE-FIRE ONCE. A small watchdog (the [[FIX-1063]] jobid-44 pattern) scans for a startup-timeout row whose job has not since succeeded and re-invokes the command once, with a lockout so a persistently-starved job cannot spin. Pro: recovers the lost work the same day, which is the actual harm. Con: it re-fires INTO the same starved window that killed the first attempt, so it must carry a delay and a give-up count, and any job that is not idempotent must be excluded by name — that exclusion list is the real design work, not the watchdog. (B) ALERT TIER. Leave the firing lost but make the LOSS loud: give the canary a distinct condition for consecutive-startup-timeouts-on-one-job and for a burst across many jobs, separate from the existing report-only line, so the noise concern is handled by tiering rather than by silence. Pro: no new execution paths, no idempotency risk. Con: recovers nothing; a human still has to re-run it. RECOMMENDATION IF FORCED: (B) first because it is safe and immediately informative, then (A) narrowly scoped to the jobs whose procedures are already resumable and idempotent — which after [[FIX-1069]] includes the EC rebuild. PREREQUISITE: [[FIX-1072]] relocated the mechanism from bgworker-slot exhaustion to connection-accept pressure, so any re-fire design should assume the constraint is the postmaster accepting connections, not a worker pool draining. Cross-ref [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-1022]], [[FIX-1052]], [[FIX-1058]], [[FIX-1063]], [[FIX-1072]]. <!--id:FIX-1073-->

FIX-1063's own function comment asserts that its cancel lands in the target procedure's FIX-1028 or FIX-1021 WHEN query_canceled handler, which closes the row partial rather than leaving it stranded. That assertion is FALSE for two of the seven jobs it budgets. Probed pg_proc.prosrc on prod: refresh_derived_mvs, refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental and run_entity_connections_rebuild all contain a query_canceled handler, while refresh_financial_entity_totals_incremental and run_rule_taggers contain only WHEN OTHERS. Per [[FIX-1028]], PL/pgSQL's OTHERS does NOT match query_canceled (57014) or assert_failure, so pg_cancel_backend blows straight through the handler and out of the procedure, skipping the terminal UPDATE. This is the exact defect FIX-1028 was filed for, in two procedures the FIX-1028 sweep did not reach. CONSEQUENCE beyond the untidy row: a stranded running row is indistinguishable from a live run to anything that reads data_sync_log for liveness, which is why [[FIX-1101]]'s widened FEC interlock deliberately probes pg_locks and pg_stat_activity instead of a status column. It also means the runtime of a cancelled job is unrecoverable from the log — started_at to now is arithmetic, not a measurement ([[FIX-1035]]). FIX SHAPE: add WHEN query_canceled handlers to both procedures on the FIX-1028 pattern (by name, FIRST, before WHEN OTHERS), closing the row partial with the elapsed span and the cancel detail. Then re-audit: grep every procedure named in cron_job_budget for a query_canceled handler and treat a missing one as a budget that cannot land cleanly. Also reconcile the two rows already stranded. TWO SEPARATE FINDINGS. FINDING ONE, a status divergence: cron.job_run_details runid 15272 records status succeeded for 07:00:00 to 07:22:41 (1361.9s, return_message CALL), while the data_sync_log row the same procedure wrote for the same span records status failed with error chord_donor_type_party_flows_mv: could not resize shared mem. The procedure caught its unit failure, recorded it honestly in its own log, and then RETURNED NORMALLY — so pg_cron sees a clean CALL. Anything monitoring cron.job_run_details for weekly-MV health is therefore blind to a failed unit by construction, and the two sources of truth disagree about the same run. FINDING TWO, the failure itself: chord_donor_type_party_flows_mv could not resize shared memory — a parallel-worker DSM allocation failure. This is the same MV family that took prod down twice ([[FIX-1015]] era, the reason jobid 10 was switched off in the first place), so the fence held and the box survived, which is the good news and should be recorded as such: the FIX-1030 unit watchdog and the FIX-1021 per-unit budget did their job, five units succeeded, one failed, nothing cascaded. - [x] 🔴 S — **The supervised EC drain is the one window driver FIX-1101's watchdog cannot see — and --until cannot interrupt a window already running** — MEASURED on prod during the FIX-1101 acceptance drain, 2026-08-25 23:59 to 2026-08-26 01:58 UTC. The drain banked 12 of 16 windows cleanly at a mean of 343s (sigma 16s) and 1,794,291 edges, then window 13 ran 1,902s and took the box into connection starvation: jobids 40 and 44 failed on job startup timeout at 01:52, 01:54, 01:56 and 01:58, recovering only at 01:58:07. THREE DISTINCT DEFECTS, all in the operator path rather than the scheduled path. ONE, scripts/drain-ec-donations.mjs does not publish pipeline_state.entity_connections_window_inflight, so enforce_ec_window_budget() (FIX-1101) is structurally blind to it. The 30-minute per-window bound shipped the same night would have cancelled window 13 at 1,800s; instead it ran unbounded. The scheduled driver publishes and is bounded; the hand-driven one that runs for two hours in a quiet window is not, which is exactly backwards. TWO, --until is checked only BETWEEN windows (the loop tests the deadline before starting window i). Window 13 started at about 01:26, legally ahead of the 01:45 stop, and then overran it by 13 minutes. The flag is documented as a hard stop and is not one; it is a hard START gate. THREE, and this is the operationally nastiest: KILLING THE CLIENT DOES NOT STOP THE QUERY. The node process and its psql child were killed at 01:53 and pg_stat_activity still showed pid 162913 running rebuild_ec_donations_incr_window at 1,902s two minutes later, waiting on IO DataFileRead. PostgreSQL does not notice a departed client mid-statement (client_connection_check_interval defaults to 0), so the window kept consuming I/O until a manual pg_cancel_backend(162913) at 01:58:08. Any runbook step that says stop the drain by killing it is wrong. FOURTH THING, a near-miss worth recording: killing the drain also skipped its FIX-943 vacuum tail, leaving entity_connections at 418,198 dead tuples after a 1.79M-edge bulk rewrite. That was cleaned up only because jobid 6 ec-vacuum-analyze is scheduled 0 2 star star 0,3 and 08-26 was a Wednesday — it ran 02:00:00 to 02:12:01 (721.7s vs the ~90s a clean EC vacuum takes) and restored 0 dead / 100 percent all-visible. On any other weekday the table would have sat degraded until autovacuum reached it. FIX SHAPE: (a) have the drain publish and clear the same in-flight row the driver does, so it inherits the per-window bound for free, and handle the resulting cancel as a clean early stop rather than an error; (b) rename or re-document --until honestly, and add a mid-window deadline check that cancels via pg_cancel_backend on the drain's own connection; (c) make the vacuum tail survive an interrupted run — a SIGINT handler, or accept that (a) turns a runaway into a normal cancel that reaches the tail. CONTEXT for why window 13 was slow at all: window 12 had already taken 1,385.2s against the same 343s mean on comparable work, and prod's Observability panel during the drain showed CPU 54.06 percent of which IOwait was 41.36 percent, with disk at 2,078 of a 3,000 Max IOPS cap (69.3 percent). A single drain consumes about two thirds of provisioned IOPS on an otherwise idle box, so a degraded window tips it over the cap. See [[FIX-1107]] and docs/audits/2026-08-20-fix1069-ec-incremental-windowing.md section 13. Cross-ref [[FIX-1101]], [[FIX-1069]], [[FIX-943]], [[FIX-1035]], [[FIX-1063]]. <!--id:FIX-1110-->
- [x] 🟠 L — **EC rebuild becomes a paced background crawl — one bounded unit per firing, spend under refill** — **Structural answer to [[FIX-1107]]/[[FIX-969]]'s "no scheduled writer knows the I/O budget exists": the EC rebuild becomes a background crawl — ONE bounded unit per firing, paced so spend is under refill.** Craig locked the scheduling philosophy on 2026-08-27 after three measured I/O-budget exhaustions in three days (08-24 EC window 5; 08-25 jobid 13; 08-26 the FIX-1101 acceptance drain): derived-layer staleness of a few days is acceptable, the box's daily Disk IO burst budget is the constraint, and bulk work becomes a slow constant background crawl that yields to users. SHIPPED (migration 20260827000000): (1) `p_max_units int DEFAULT NULL` on the EXISTING `run_entity_connections_rebuild()` — NULL is byte-for-byte the prior behaviour, N runs at most N PENDING units (one donations window, or one non-donations arm — exactly what [[FIX-1056]]/[[FIX-1069]] already made bankable) and exits 'partial' with `unit_capped=true` and a resumable cursor. NOT a fork: one body, one truth. (2) A unit-duration ring of the last 50 in `pipeline_state.ec_crawl.recent_units` plus a 2x-rolling-median backoff (2 h) — the throttle sensor. Duration is the sensor because the burst balance is readable from no catalog, and because the throttle announces itself in duration: prod 08-25 jobid 13 went ~3 s -> ~8 s -> >1,680 s per chunk across the 11:15 throttle inflection. Median not mean, per unit CLASS, with a 5-sample cold-start guard. (3) Blackout windows (UTC, wrap-around supported) — mechanism ships, policy is data, default empty. (4) `ec-crawl` pg_cron job at `*/15` with a [[FIX-1071]] outside budget row at 1,800 s, created INACTIVE for a Craig-gated Phase 4. THE PACING ARITHMETIC, from FIX-1101's clean 08-26 receipt (jobid 2, 2,654 s, arm_timings donations_incr_windows 1385 / _external 878 / _contracts 307 / eight arms 0-26 s each): a donations window is ~346 s at ~2,500 IOPS against a 1,000 IOPS baseline, which is ~540 s of burst refill, which is why 12-13 back-to-back windows exhaust the pool and match the measured 75-minute 08-25 burst. Pacing is per-FIRING not per-cycle, so the ceiling does not depend on cycle composition: 96 firings/day x 346 s = 33,216 writer-s = 51,817 refill-s = 60 percent of the day's refill, with 40 percent headroom, and no cycle shape can exceed it. ONE KNOB THE ARITHMETIC ADDED, not in the original design: `min_cycle_interval_minutes` (default 360). The ten non-donations arms are UNCONDITIONAL full rebuilds and rerun every cycle; because already-banked windows skip WITHOUT consuming a firing, a small-dirty-set cycle completes in ~13 firings ~3.3 h, which would spin those arms 6-7x/day against once-a-week today. Not a budget problem (8 of 10 cost <=26 s) but `_external` 878 s + `_contracts` 307 s is ~2 h/day of recomputing unchanged edges. HAZARD FOUND AND FIXED IN THE MIGRATION, worth recording: adding a parameter creates a SECOND procedure, it does not replace the old one, and `CALL run_entity_connections_rebuild('incremental')` then fails with `procedure ... is not unique` — a HARD ERROR that would have silently stopped the EC arm entirely. Measured on local before writing. The migration DROPs `(text)` before creating `(text,int)`; any future parameter add must do the same. PROVEN ON LOCAL against a 25,932-donor / 214,031-edge dirty set: (i) EQUIVALENCE — 26 firings of `p_max_units := 1` produced 214,031 edges and one `p_max_units := NULL` run produced 214,031 edges, symmetric difference 0 in BOTH directions over every column with evidence_ids sorted, and identical closed cycle (staging truncated, all 16 window watermarks at target, cursor cleared); (ii) BACKOFF — a 7 s unit against a seeded 1 s median over 5 samples set backoff_until, the next firing gate-skipped with a distinct `skipped` data_sync_log row, expiry resumed; (iii) BLACKOUT — a window covering now skipped (including the midnight wrap case 23:13-01:13), one not covering now ran; (iv) INTERLOCK — `fec_bulk_run_state` present deferred, cleared ran; (vi) the [[FIX-1063]] outside bound CANCEL BRANCH, never before exercised anywhere, fired on a forced overrun (ec-crawl cancelled at 16 s against a 10 s budget, signaled=t, `cron_job_budget_action` row written) while the FIX-1101 inside bound correctly declined on the same firing (16 s < 1,800 s) — the two bounds layering exactly as designed; (vii) CYCLE COOLDOWN — a closed cycle 3 min old under a 360-min minimum skipped, an OPEN cycle (cursor present) correctly ignored the cooldown and ran. Phase 4 (Craig-gated, quiet window): activate ec-crawl, pause jobid 2 `rebuild-ec-incremental` BY NAME, confirm jobid 22 stays paused; both stay defined for their cron.job_run_details history and the un-pause condition is "never, unless the crawl is retired". Ledger and the crawl's own daily consumption: docs/audits/2026-08-27-io-budget-burst-ledger.md. Cross-ref [[FIX-1107]], [[FIX-969]], [[FIX-1101]], [[FIX-1069]], [[FIX-1056]], [[FIX-1063]], [[FIX-1071]], [[FIX-1110]], [[FIX-1030]], [[FIX-1035]], [[FIX-1028]]. <!--id:FIX-1111-->
- [x] 🔴 M — **Watermark-ratchet census: three budget-cancellable cron procedures bank chunks but not progress** — **Census: three budget-cancellable cron procedures write their progress watermark ONLY at end-of-run, so a watchdog cancel discards every chunk they committed and the job can never converge.** MECHANISM, established by [[FIX-1107]]'s attribution of the 08-25 stall: `QUERY_CANCELED` (57014) is NOT matched by `EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS` — PL/pgSQL's OTHERS matches every error except query_canceled and assert_failure — so a cancel from `enforce_cron_job_budgets()` ([[FIX-1063]]) or the unit watchdog propagates straight out of the procedure, skipping the terminal watermark write. The work the per-chunk COMMITs already banked is real and durable; the watermark that would let the next run SKIP it is not. So the next firing redoes everything from the old watermark, hits the same budget, and is cancelled again. This is not a slow job — it is an UNCONVERGEABLE one. INSTRUMENT: pg_proc.prosrc on prod (bodies verified byte-identical to local by md5), classifying each procedure by (a) does it carry a `cron_job_budget` row or fall under `enforce_derived_mvs_unit_budget()`, (b) is the watermark write inside the chunk loop or after it; plus cron.job_run_details across the full retained window for whether a cancel has ALREADY happened. AT RISK — (a) AND (b) both true, zero `WHEN query_canceled` handlers in all three: (1) `refresh_financial_entity_totals_incremental` (jobid 13, budget 7,200 s), watermark key `financial_entity_totals_watermark`, written after all three chunk loops at ~84 percent through the body while the loops commit at 60/71/80 percent — **2 budget cancels already, most recently 2026-08-25 10:00 runid 15453 at 8,047.8 s**, which is the confirmed case this census generalises; (2) `refresh_donor_party_rollup_incremental` (jobid 17, budget 1,800 s), key `donor_party_rollup_watermark`, written at ~87 percent after loops committing at 72 and 84 percent — 0 budget cancels but **1 statement_timeout cancel already**, and a timeout cancel is the same 57014 through the same unguarded OTHERS; (3) `run_rule_taggers` (jobid 12, budget 7,200 s), key `size_tags:donation_watermark` — DIFFERENT SHAPE and a partial exception: the signature write and the rebuild share one transaction and roll back together, so there is no watermark ratchet, but the unguarded OTHERS still lets a cancel skip the terminal data_sync_log update and strand the row 'running' ([[FIX-1028]]'s class) — **1 budget cancel already, 2026-08-25 16:00 at 7,325.8 s**, plus 3 statement_timeout cancels. NOT AT RISK, and worth recording so the pattern is legible: `refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental` (jobid 24) writes its watermark INSIDE the chunk loop and carries a query_canceled handler (5 timeout cancels survived, [[FIX-1002]]/[[FIX-1003]]); `refresh_treemap_individuals_global` (jobid 26) updates a per-chunk cursor inside the loop (1 budget cancel survived); `run_entity_connections_rebuild` (jobids 2/22/ec-crawl) carries per-window watermarks and three query_canceled handlers ([[FIX-1069]]/[[FIX-1028]], and [[FIX-1111]] preserves this); `refresh_agency_staffing_rollup` (jobid 25) has no watermark at all so there is nothing to ratchet; `refresh_contract_flow_rollups` (jobid 28) has ZERO COMMITs — the whole procedure is one transaction, so a cancel is atomic and mis-records nothing, but it is also unresumable, which is a different and currently-unexercised risk at a 10,800 s budget on a job measured at 1,053 s. THE RULE THIS ESTABLISHES: **a procedure that can be cancelled from outside must either write its watermark in the same transaction as the chunk that earned it, or catch `query_canceled` BY NAME and write the watermark before re-raising. A per-chunk COMMIT without a per-chunk watermark is not resumability — it is work that will be done again.** Filed as a census only; nothing is fixed here except what [[FIX-1111]] already covers for the EC arm. Fix order should follow the evidence: jobid 13 first (2 cancels, currently PAUSED for exactly this reason), then jobid 17, then jobid 12's stranded-row leg. Cross-ref [[FIX-1107]], [[FIX-1063]], [[FIX-1028]], [[FIX-969]], [[FIX-1031]], [[FIX-1111]]. <!--id:FIX-1112-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **anon can EXECUTE refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental() on prod; no sweep exists for re-widened grants** — **`refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental()` is EXECUTE-able by `anon` on prod — an unauthenticated /rest/v1/rpc/ request is one connection away from starting the 4-hour donor rollup.** MEASURED on prod 2026-08-27 while auditing grants after [[FIX-1111]] recreated a sibling procedure: `pg_proc.proacl` carries `anon=X/postgres | authenticated=X/postgres`. This is Supabase's default-grant behaviour on newly created routines (project_rpc_execute_grant_hardening), not something anyone chose. SCOPE OF THE AUDIT: of six cron-only procedures sampled, four are already correctly revoked (`enforce_cron_job_budgets`, `refresh_treemap_individuals_global`, `rebuild_official_vote_stats`, and FIX-1111's own `ec_crawl_gate`/`ec_crawl_record_unit`), and `run_entity_connections_rebuild` was revoked by FIX-1111 (migration 20260827000200) because FIX-1111's own DROP+CREATE is what re-applied the default to it. **This one is the remaining outlier and was NOT touched, because it is not FIX-1111's object to change.** WHY IT MATTERS: jobid 24 `donor-rollup-refresh` carries a 14,400 s [[FIX-1063]] budget and has been measured at 7,171.9 s and 7,186.6 s in a single day; [[FIX-1107]] establishes that the box's whole daily I/O burst pool is 30-75 minutes, so an attacker-triggered or accident-triggered firing is materially expensive, not merely untidy. It is also idempotent and advisory-locked, so the blast radius is I/O and connections rather than data corruption. WHY IT IS PROBABLY SAFE TO FIX: no PostgREST caller exists. Every reference in the tree is a pg_cron command, a dashboard display string (`apps/civitics/app/dashboard/DashboardClient.tsx` retryCmd), or a `packages/data` script using a direct `pg.Client` that connects as `postgres` — verified by grep 2026-08-27. FIX SHAPE: a one-line migration, `REVOKE ALL ON PROCEDURE public.refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental() FROM PUBLIC, anon, authenticated;` plus `NOTIFY pgrst`, mirroring 20260827000200 exactly. BROADER FOLLOW-UP worth doing at the same time: this was a six-procedure spot check, not a sweep. The real work is enumerating EVERY `public` routine whose `proacl` grants anon/authenticated EXECUTE, classifying each as route-called or cron-only, and revoking the cron-only set — and adding that check to the daily canary so a future CREATE OR REPLACE cannot silently re-widen one, which is exactly the trap FIX-1111 fell into and caught. Cross-ref [[FIX-1111]], [[FIX-1101]], [[FIX-1107]], [[FIX-1063]], [[FIX-1002]], [[FIX-1003]]. <!--id:FIX-1113-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **Ship get_ec_crawl_health() — the lag metric the tier-vs-ingest decision reads from** — FIX-1111 made the EC rebuild a paced crawl, which converts an availability problem into a LATENCY one: the crawl cannot starve the box, but it can fall arbitrarily far behind ingest and nothing measures that. This ships the instrument. get_ec_crawl_health() returns ONE jsonb aggregate (PostgREST caps set-returning RPCs at 1000 rows) carrying: EC scalar watermark age in days, dirty-set rows/donors, trailing-7d firing census split into units-run vs skipped vs backoff vs failed, cumulative per-reason skip counters, units-per-cycle for the last 5 closed cycles, last cycle closed at, the open cycle, and the live ec_crawl config. Wired into the persisted status-snapshot payload as section ec_crawl_health — NOTE the payload cutover lag: the dashboard reads the PERSISTED snapshot, so the tile appears only after platform-snapshot (every 10 min) picks it up, not at deploy. THE DECISION RULE IT SERVES, recorded verbatim: lag greater than 7 days for two consecutive weeks WITH backoffs on more than about 25 percent of firings means a compute-tier conversation; lag greater than 7 days with backoffs rare and units-per-cycle growing means an INGEST conversation (delta aggregation, write amplification, replay pacing). The two-consecutive-weeks half cannot be evaluated from one snapshot, so the RPC exposes lag_days and backoff_rate_7d and emits a signal of ok / lag_high_backoff_high / lag_high_backoff_low; the two-week persistence is the human read across two snapshots, deliberately not faked in SQL. Cross-ref [[FIX-1111]] (the crawl), [[FIX-1107]] (the I/O budget that forced it), [[FIX-1110]] (the supervised drain that shares its path). <!--id:FIX-1114-->
- [x] 🔴 M — **Rebuild entity_connection_stats as a bounded unit — the current procedure OOMs a 2GB box and takes the postmaster with it** — jobid 16 entity-connection-stats-rebuild is PAUSED as of 2026-08-28 (see [[FIX-1103]] for the correlation that justified it). This bullet is the replacement shape. WHY THE CURRENT ONE CANNOT STAY: rebuild_entity_connection_stats() does SET work_mem = 256MB and then CREATE TEMP TABLE ecs_stage AS SELECT ... FROM (SELECT from_id FROM entity_connections UNION ALL SELECT to_id FROM entity_connections) GROUP BY id — an unbounded HashAggregate over TWICE the entity_connections row count, producing about 2.66M groups, on a box with 2GB RAM and 256MB shared_buffers. The apply half is already disciplined (16 uuid-range windows, DELETE+INSERT, COMMIT per window, FIX-703) but the STAGE BUILD is one unbounded statement and it is the half that kills the box. Evidence: 2026-08-10 died at 21610s on statement timeout INSIDE the CREATE TEMP TABLE; the two firings after that both ended in a postmaster restart. REQUIRED SHAPE: make the stage build bounded the way the crawl bounds its units. Either (a) build the stage per uuid-range window so each statement aggregates 1/16th of the keyspace and commits, trading FIX-734's single-scan property for survivability, or (b) keep the single scan but drive it from a watermark so only entities whose edges CHANGED are re-aggregated, which is the same delta shape entity_connections_rebuild already uses. Option (b) is preferred and is a genuine crawl-class unit: it would slot into run_entity_connections_rebuild as one more arm and inherit the pacing, the budget bound, the sensor and the cycle cooldown for free, which also deletes the separate cron job. Whatever ships must lower work_mem to something the box can actually hold and must be measured against prod cardinality before it is scheduled. NOTE the staleness this leaves: entity_connection_stats_mv last rebuilt successfully 2026-08-05, so connection counts are already weeks stale and drifting further while the crawl writes edges continuously — the replacement is not optional maintenance. Cross-ref [[FIX-1103]], [[FIX-1052]], [[FIX-985]], [[FIX-734]], [[FIX-703]], [[FIX-1111]]. <!--id:FIX-1115-->

- [x] 🟠 M — **The EC crawl recomputes unchanged arms every cycle — _external and _contracts rebuild byte-identical row counts for ~1,250 s/cycle** — MEASURED on prod from the FIX-1111 crawl ring, 2026-08-27. The ten non-donations arms in run_entity_connections_rebuild are UNCONDITIONAL full rebuilds: each one DELETEs its connection_type and reinserts from source, every cycle, whether or not the source changed. The ring proves the waste is exact, not approximate — rebuild_entity_connections_external ran twice for 1,148,418 rows total (2 x 574,209, byte-identical) at a median 899.1 s, and rebuild_entity_connections_contracts ran three times for 569,847 rows total (3 x 189,949, byte-identical) at a median 344.6 s. That is ~1,244 s of writer per cycle spent recomputing edges that did not change, against a measured whole-cycle cost of roughly 1,830 s. On a box whose scarce resource is the daily disk burst budget (FIX-1107) this is the single largest remaining source of pure waste in the crawl. FIX SHAPE: a cheap per-arm source-change gate. For each non-donations arm, a fingerprint over that arm's OWN source scope — count plus max timestamp, chosen per arm because the sources differ (votes.updated_at, career_history.updated_at, agencies.updated_at, evidence_cards.updated_at, external_relationships.ingested_at, proposal_cosponsors.created_at which has no updated_at at all, and financial_relationships scoped by the arm's own relationship_type so the four FR-sourced arms do not all fire on any FR write). Skip the arm when the fingerprint is unchanged since its last successful build, banking it for the cycle so the cycle can still close, and record a skipped-unchanged mark so the lag metric can tell idle from gated. THE GATE MUST FAIL OPEN — a fingerprint probe that errors or times out means RUN the arm, never skip it. A gate that silently freezes an arm is the FIX-885 stranded-flag class and would be strictly worse than the waste it replaces. Measured probe costs on the local clone: external_relationships 586 ms, agencies 7 ms, evidence_cards 4 ms, financial_relationships scoped to contract 15,975 ms — all pennies next to the arms they skip. Cross-ref FIX-1111, FIX-1107, FIX-969, FIX-885, FIX-1115. <!--id:FIX-1117-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **The FIX-1117 contracts gate needs a partial index on financial_relationships(updated_at) WHERE relationship_type IN (contract,grant) — the probe costs 98s without one** — MEASURED ON PROD 2026-08-28, immediately after FIX-1117 landed. Nine of the ten per-arm source fingerprints are pennies exactly as designed — oversight 46 ms, gifts/holds/lobbying/cosponsors/appointments/investigation 20-35 ms each, the entity_connections stats fingerprint 1,440 ms, external_relationships 3,365 ms, votes 4,154 ms. One is not: rebuild_entity_connections_contracts measured 111,575 ms on its first prod call and 98,204 ms on a warm second call, so it is NOT a cold-cache artifact. Its scope is financial_relationships WHERE relationship_type IN ('contract','grant') = 3,908,956 rows inside a 12 GB table, and the plan is a Parallel Bitmap Heap Scan driven by financial_relationships_type: the bitmap index scan is cheap, the 3.9M heap fetches are not. Dropping max(updated_at) does not help — count(*) alone measured 98,692 ms with the identical plan, because no existing index can serve it index-only (financial_relationships_derivation leads with relationship_type but does not carry updated_at, and FR's visibility map is too degraded for an index-only scan to be chosen anyway; cf FIX-1034 and the FR dead-tuple work). CONSEQUENCE AND WHAT SHIPPED INSTEAD: 98 s to avoid a 344.6 s arm is still a net win, but it is a poor ratio and it spends the exact resource — prod's daily disk burst budget, FIX-1107 — that the whole FIX-1111 line of work exists to protect, on every cycle, up to four times a day. So FIX-1117 shipped a disabled_arms escape in pipeline_state.ec_arm_source_fingerprints, and rebuild_entity_connections_contracts is in it: a disabled arm returns a NULL fingerprint, which is the gate's fail-open value, so that arm simply runs every cycle exactly as it did before FIX-1117. Nothing is broken; one arm is un-gated. THE FIX: build CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY financial_relationships_contract_grant_updated_at ON public.financial_relationships (updated_at) WHERE relationship_type IN ('contract','grant') — roughly 3.9M entries, on the order of 90 MB — which makes max(updated_at) an O(1) backward index scan and count(*) an index-only scan over 90 MB instead of 3.9M heap fetches. CONCURRENTLY because a plain CREATE INDEX takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on a 12 GB table, and it cannot run inside a migration transaction, so this wants a supervised quiet window rather than a db:push:prod. Then remove rebuild_entity_connections_contracts from disabled_arms with a single UPDATE — no migration needed, which is why the escape is data rather than code — and re-measure. Expected saving once enabled: 344.6 s of writer per no-change cycle, which is the second largest arm after _external. Cross-ref FIX-1117, FIX-1111, FIX-1107, FIX-1034, FIX-943. <!--id:FIX-1118-->

- [x] 🟠 S — **platform-snapshot GHA cron fires every ~3 hours, not every 10 minutes** — Surfaced while verifying [[FIX-1121]] on prod 2026-08-29. The workflow header for .github/workflows/platform-snapshot.yml documents a 10-minute cadence with expected GHA drift of 5-15 min, and every downstream comment (status routes, dashboard SSR, SNAPSHOT_STALE_MS tuning) reasons from that number. The actual schedule-triggered runs over the last 51 hours: 2026-08-27T15:08, 08-28T00:23, 08-28T11:35, 08-28T21:30, 08-29T03:20, 08-29T10:16, 08-29T15:05, 08-29T18:23. That is EIGHT scheduled firings in 51 hours - a mean interval of about 6.4 hours and a shortest gap of 3.2 hours, against an advertised 10 minutes. GitHub drops scheduled workflow runs under platform load and offers no delivery guarantee; this is not drift, it is wholesale skipping. Consequences: (1) status_snapshot is routinely 3+ hours stale, which is inside SNAPSHOT_STALE_MS (4h) only by luck - one more skipped window and every dashboard read crosses into stale; (2) the FIX-1121 investigation had only 10 retained ticks over 51 hours to reason from, which is why the retention interaction looked worse than it is; (3) any per-10-min assumption in cost or freshness math is wrong by a factor of ~38. Options: move the schedule to a Supabase pg_cron job that curls the route (the project already runs pg_cron for the EC and donor rollups, see project_pgcron_rebuild_cron_resilience), move it to a Vercel cron now that the project is on Pro (the header comment notes Hobby was the original reason for GHA and that swapping back is a one-line change), or accept the real cadence and re-tune SNAPSHOT_STALE_MS and the docs to match it. Cross-ref [[FIX-281]], [[FIX-297]], [[FIX-327]], [[FIX-1094]], [[FIX-1121]]. <!--id:FIX-1127-->

- [x] 🔴 M — **Nothing detects a wedged front door — the REST/pooler layer fails independently of the DB and only a project restart clears it** — The Supabase front door (REST + pooler) can wedge on its own and STAY wedged long after the database underneath is healthy, and no instrument in this repo notices. Reported shape: on 2026-08-31 it stayed wedged about 11 hours after the DB had recovered, and only a Supabase project restart cleared it. Measured corroboration pulled 2026-09-01 from the Logs API (analytics/endpoints/logs.all over edge_logs): the 08-31 22:00 UTC hour is 17 requests and 17 of them are Cloudflare-class 52x, i.e. 100 percent front-door failure, and the 23:00 hour is 1000 requests with 49 x 52x plus 61 total 5xx — while the Postgres side shows nothing that would explain it. The 52x family (520/521/522/525) is the tell: those are edge-to-origin failures, NOT application errors, so every DB-side instrument we own is blind to them by construction. Note the asymmetry that makes this dangerous: Cloudflare in front of the WEBSITE showed ZERO 5xx across the same 24h (verified via scripts/cf-analytics.mjs --by edgeResponseStatus: 403/200/400/301/307/404/204/401/499/302 and no 5xx at all), so a wedged data-plane front door does not necessarily surface as a red website. THE FIX: a detector for sustained front-door 5xx — poll the Logs API edge_logs 5xx rate on a schedule, and when it stays above a threshold for N consecutive intervals, send email on the EXISTING alerting rails (the same ones the canary uses, see FLAGS/EMAIL_ALERTS_ENABLED) rather than inventing a new channel. Pair it with a runbook line naming the only known remediation (project restart) so the on-call path is one step, not a diagnosis. Explicitly IN SCOPE: the detector must not depend on a Postgres connection succeeding, because the failure mode being detected is precisely one where the front door in front of Postgres is the broken component. Cross-ref [[FIX-1125]] for the sibling lesson that a guard starved by the condition it exists to end is not a guard. <!--id:FIX-1130-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines derives cadence from the FIRING schedule, so both crawl arms read permanently stale to the canary** — Measured on prod 2026-09-02 01:35 UTC while re-taking the [[FIX-990]]/[[FIX-992]]/[[FIX-993]] freshness readings. list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines() (FIX-977) derives each pipeline's cadence_hours from its cron schedule, and canary-check.ts fetchRollupRegistry() feeds that straight into report_after_hours / escalate_after_hours. That mapping is correct for a job that does its whole unit of work in one firing. It is WRONG for the two bounded crawl arms, which park status=partial on EVERY firing by design and only write status=complete when a full cycle closes. Consequence, both measured: entity_connections_rebuild is keyed off jobname ec-crawl (jobid 45, schedule */15) so its derived cadence is 0.25h, giving report_after 0.4h and escalate_after 0.6h — against a real last_complete_at of 2026-08-31 19:20:45, i.e. 30.2h, so it escalates on every canary run and can never not escalate. get_ec_crawl_health() reports signal=ok, backoff_rate_7d 0.0217, and cycles_last5 ALL closed with spans of 240-1005 minutes, so the pipeline is healthy and converging while the registry calls it 121 cadence cycles behind. financial_entity_totals_refresh is the same shape (jobnames fe-crawl + financial-entity-totals-incremental, derived cadence 37h, 599.0h since complete) and is additionally a long linear replay whose watermark is deliberately weeks behind. This is not cosmetic: it is a permanent false escalation on the daily canary in exactly the detector FIX-977 built to stop pipelines going unwatched, and per the FIX-968 precedent a detector that always fires is a detector nobody reads. It also makes the registry unusable as the instrument for future EC freshness re-takes — the 84h Mon+Wed figure FIX-990 was judged against no longer exists anywhere in the registry, because jobids 2 and 22 are both inactive. Fix shape: give the registry a per-pipeline cycle-cadence override, or teach it that a pipeline whose recent rows are status=partial with sweep_in_progress should be judged on cycle closes rather than firings — the get_ec_crawl_health() cycles_last5 span is the honest denominator for the EC arm. Cross-ref [[FIX-977]], [[FIX-990]], [[FIX-1115]], [[FIX-1031]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-968]]. <!--id:FIX-1135-->

- [x] 🟠 S — **rebuild_entity_connections_votes carries the FIX-983 watermark defect on votes.updated_at — same mechanism, different table, still unfixed** — CONFIRMED on live prod pg_proc 2026-09-03 while enumerating the FIX-983 census by mechanism. FIX-983 shipped the head-lag horizon for every financial_relationships.updated_at watermark (13 clamp sites, helper public.fr_watermark_horizon()). It deliberately did NOT touch the votes twin, which is byte-for-byte the same defect one table over. THE EVIDENCE. public.votes carries trigger votes_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ... EXECUTE FUNCTION set_updated_at(), whose whole body is NEW.updated_at = NOW(); RETURN NEW; — NOW() is transaction_timestamp(), the moment the writing transaction BEGAN. rebuild_entity_connections_votes() then reads pipeline_state key entity_connections_votes -> last_indexed_at, builds its dirty set at line 28 as WHERE v.updated_at > v_last_indexed_at with NO upper bound, captures SELECT MAX(v.updated_at) at line 32, and writes COALESCE(v_new_max_updated_at, NOW()) as the new watermark at lines 41 and 95. rebuild_entity_connections_votes_full() writes a bare NOW() at line 49. So a vote-writing transaction that starts before the watermark read and commits after it stamps rows BELOW the new watermark that were invisible at read time, and no later run ever sees them: permanent, silent row loss in the vote-derivation arm of entity_connections. THE FIX IS ALREADY BUILT AND IS THREE LINES PER SITE. Apply the same invariant FIX-983 applied: (a) v_new_max_updated_at := LEAST(COALESCE(v_new_max_updated_at, v_horizon), v_horizon) where v_horizon := public.fr_watermark_horizon(); (b) bound the dirty set with AND v.updated_at <= v_new_max_updated_at; (c) add the caught-up branch so a clamped target at or below the watermark returns without moving the watermark BACKWARDS; and in _votes_full() replace the bare NOW() watermark write with the horizon. The helper is generic — it reads a clock and a GUC, nothing FR-specific — so it needs no votes-specific twin, though a rename to watermark_horizon() would read better once a second table uses it. WHY IT WAS SPLIT OUT rather than folded into FIX-983: the FIX-983 bundle was scoped to the financial_relationships population and its proofs were built against FR fixtures; landing a votes change on the same commit would have shipped an unproven edit next to three proven ones. EXPOSURE. Smaller than the FR case but the same class: the vote writer is the congress-votes ingest, which UPDATEs existing rows on re-fetch (that is what arms the BEFORE UPDATE trigger at all), and the arm runs inside run_entity_connections_rebuild. Size it before fixing by measuring the vote writer's transaction duration the way FIX-983 sized the FR writer (631 calls, mean 4.1 s, max 19.5 s from pg_stat_statements). Cross-ref [[FIX-983]], [[FIX-1074]], [[FIX-972]], [[FIX-747]]. <!--id:FIX-1139-->
- [x] 🔴 S — **The FIX-983 caught-up branch logged status=skipped, which does not reset the freshness clock — jobid 24 would have paged on a healthy rollup at the next firing** — SELF-INFLICTED BY [[FIX-983]], caught in the same session, one hop after the prod landing, before it fired. FIX-983's invariant (c) says a routine whose horizon-clamped target has not cleared its watermark must no-op cleanly rather than write the watermark BACKWARDS. In the two rollup PROCEDUREs that keep a data_sync_log row that was implemented as an early RETURN logging status = skipped. THE DEFECT. public.check_rollup_freshness() measures staleness as hours since the last data_sync_log row for the pipeline with status = complete, and canary-check.ts escalates off that; a skipped row does not reset the clock. So a stretch of legitimately caught-up firings would have driven donor_rollup_refresh past its freshness ceiling and paged with the rollup perfectly healthy — the exact FIX-968 shape (a frozen signal making a healthy system look broken) that the playbook's E1 entry exists to prevent. IT WAS REACHABLE ON THE VERY NEXT FIRING, measured on prod 2026-09-03 01:45 UTC, not argued from theory: pipeline_state.donor_rollup_watermark.last_indexed_at = 2026-09-01 07:28:45.938461 and MAX(fr.updated_at) over donation/ie_support/ie_oppose = 2026-09-01 07:28:45.938461 — EQUAL, because financial_relationships has taken no write in over 24h. LEAST(max, horizon) is therefore at or below the watermark, so jobid 24 donor-rollup-refresh would have taken the skip branch at 09:00 UTC that morning and at 12:00, and every firing until FR moves; last_complete was 2026-09-02 12:00 so the 48h ceiling would have tripped 2026-09-04. THE FIX IS TO DELETE THE BRANCH, NOT RELABEL IT. The early RETURN was only ever protecting against a backwards watermark write, and a floor does that in one line with no new control flow and no new status vocabulary: v_new_max := GREATEST(v_new_max, v_watermark). With the target floored at the watermark the dirty predicate (> v_watermark AND <= v_new_max) is empty BY CONSTRUCTION, the loop is a no-op, and the terminal write rewrites the SAME watermark — so the run reports complete, because it IS complete: everything readable has been read. GREATEST ignores NULLs so the bootstrap path (v_watermark IS NULL) is untouched. This is the same construction FIX-983 already used for donor_rollup_rebuild_bulk and [[FIX-987]] used for refresh_agency_staffing_rollup, both of which log complete on an empty dirty set and were never affected — the inconsistency was the tell. NOT CHANGED: refresh_donor_party_rollup_mv() and refresh_official_donor_rollup_mv() keep their RAISE NOTICE plus RETURN, because they write NO data_sync_log row at all and so cannot move a freshness clock in either direction. THE GENERAL LESSON, worth a playbook line: a new early-return path in a scheduled routine is a change to its OBSERVABILITY contract, not just its control flow. Before adding one, check what the freshness/canary layer counts — here it counts exactly one status value. Cross-ref [[FIX-983]], [[FIX-987]], [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-1011]], [[FIX-1135]]. <!--id:FIX-1140-->

(c) financial_entities and entity_connections index-only scans degrade with visibility-map decay and this unit reads both; check pg_stat_user_tables.last_vacuum against the slow days before blaming the query. EXPLICIT NON-ACTION: do not raise the 900s unit budget to make the slow days fit. Confirmed intact on prod 2026-09-04: entity_search_index holds 364,129 rows, so the 09-03 cancel did NOT strand a TRUNCATE (the function TRUNCATEs then INSERTs in one unit transaction, and the cancel rolled both back together). Cross-ref [[FIX-1123]] [[FIX-1125]] [[FIX-1128]] [[FIX-1030]] [[FIX-1073]]. APPEND 2026-09-07: CLOSED as superseded by [[FIX-1152]], which answers all three of this bullet's candidates. FIX-1152 ships the durable fix: both vacuum owners go daily at 04:30 / 04:50 UTC ahead of the 06:00 daily, and the daily records the visibility map it ran against. (b) co-tenancy is ruled out as the EXPLANATION — the Sunday 09-06 nightly started 06:54:07 against the daily's 06:00:00-06:05:30, a 48-minute gap with no overlap, and that day read 234.8s; hour 06 does measure 9.2% startup timeouts on the 14-day histogram, but that is a scheduling concern now carried by [[FIX-1163]] and [[FIX-1124]], not an account of the 5x swing. (a) per-stage instrumentation is NOT implementable as written, so it is superseded rather than deferred: rebuild_entity_search_index runs as ONE statement inside the unit's own transaction, so any per-stage timing row it wrote would roll back with the watchdog cancel — precisely the runs the instrumentation exists to explain. - [x] 🟡 S — **A newly scheduled daily pg_cron job escalates the canary until its first firing** — check_cron_job_health()'s missing_daily arm selects active jobs whose schedule is daily (fields 3-5 all star) with NOT EXISTS any cron.job_run_details row inside the lookback window, and canary-check.ts ESCALATES on every entry. What remains is a correctness-of-record problem rather than a live money problem: 55 officials rows assert an FEC candidate identity their role forbids, which is exactly the claim FIX-1153 retires for the money-holding half, and any future reader that trusts source_ids fec_id without re-checking the role inherits the bug. - [x] 🟠 S — **Daily canary has no alarm for 'a FEC drop is pending and nobody collected it'** — FIX-1163 made the FEC drop probe durable: the enrichment-light phase now writes pipeline_state.fec_drop_probe with cycle, pending, remote_last_modified, watermark_last_modified, probed_at and phase, every nightly, independent of whether fec-phase ran. Nothing READS that key yet, so the evidence exists but no one is watching it. Ask: teach the daily canary (the FIX-1011 registry/canary pipeline_state readers) to escalate when fec_drop_probe.pending is true AND the newest data_sync_log row for pipeline='fec_bulk' with status='complete' is older than fec_drop_probe.probed_at by more than 2 days. That is the condition FIX-1156 was really about — not 'did the nightly fail' but 'is there money sitting at FEC that nothing has collected'. Two days is deliberate: FEC publishes indiv{yy}.zip Sundays around 15:20 UTC, the Sunday nightly probes last week's file, so a one-day lag is normal and a two-day lag means the collector missed its window. Fail-closed detail the alarm must respect: a probe whose HEAD failed records pending=false with remote_last_modified NULL, so 'pending=false' alone is not proof of health — a run of NULL remote_last_modified is its own (quieter) signal that the probe cannot see FEC at all. Cross-ref FIX-1011, FIX-1156, FIX-1163, FIX-903. <!--id:FIX-1166-->

A revocation UI that reports success and does not revoke is a security finding, not data hygiene. Shape of the 13: one row then SIX PAIRS ~200-250ms apart — a double-submitting grant path with no idempotency, a second defect no dedupe fixes. NOT the same 13 as integrity-audit/checks/grants.ts:124 (those are anon/authenticated-EXECUTEable PROCEDUREs from [[FIX-1113]]); coincidence of number, do not conflate. NOTHING APPLIED. - [x] 🔴 M — **Saved views still vanish on prod after FIX-782: post-save reload GET races the auth-cookie rotation → anon empty-200 wipe** — FIX-782 (non-destructive reload catch) shipped + deployed but the bug persists on prod: saving on /search or /graph still makes the view vanish, and the /graph Save View never lists the row. Prod evidence: the POST persists (rows land in user_custom_groups owned by the user, is_public=false) but the client's post-save reload GET returns 200 with an empty/anon list — that request authenticates as ANON while the mount GET authes fine. The only difference is timing: the reload GET fires immediately after the POST, and the POST's middleware rotates the session cookie writing it to the RESPONSE only (not the forwarded request; see apps/civitics/middleware.ts setAll) so the chained GET races a rotated-out token. FIX-782's catch only guards GET REJECTION; a GET that succeeds with {groups:[]} still runs setItems([]) and wipes. The /graph path has no optimistic insert so it depends wholly on that racing GET. Fix: stop re-fetching the whole list after our own write — the bus broadcasts the confirmed POST row object (upsert) / deleted id (remove) and each rail applies the delta, immune to the cookie race. Keep the single mount fetch (authes fine) + FIX-782 non-destructive catch. Also add graph-path optimistic insert via the broadcast. FOLLOW-UP: the middleware cookie-rotation pattern (response-only setAll) is a latent auth race for any POST-then-GET flow — investigate separately. References [[FIX-782]] [[FIX-770]]. <!--id:FIX-784-->
- [x] 🔴 S — **Per-user authed API endpoints are CDN-cached by the next.config catch-all (stale-after-write + cross-user leak)** — THE real cause of the saved-views 'revert on refresh' (FIX-782/784 chased client-side theories; the server was always fine). next.config.mjs headers() has a catch-all that stamps CDN-Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=600 on everything except a short denylist (api/auth, api/admin, auth, profile, dashboard). /api/graph/custom-groups (and other per-user authed GET routes) are NOT excluded, so the Vercel/Cloudflare edge caches a user's saved-views list for 300s, and the cache key does NOT vary by Cookie. Result: a save/delete persists in the DB (POST returns 201) but a refresh serves the stale edge-cached list → the view 'reverts'. SECURITY: because the cache doesn't vary by user, one user's saved views (and other per-user responses) can be served to another. Confirmed by the live response headers on prod (cf-cache-status DYNAMIC, cdn-cache-control s-maxage=300). Fix: denylist the clearly per-user authed API routes (graph/custom-groups, graph/me, graph/my-representatives, notifications, follows, api/profile, constituent-status, officials/claim-status, representatives) from the cdnHot catch-all and pin them CDN no-store. FOLLOW-UP: audit the ambiguous public-or-private authed GET routes (comments, positions, statements, initiatives, investigations, questions) individually. References [[FIX-784]] [[FIX-782]]. <!--id:FIX-786-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **FIX-786 audit: no-store 4 more per-user authed API routes (positions/statements/questions/investigations)** — FIX-786 security audit follow-through. Four more authed GET routes vary by the signed-in viewer and were still CDN-cached by the next.config catch-all (same cross-user disclosure class as [[FIX-786]]): api/positions (returns the caller's own stance -3..3), api/statements + api/questions (their RPCs embed my_vote keyed to auth.uid()), api/investigations (RLS status<>archived OR created_by=auth.uid() → creators see own archived rows). Fix: add to the userScopedApi CDN no-store denylist. api/positions uses an EXACT source (not /:path*) and a not-followed-by-slash exclusion so its PUBLIC /api/positions/rollup aggregate stays cached. Verified via response headers. References [[FIX-786]]. <!--id:FIX-787-->
- [x] 🔴 S — **CDN cache hotfix: per-user pages cross-user cached + comments read-your-own-writes broken** — Prod, authed (2026-07-11 captures): the cdnHot(300,600) catch-all in next.config.mjs headers() stamps CDN-Cache-Control on every route not in the [[FIX-786]]/[[FIX-787]] denylist — which only ever listed API routes. - [x] 🟠 S — **plum-book: escape comma-bearing names in the ilike OR-filter** — plum-book builds full_name.ilike.<name> conditions joined by commas into a PostgREST .or(); a name with a comma ('joseph knouff, jr.') breaks the logic-tree parser (failed to parse logic tree, column 514) → the whole ilike chunk's official lookup fails and those plum_id bindings silently drop. - [x] 🔴 M — **Harden the rebuild against GHA cancel/timeout — orphaned backends + stranded autovacuum** — Surfaced 2026-06-15 running mode=full ad-hoc: when GHA cancels a run (manual OR the 4h timeout-minutes cap — same path), it kills the node client but Postgres keeps executing the in-flight query as an ORPHANED backend that hammers prod until the session statement_timeout (observed run-1 finalize() orphaned 1h10m + run-2 prepare() DELETE orphaned 16m, together I/O-saturating Pro Small → request-path 503s / 57014 on the live site). Two compounding bugs: (1) GHA's SIGKILL skips the script's `finally`, so FIX-590's `autovacuum_enabled=false` is left stranded → the table never gets autovacuumed. (2) the donations prepare()→windows split is NON-atomic: if a run is cancelled after prepare()'s DELETE-all commits but before the windows finish, donation edges are left empty/partial (the old monolith DELETE+INSERT was one transaction → a cancel rolled back to the prior good data). Fix landed (script-only, rebuild-entity-connections.ts): tag the connection `application_name='entity_connections_rebuild'`; a SIGTERM/SIGINT handler opens a fresh connection, `pg_cancel_backend(myPid)` + re-enables autovacuum (GHA sends SIGTERM before SIGKILL, so this catches the timeout case); and a STARTUP RECONCILE that, before doing anything, cancels+terminates any orphaned backend carrying our application_name (workflow concurrency is cancel-in-progress:false so it's always a prior orphan, never a peer) and unconditionally re-enables autovacuum — self-healing after any dirty exit. Incident recovery (2026-06-15): cancelled both orphans via pg_cancel_backend (run-2 prepare DELETE rolled back → 4.48M donation edges preserved, no data loss), manually re-enabled autovacuum, refreshed group_donor_rollup. RESIDUAL (low-risk now, follow-up): the non-atomic empty/partial-donations-on-cancel (bug 2) is only fully closed by making each window an atomic DELETE+INSERT for its from_id range (needs a `(connection_type, from_id)` index on entity_connections for an efficient ranged DELETE) instead of the upfront prepare() DELETE-all; exposure is small now that donations finish in ~1h vs the 4h budget. OPERATIONAL: the full rebuild saturates Pro Small I/O for its whole duration — run ONLY at low traffic (the 08:00 UTC=midnight PT schedule exists for this); do not trigger ad-hoc during active hours. Cross-ref [[FIX-590]] [[FIX-588]] [[FIX-589]] (compute is the durable relief). <!--id:FIX-591-->
